blocks.source: 0. Overview

This manuscript constructs the one-loop quantum Batalin–Vilkovisky theory of four-dimensional $\mathcal N=4$ super Yang–Mills theory on Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$, together with the transformations of its local operators under the whole superconformal algebra, in the renormalisation formalism of Costello [C07] and Costello–Gwilliam [CG2]. The single regulator is a lower cutoff $\varepsilon>0$ on Schwinger time; the upper end of every Schwinger integral is $\infty$, and no infrared scale and no dimensional continuation enter. This overview states what is constructed, where the construction needs care, how the chapters are organised, and the results of this first step.
0.1 What is constructed

The fields are those of ten-dimensional super Yang–Mills theory reduced to $\mathbb R^4$ [ESW, Prop 2.20, §10.3], complexified. Write $V$ for the complexification of $\mathbb R^4$ and $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ for the six transverse directions, and $\mathfrak g$ for the complexified gauge Lie algebra with its invariant pairing $(-,-)$, which carries the coupling. The gauge field $A$ is a ten-component one-form with values in $\mathfrak g$: its components along $V$ form the connection $A|_V$, and its components $\iota_wA$, $w\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$, are the six scalars. The gaugino $\lambda$ takes values in the ten-dimensional semi-spin representation $\Sigma$, which in four dimensions is $S_+\otimes W\oplus S_-\otimes W^*$, with $S_\pm$ the two Weyl spinor representations and $W$ the four-dimensional R-symmetry space [ESW, §10]; spinors stay index free throughout. The ghost $c$ and the antifields $A^*$, $\lambda^*$, $c^*$ complete the fields [ESW, Def 3.2, Rem 1.36]. The action $S$ is [ESW, (31)] reduced to four dimensions; its quadratic part defines the linear differential $Q$, the rest is the interaction $I$, and $\{-,-\}$ is the odd Poisson bracket [C07, Lemma 4.3.2].

Costello's construction needs three more objects. A gauge-fixing operator $Q^{GF}$, here of Feynman type, makes $H=[Q,Q^{GF}]$ the Laplacian on every field. The heat kernel $K_t$ of $H$ at Schwinger time $t$ [C07, §6.5] gives the propagator
P(\varepsilon,\infty)=\int_\varepsilon^\infty(Q^{GF}\otimes1)K_t\,dt ,
and Feynman graphs with these edges assemble into the renormalisation group flow of an even functional $J$,
W\big(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J\big)=\hbar\log\Big(e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}e^{J/\hbar}\Big)\qquad[\text{CG2, §7.2.7}],

with $\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}$ the second-order operator contracting two fields with the kernel $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ [C07, §6.4]; this is the functional called $\Gamma$ in [C07, Def 6.6.1]. As in Theorem B of [C07], the counterterm $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ is the singular part of the graph expansion, extracted graph by graph, with coefficients in the span of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $\log\varepsilon$ at one loop; it is local, and $W\big(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]\big)$ has a limit as $\varepsilon\to0$. A local operator $O$, for instance $\int\omega\,(\iota_{w_1}A,\iota_{w_2}A)$ with $\omega$ a compactly supported four-form [CG2, Lemma 10.1.1.3], enters through a square-zero parameter $\delta$ [CG2, Def 8.3.1.1]: the counterterm $\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ of the family $I+\delta O$ defines the local operator at the UV end, $O(\varepsilon)=O-\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$, and its quantum observable is
O[\infty]=\lim_{\varepsilon\to0}\partial_\delta W\big(P(\varepsilon,\infty),\,I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]+\delta\,O(\varepsilon)\big)\qquad[\text{CG2, Def 8.3.1.3}].

The superconformal algebra $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ [SW, (7), (17)] acts through an equivariant action $S+S^{(1)}+S^{(2)}$, a Maurer–Cartan element of the Chevalley–Eilenberg complex of [ESW, Def 1.26–1.27] with differential $d_{CE}$. Building $O[\infty]$ from the equivariant interaction, the transformation of $O$ along a generator $x_1\in\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ is the component $[(d_{CE}+Q)O[\infty]](x_1)$. Along the dilatation $\Delta$, the generator $2E$ of [SW, (17)] with $E$ the Euler vector field [SW, (3)], it is the anomalous dimension; along the supercharges $Q^i_\alpha$, $\bar Q_{\dot\alpha i}$ and the special supercharges $S^\alpha_i$, $\bar S^{\dot\alpha i}$ (the names of [SW, (8)]) it is the quantum-corrected supersymmetry; along the special conformal generators it is the primary condition. The program therefore has two outputs: the quantised interaction, with its counterterms and its quantum master equation, and, for every local operator, its observable and its transformations along all of $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$.
0.2 Three points that need care

Operators. Inserting a composite operator produces divergences, and the limit defining $O[\infty]$ exists for many choices of the functional $O(\varepsilon)$. At scale $\infty$, however, $K_\infty=\lim_{t\to\infty}K_t=0$ on $\mathbb R^4$, and $P(0,\infty)$ is a contracting homotopy for $Q$: for compactly supported $\alpha$,
Q\big(P(0,\infty)\star\alpha\big)+P(0,\infty)\star(Q\alpha)=\alpha ,

where $P(0,\infty)\star$ is the operator with kernel $P(0,\infty)$ [C07, §6.3]. Away from finitely many zero-mode classes, every $Q$-closed functional at scale $\infty$ without constant term is therefore $Q$-exact, and an arbitrary $O(\varepsilon)$ carries no cohomological information. The content of an operator is the locality of $O(\varepsilon)$: $O(\varepsilon)=O-\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ with local coefficients in the span of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $\log\varepsilon$. Locality and the existence of the limit fix the singular part uniquely, and the finite part is the scheme. An equation $[(d_{CE}+Q)O[\infty]](x_1)=Y[\infty]$ has content because $Y$ is required to be local, and anomalous dimensions are classes in the cohomology of local functionals.

Counterterms. Theorem B fixes the singular part $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ uniquely. The cutoff on every edge breaks gauge invariance and superconformal symmetry, and $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ contains $\varepsilon^{-1}$ mass terms with nonzero image under $Q$. The quantum master equation, transported to the UV boundary, then forces finite local counterterms. They are constrained by the master equation and fixed up to a choice; this choice is the renormalisation condition, part of the definition of the quantum theory and of every operator.
The UV boundary. The lower end $t=\varepsilon$ of the Schwinger integral carries two kernels,
\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}P(\varepsilon,\infty)=-\varepsilon L_\varepsilon,\qquad (Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q)P(\varepsilon,\infty)=K_\varepsilon,\qquad L_\varepsilon=(Q^{GF}\otimes1)K_\varepsilon ,

the second being [C07, Lemma 10.2.1] with $K_\infty=0$. Edges pinned at $t=\varepsilon$ and carrying $L_\varepsilon$ produce the singular coefficients and the scaling behaviour. Edges carrying $K_\varepsilon$ produce the defects of the quantum master equation and the transformations of observables, through

(d_{CE}+Q)\,e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}=e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}\big(d_{CE}+Q+\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon\big),\qquad \Delta_\varepsilon=-\partial_{K_\varepsilon}\quad[\text{C07, §10.1}].
Every singular or anomalous coefficient of this manuscript is carried by such boundary edges.
0.3 Plan of the chapters

Chapter 1 fixes the fields, the odd pairing, the reduced action with its linear differential and vertices, and the classical master equation. Chapter 2 realises $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ on Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$ and constructs the equivariant action $S+S^{(1)}+S^{(2)}$ in the Chevalley–Eilenberg complex. Chapter 3 constructs the Feynman-gauge $Q^{GF}$, records which axioms of [C07, Def 4.3.3] it satisfies, and proves the UV-boundary identity, the acyclicity at scale $\infty$ and the one-loop formula. Chapter 4 computes the one-loop counterterms of the action in the two-, three- and four-point sectors and the quantum master equation at the UV boundary. Chapter 5 computes $O(\varepsilon)$ for the single letters and the scalar bilinears, Chapter 6 their dilatation through the scaling covariance of the regulator, and Chapter 7 the selection rules for the other superconformal components and the program of Steps 2–5.
0.4 Results of Step 1
All one-loop coefficients are rational multiples of
\frac{\hbar\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2\,(X,Y)},
which is independent of $X,Y\in\mathfrak g$ for simple $\mathfrak g$; below it is called the unit and written out in every formula.

• Chapter 2. The equivariant action $S+S^{(1)}+S^{(2)}$, with $S^{(k)}=0$ for $k\ge3$, satisfies its master equation for every $\mathfrak g$ on the Poincaré supersymmetry subalgebra, in arity $0$, in arity $3$ with at most one or with three odd arguments, and in every arity $\ge4$; the remaining components, of arities $1$ to $3$, hold for $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ at sampled generators, with the probability bound stated there.
• Chapter 3. With the Feynman-gauge operator, $d^*d$ being the positive Laplacian,
H=[Q,Q^{GF}]=d^*d\otimes\mathrm{id},\qquad (Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q)P(\varepsilon,\infty)=K_\varepsilon,\qquad (Q^{GF})^2\neq0 ;
conditions (1), (2), (4) of [C07, Def 4.3.3] hold and (3), (5) fail, and every identity used later rests on the conditions that hold.
• Chapter 4. The part of $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ quadratic in the fields is, with $\mathrm{dvol}$ the Euclidean volume form and ${\not d}$ the Dirac operator [ESW, §2.1],
• Chapter 4. Through the cubic and quartic sectors the $\log\varepsilon$ part of $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ is
\log\varepsilon\,\frac{\hbar\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\,\big(Q+\{I,-\}\big)\int\mathrm{dvol}\Big(2(A,A^*)-4(\lambda^*,\lambda)-(c^*,c)\Big),

which multiplies the tree vertices $(A|_V)^3$, $A|_V(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})^2$, $\lambda\lambda A|_V$, $\lambda\lambda A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$, $cA|_VA^*|_V$, $cA|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}A^*|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$, $c\lambda\lambda^*$, $ccc^*$, $(A|_V)^4$, $(A|_V)^2(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})^2$, $(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})^4$ by $6,6,10,10,1,1,1,1,8,8,8$ units; its component along the coupling vanishes, so the coupling is unrenormalised at one loop, and the $\varepsilon^{-1}$ terms lie in the quadratic sector.

• Chapter 4. In the sector $(c,A|_V)$ of the quantum master equation the $\varepsilon^{-1}$ parts cancel against $-Q$ of the mass counterterm, no $\log\varepsilon$ appears, and the finite obstruction is

-\frac{27}{8}\,\frac{\hbar\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*dc,d^*A|_V)=\frac{27}{16}\,\frac{\hbar\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\,Q\!\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V),
removed by the finite change $I\mapsto I-\frac{27}{16}\frac{\hbar\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V)$.

• Chapter 5. The single letters $\int\omega\,(X,\iota_wA)$, $\int\omega\,(X,\iota_v(A|_V))$, $\int\omega\,(\zeta,\lambda)$, $\int\omega\,(X,c)$, with fixed $X\in\mathfrak g$, $v\in V$, $\zeta\in\Sigma^*\otimes\mathfrak g$, have $O(\varepsilon)=O$. For $O=\int\omega\,(\iota_{w_1}A,\iota_{w_2}A)$, with $w$ running over an orthonormal basis of $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$,

\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]=\frac{\hbar\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\log\varepsilon\Big[4\,O-2(w_1,w_2)\sum_w\int\omega\,(\iota_wA,\iota_wA)\Big]+\frac{2\hbar\dim\mathfrak g\,(w_1,w_2)}{16\pi^2\varepsilon}\int\omega ;
for $(w_1,w_2)=0$, where $O$ lies in the traceless part, and for the trace $\sum_w\int\omega\,(\iota_wA,\iota_wA)$ this gives

• Chapter 6. Let $O$ have Weyl weight $w_O$ (the sum of the weights $1$ of $A$, $\tfrac32$ of $\lambda$, $0$ of $c$, plus the number of derivatives), so that $\Delta=2E$ acts on it classically by $2(E+w_O)$, $E$ acting on its density. The scaling covariance of the regulator, together with the identification of the Weyl scaling with the dilatation cochain that Chapter 6 states as the task of Step 2, gives
[(d_{CE}+Q)O[\infty]](\Delta)=2\Big(E+w_O+\text{coefficient}\cdot\frac{\hbar\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\Big)O[\infty]+\cdots,

For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(N)$ with $(X,Y)=-\frac{4\hbar}{g^2}\operatorname{tr}(XY)$, $\operatorname{tr}$ the trace in the defining representation and $g$ the Yang–Mills coupling (Chapter 6), the unit equals $-g^2N/(32\pi^2)$, and $-24$ units equal $3g^2N/(4\pi^2)$, the one-loop anomalous dimension of the Konishi operator; this serves as a consistency check.

• Chapter 7. Translations, rotations and the R-symmetry commute with $Q^{GF}$ and $H$; their components can be chosen with no one-loop correction, and the counterterms of the traceless and the trace scalar bilinears stay in their own representations. Along the supercharges, the special supercharges and the special conformal generators the regulator moves, and the one-loop output lies in an explicit list of local structures; for the traceless scalar bilinear the supercharge component is a multiple of its classical structure.
1. The classical theory

Every number computed in the following chapters is a coefficient in front of a local functional, and its sign and normalisation are inherited from three classical data: the odd pairing on the fields, the BV action and the linear differential $Q$ [C07, §4.3]. The sources supply the ten-dimensional action [ESW, (31)] and its dimensional reduction [ESW, Prop 2.20, §10.3], while the pairing on the antifields stays implicit in the phrase “natural $(-1)$-shifted symplectic structure” [ESW, Def 1.34]. This chapter fixes all three data for the reduction to Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$, writes the interaction vertex by vertex, and shows that the classical master equation determines the relative signs of the pairing.
1.1 Spaces and the dimensional reduction
Definition 1.1 (Spaces).

The ten-dimensional space is $V_{10}=V_{\mathbb R}\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C$, where $V_{\mathbb R}=\mathbb R^{10}$ carries its Euclidean form and the orthogonal decomposition $V_{\mathbb R}=W_{\mathbb R}\oplus W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ of [ESW, §2.2, §2.6]: $W_{\mathbb R}=\mathbb R^4$ is spacetime and $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ consists of the six transverse directions. With $V=W_{\mathbb R}\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C$ the complexification of $\mathbb R^4$,
V_{10}=V\oplus\big(W_{\mathbb R}^\perp\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C\big),

and from here on $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ and $\mathfrak{so}(W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)$ denote these complexifications. The nondegenerate symmetric form $(-,-)$ of $V_{10}$ is the complex-bilinear extension of the Euclidean form. The letter $W$ alone denotes the multiplicity space of [ESW, §10].

The gauge Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ is complex, with bracket $[-,-]$ and a nondegenerate invariant symmetric pairing $(-,-)$ [ESW, §3.1], chosen positive definite on the compact real form, so that $\langle e,Qe\rangle$ is negative definite on the real slice of [C07, §6.6] (Remark [1.10](#b-00130)). The coupling constant sits in $(-,-)$. The inverse pairing is the element $(-,-)^{-1}\in\mathfrak g\otimes\mathfrak g$.

The two sixteen-dimensional semi-spin representations $\Sigma$ and $\Sigma^*$ of $\mathfrak{so}(V_{10})$ form the $\mathbb Z/2$-graded Clifford module $\Sigma\oplus\Sigma^*$ with Clifford action $\rho$ and pairing $(-,-)\colon\Sigma\otimes\Sigma^*\to\mathbb C$ [ESW, §2.1]:
\rho(v_1)\rho(v_2)+\rho(v_2)\rho(v_1)=2(v_1,v_2),\qquad (\rho(v)Q_1,Q_2)=(Q_1,\rho(v)Q_2),\qquad v,v_1,v_2\in V_{10}.
The $\Gamma$-pairing $\Gamma\colon\mathrm{Sym}^2(\Sigma)\to V_{10}$, $\Gamma\colon\mathrm{Sym}^2(\Sigma^*)\to V_{10}$ is defined by [ESW, (28)]

The map $q\colon\wedge^\bullet V_{10}\to\mathrm{Cl}(V_{10})$ is antisymmetrisation, $q(v_1\wedge v_2)=v_1v_2-(v_1,v_2)$ [ESW, (29)]. Applied to a two-form, such as $F_A$, the symbol $\rho$ means $\rho\circ q$, as in $\rho(F_A)$ [ESW, (33)].

The exterior derivative $d$ acts along $\mathbb R^4$, and every field is constant along $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$. The operator $d^*$ is the formal adjoint of $d$ for the Euclidean metric, $\mathrm{dvol}$ is the Euclidean volume density of $\mathbb R^4$, and ${\not d}=\rho\circ d$ is the Dirac operator from $\Sigma$-valued to $\Sigma^*$-valued functions [ESW, §2.1]; the same formula on $\Sigma^*$-valued functions is written ${\not d}|_{\Sigma^*}$.
The four-dimensional content of $\Sigma$ is [ESW, §10, §10.3]
\Sigma\cong S_+\otimes W\oplus S_-\otimes W^*,\qquad \dim W=4,\qquad W\cong S_+^6\ \text{as a representation of}\ \mathrm{Spin}(6;\mathbb C)\cong SL(4,\mathbb C),
with $S_\pm$ the two-dimensional semi-spin representations of $\mathrm{Spin}(4,\mathbb C)$.
Proposition 1.2 (Four-dimensional chirality).

Fix an orientation of $V$. For an oriented orthonormal basis $v_1,\dots,v_4$ of $V$ the element $q(v_1\wedge v_2\wedge v_3\wedge v_4)=v_1v_2v_3v_4$ of $\mathrm{Cl}(V_{10})$ depends on the orientation alone. The operator $\rho(v_1v_2v_3v_4)$ squares to $1$ on $\Sigma$ and on $\Sigma^*$, with eigenvalues $+1$ and $-1$ each of multiplicity $8$. Writing
one has, for $v\in V$ and $w\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$,
\rho(v)\colon S_+\otimes W\to S_-\otimes W,\qquad \rho(w)\colon S_+\otimes W\to S_+\otimes W^*,
and correspondingly on the other summands: $\rho(v)$ exchanges the four-dimensional chiralities and $\rho(w)$ preserves them.
Proof.

The element $v_1v_2v_3v_4$ is the antisymmetrisation $q$ of the oriented unit element of $\wedge^4V$, hence depends on the orientation alone. By the Clifford relation the $v_i$ anticommute pairwise and square to $1$, hence

Moving $v_1$ through $v_1v_2v_3v_4$ meets $v_2,v_3,v_4$ once each, so $v_1\,(v_1v_2v_3v_4)=-(v_1v_2v_3v_4)\,v_1$; the same holds for each $v_i$, hence for every $v\in V$ by linearity. For $w\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$, $w$ anticommutes with all four $v_i$, so $w\,(v_1v_2v_3v_4)=(+1)(v_1v_2v_3v_4)\,w$. Since $\rho(v)$ maps $\Sigma\to\Sigma^*$, the first relation reads $\rho(v)\rho(v_1v_2v_3v_4)|_{\Sigma}=-\rho(v_1v_2v_3v_4)|_{\Sigma^*}\rho(v)$, so $\rho(v)$ maps the $+1$ eigenspace on $\Sigma$ to the $-1$ eigenspace on $\Sigma^*$; the second relation gives $\rho(w)$ mapping the $+1$ eigenspace on $\Sigma$ to the $+1$ eigenspace on $\Sigma^*$. For the multiplicities, take a unit vector $w\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$. The even element $v_1w$ satisfies $(v_1w)^2=-v_1^2w^2=-1$ and $v_1w\,(v_1v_2v_3v_4)=-(v_1v_2v_3v_4)\,v_1w$, so $\rho(v_1w)$ is an invertible endomorphism of $\Sigma$ (and of $\Sigma^*$) exchanging the two eigenspaces of $\rho(v_1v_2v_3v_4)$; hence each eigenspace has dimension $16/2=8$. ∎
Remark 1.3.

The names of the eigenspaces depend on the orientation of $V$; the opposite orientation exchanges $S_+\leftrightarrow S_-$ in all four of them. This orientation is fixed once; Chapter 2 uses it to name the supercharges.
1.2 Fields, degrees and parities
Definition 1.4 (Fields).
The BRST fields of [ESW, Def 3.2], reduced along $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ [ESW, Def 1.55, Prop 1.56, Prop 2.20], form
F_{\rm gauge}=\Omega^0(\mathbb R^4;\mathfrak g[1])\oplus\Omega^0(\mathbb R^4;V_{10}^\vee\otimes\mathfrak g)\oplus\Omega^0(\mathbb R^4;\Pi\Sigma\otimes\mathfrak g),
with sections $(c,A,\lambda)$. The space of BV fields is $\mathscr E$ [C07, §4.1],
\mathscr E=F_{\rm gauge}\oplus F_{\rm gauge}^![-1]\qquad[\text{ESW, Rem 1.36}],

with antifields $(c^*,A^*,\lambda^*)$; duals are identified through $(-,-)$ on $\mathfrak g$, the metric of $V_{10}$, the pairing $\Sigma\otimes\Sigma^*\to\mathbb C$ and $\mathrm{dvol}$. The component of $A$ along $V$ is the connection $A|_V$, the component along $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ is $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$, and $\iota_wA=A(w)$ for $w\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ are the six scalars. The compactly supported elements of $\mathscr E$ form $\mathscr E_c$ ($\mathcal E_c$ in [ESW, §1.1]).

The degrees are those of [ESW, Rem 1.33]: the ghost $c$ is a section in degree $-1$, which forces $A^*$ in degree $+1$ and $c^*$ in degree $+2$. Signs follow the Koszul rule for the total parity, the sum of the $\mathbb Z$-degree and the $\mathbb Z/2$-degree modulo $2$ [ESW, §1.1].

1.3 Pairing and bracket
Definition 1.5 (Odd pairing).

The odd pairing $\langle\,,\rangle$ on $\mathscr E$ [C07, Def 4.3.1; ESW, Def 1.13, Def 1.16] is nonzero exactly between a field and its antifield. For each of the three pairs, call the member of even total parity the even member: $A$, $\lambda^*$, $c^*$; their partners $A^*$, $\lambda$, $c$ are odd. For a section $e_0$ in the slot of an even member and a section $e_1$ in the slot of its partner,
\langle e_0,e_1\rangle=\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(e_0,e_1),\qquad \langle e_1,e_0\rangle=-\langle e_0,e_1\rangle ,

where $(e_0,e_1)$ is the fibre pairing of Definition [1.4](#b-00081); for the pair $(\lambda^*,\lambda)$ it is $(e_1,e_0)$ with $(-,-)\colon\Sigma\otimes\Sigma^*\to\mathbb C$ tensored with $(-,-)$ on $\mathfrak g$.
Definition 1.6 (Bracket and the kernel of the identity).
The kernel $K_0$ of the identity [CG2, §7.2.3] has nonzero components exactly in the slot pairs
A\otimes A^*,\quad A^*\otimes A,\quad \lambda^*\otimes\lambda,\quad \lambda\otimes\lambda^*,\quad c^*\otimes c,\quad c\otimes c^*,

each equal to $-\delta(x-y)$ times the inverse of the fibre pairing: $(-,-)^{-1}$ tensored with the inverse metric of $V_{10}$ for $A$, $A^*$, with the canonical element of $\Sigma\otimes\Sigma^*$ for $\lambda$, $\lambda^*$, and with $1$ for $c$, $c^*$; here $x,y\in\mathbb R^4$ are the two positions and $\delta(x-y)$ is the delta distribution of the diagonal, always written with its argument. The bracket is the odd Poisson bracket of [C07, Lemma 4.3.2], defined for $f$ local and $g$ arbitrary; it is given by the formula of [C07, §10.1] for the manifold a point,
\{f,g\}=\Delta_0(fg)-\Delta_0(f)g-(-1)^{|f|}f\Delta_0(g),\qquad \Delta_0=-\partial_{K_0},
with $\partial_\phi$ the order-two operator of [C07, §6.4] and $f$ local. It satisfies
the graded symmetry of [ESW, Def 1.15].
Remark 1.7.

The overall sign of $\langle\,,\rangle$ is a convention: reversing it reverses $K_0$ and the bracket, and leaves the master equation $\{S,S\}=0$ invariant. The relative signs of the three pairs are fixed by the master equation (Proposition [1.14](#b-00173)).
1.4 The action
Definition 1.8 (Action).
The action is the dimensional reduction of [ESW, (31)]:
S=\int_{\mathbb R^4}\mathrm{dvol}\Big(-\tfrac14(F_A,F_A)+\tfrac12(\lambda,{\not d}_A\lambda)+(d_Ac,A^*)+([c,\lambda],\lambda^*)+\tfrac12([c,c],c^*)\Big), \tag{1.1}
with
F_A=dA+\tfrac12[A\wedge A],\qquad d_A=d+[A,-],\qquad {\not d}_A=\rho\circ d_A .

Here $A$ is regarded as a one-form on $V_{10}$ constant along $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$; $d$ acts along $\mathbb R^4$, and $d_A$, ${\not d}_A$ use all ten components of $A$. The pairing $(F_A,F_A)$ is the Hodge pairing on $\wedge^2V_{10}^\vee$ tensored with $(-,-)$ on $\mathfrak g$, normalised by

Every pairing in [(1.1)](#b-00108) is read with its left entry first, as printed in [ESW, (31)]. In [ESW] the full action is $S$ and the interaction is $I$; in [C07] the letter $S$ denotes the interaction. Here $S$ is always the full action and $I$ the interaction.
Splitting $A=A|_V+A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$,

(F_A,F_A)=(F_{A|_V},F_{A|_V})+\big(d_{A|_V}A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp},\,d_{A|_V}A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}\big)+\big(\tfrac12[A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}\wedge A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}],\,\tfrac12[A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}\wedge A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}]\big),
{\not d}_A\lambda={\not d}\lambda+\rho([A|_V,\lambda])+\rho([A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp},\lambda]),\qquad (d_Ac,A^*)=(dc,A^*|_V)+([A,c],A^*),
where $\rho([A,\lambda])$ is Clifford multiplication by the $V_{10}^\vee$ factor of $A$ (through the metric) together with $[-,-]$ on the $\mathfrak g$ factors, i.e. $({\not d}_A-{\not d})\lambda$.
Proposition 1.9 (Normalisation of the gauge kinetic term).
For $Q_1\in\Sigma$ put
S^{(1)}(Q_1)=\int\mathrm{dvol}\Big(-(\Gamma(Q_1,\lambda),A^*)+\tfrac12(\rho(F_A)Q_1,\lambda^*)\Big)\qquad[\text{ESW, (33)}].

For abelian $\mathfrak g$ the bracket $\{S,S^{(1)}(Q_1)\}$ is an affine function of the coefficient of the Hodge pairing $(F_A,F_A)$ in [(1.1)](#b-00108), and the identity $\{S,S^{(1)}(Q_1)\}=0$ of [ESW, Lemma 3.4] fixes this coefficient to $-\tfrac14$. The coefficients $+\tfrac14$ and $-\tfrac12$ (the reading of $(F_A,F_A)$ as a sum over ordered pairs of directions, twice the Hodge pairing) give a nonzero bracket.
Proof.

For abelian $\mathfrak g$ the bracket is affine in the coefficient of $(F_A,F_A)$: this coefficient times $(dA,dA)$ meets $-(\Gamma(Q_1,\lambda),A^*)$ through the $(A,A^*)$ pair, $\tfrac12(\lambda,{\not d}\lambda)$ meets $\tfrac12(\rho(dA)Q_1,\lambda^*)$ through the $(\lambda^*,\lambda)$ pair, and $(dc,A^*)$ meets $\tfrac12(\rho(dA)Q_1,\lambda^*)$ in $(\rho(d\,dc)Q_1,\lambda^*)=0$. With the coefficient $-\tfrac14$ the bracket vanishes for every $Q_1\in\Sigma$ and every $\mathfrak g$: this is [ESW, Lemma 3.4] in ten dimensions, pulled back along the reduction [ESW, Prop 2.20], and for $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ and $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(3)$ it holds on every element of a basis of $\Sigma$ (Remark [1.15](#b-00197)); the part of this bracket quadratic in the fields is the abelian bracket. With the coefficient $+\tfrac14$ the abelian bracket is a nonzero local functional at an element $Q_1\in\Sigma$ (Remark [1.15](#b-00197)). An affine function that vanishes at $-\tfrac14$ and is nonzero at $+\tfrac14$ has $-\tfrac14$ as its unique zero; in particular it is nonzero at $-\tfrac12$. ∎
The free part of $S$ is
\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle=\int\mathrm{dvol}\Big(-\tfrac14(dA,dA)+\tfrac12(\lambda,{\not d}\lambda)+(dc,A^*)\Big)\qquad[\text{C07, §1, §4.3}], \tag{1.2}
and $I=S-\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle$ is the interaction.
Fields and kernels on $\mathbb R^4\times\mathbb R^4$ are Fourier transformed as
\int\frac{d^4p}{(2\pi)^4}e^{i(p,x)}(\cdots)(p),\qquad \int\frac{d^4p}{(2\pi)^4}e^{i(p,x-y)}(\cdots)(p),
with $p\in V$ and $|p|^2=(p,p)$; thus $d$ becomes $i(p,-)$.
Remark 1.10 (Real slice).
The weight is $e^{+S/\hbar}$, with $\langle e,Qe\rangle$ negative definite on the real slice [C07, §6.6]. For $A$ real with respect to the compact real form of $\mathfrak g$,
\langle A,QA\rangle=-\tfrac12\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dA,dA)\le0,

and for a fixed nonzero momentum $p$ the quadratic form on the fibre $V_{10}^\vee$ has eigenvalues, in units of $(-,-)$, equal to $-\tfrac12|p|^2$ with multiplicity $9$ and $0$ with multiplicity $1$; the zero eigenvector is the longitudinal part of $A|_V$, which lies in $\operatorname{Im}Q$.

Proof.
$Q^2=0$: the composable pairs of arrows of $Q$ are $c\to A|_V\to A^*$ and $A\to A^*\to c^*$. On the first,
Q^2c=-\tfrac12\,d^*d(-dc)=\tfrac12\,d^*(d\,dc)=0 ;

and the sum vanishes. For $e_0$ in the $A^*$ slot (odd) and $e_1$ in the $c$ slot,

\langle Qe_0,e_1\rangle-\langle e_0,Qe_1\rangle=\int\mathrm{dvol}\big((e_1,{\not d}e_0)+(e_0,{\not d}e_1)\big)=0,
by integration by parts. The kernel form is the same statement for the kernel of the identity. ∎
Remark 1.12 (A sign conflict in the sources).

[ESW, Def 1.16] prints the adjointness of the BV differential as $\int\omega(e_0,Q_{BV}e_1)=(-1)^{|e_0|}\int\omega(Q_{BV}e_0,e_1)$, where $\omega$ and $Q_{BV}$ are the [ESW] names of $\langle\,,\rangle$ and $Q$. Combined with the graded antisymmetry $\langle e_1,e_0\rangle=-\langle e_0,e_1\rangle$ of Definition [1.5](#b-00091) for $e_0$ even and $e_1$ odd, the printed relation gives, for $e_0=e_1=A$ in the $A$ slot,
\langle A,QA\rangle=\langle QA,A\rangle=-\langle A,QA\rangle,

hence $\langle A,QA\rangle=0$, which contradicts the kinetic term $\tfrac12\langle A,QA\rangle=-\tfrac14\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dA,dA)$ of [(1.2)](#b-00125). The relation of Proposition [1.11](#b-00135), $\langle Qe_0,e_1\rangle+(-1)^{|e_0|}\langle e_0,Qe_1\rangle=0$, is the one satisfied by the action, and it is used throughout.

1.7 The classical master equation
Proposition 1.14 (Classical master equation).
For every $\mathfrak g$ as in Definition [1.1](#b-00054):
• equivalently, $\{\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle,\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle\}=0$ (that is, $Q^2=0$) and $QI+\tfrac12\{I,I\}=0$.
If moreover $[\mathfrak g,\mathfrak g]\neq0$, the master equation fixes the relative signs of the pairing and the sign of the ghost term:
• if the sign of the $(\lambda^*,\lambda)$ pairing, or of the $(c^*,c)$ pairing, or of both, is reversed relative to the $(A,A^*)$ pairing in Definition [1.5](#b-00091), then $\{S,S\}\neq0$;
• with the pairing of Definition [1.5](#b-00091) and the sign of the term $\tfrac12([c,c],c^*)$ reversed, $\{S,S\}\neq0$.
Proof.

Equivalence. Write $S=\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle+I$. Both summands are even, so by graded symmetry $\{I,\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle\}=\{\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle,I\}=QI$ (Proposition [1.11](#b-00135)), and
\{S,S\}=\{\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle,\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle\}+2\,QI+\{I,I\}.

The first term is $Q$ applied to $\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle$; by the preservation of the pairing in Proposition [1.11](#b-00135), $\langle Qe,Qe\rangle=-(-1)^{|e|}\langle e,Q^2e\rangle$, so this term is a multiple of $\langle e,Q^2e\rangle$ and vanishes by $Q^2=0$. This gives the equivalence of the first two items.

$\{S,S\}=0$ for every $\mathfrak g$. The action [(1.1)](#b-00108) is the BV action of the BRST theory of [ESW, Def 3.2], built as in [ESW, Def 1.34] with the natural pairing of the shifted cotangent bundle; it satisfies $\{S,S\}=0$ for every $\mathfrak g$, and the dimensional reduction preserves it [ESW, Def 1.55, Prop 1.56]. The natural pairing differs from Definition [1.5](#b-00091) at most by a sign on each of the three pairs, and these signs are independent of $\mathfrak g$. An overall sign leaves $\{S,S\}=0$ invariant. For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ the density of $\{S,S\}$ computed with the pairing of Definition [1.5](#b-00091) vanishes as a local functional, together with $2QI+\{I,I\}$, while $QI\neq0$; for each of the three other relative sign patterns it is nonzero (Remark [1.15](#b-00197)). Hence the natural pairing coincides with Definition [1.5](#b-00091) up to an overall sign, and $\{S,S\}=0$ holds for every $\mathfrak g$. The same exact computation gives $\{S,S\}=0$ for $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(3)$.

The relative signs. The action is linear in the antifields, so $\{S,S\}$ has antifield number $0$ and $1$. Each term of $\{S,S\}$ pairs a derivative along a field with a derivative along its partner and carries the sign of that pair. The derivatives of $S$ along the antifields are the gauge transformations $A\mapsto d_Ac$, $\lambda\mapsto[c,\lambda]$, $c\mapsto\tfrac12[c,c]$.

• Antifield number $0$: the gauge variation of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\big(-\tfrac14(F_A,F_A)+\tfrac12(\lambda,{\not d}_A\lambda)\big)$. The $A$-variation enters through the $(A,A^*)$ pair and the $\lambda$-variation through the $(\lambda^*,\lambda)$ pair.
• Linear in $A^*$: $[d_Ac,c]$ through the $(A,A^*)$ pair against $d_A(\tfrac12[c,c])$ through the $(c^*,c)$ pair, related by the Leibniz rule $d_A[c,c]=2[d_Ac,c]$.

• Linear in $\lambda^*$: $[c,[c,\lambda]]$ through the $(\lambda^*,\lambda)$ pair against $\tfrac12[[c,c],\lambda]$ through the $(c^*,c)$ pair, related by the Jacobi identity $2[c,[c,\lambda]]=[[c,c],\lambda]$.
• Linear in $c^*$: $[c,[c,c]]=0$.

Consider the part of $\{S,S\}$ with field content $(c,\lambda,\lambda)$, no $A$ and no antifield. The $(c^*,c)$ pair contributes nothing to it, since $\tfrac12[c,c]$ contains two ghosts. The $(\lambda^*,\lambda)$ pair contributes the variation of $\tfrac12\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(\lambda,{\not d}\lambda)$ along $\lambda\mapsto[c,\lambda]$, and the $(A,A^*)$ pair contributes, up to the sign of that pair, a nonzero multiple of the variation of $\tfrac12\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(\lambda,\rho([A,\lambda]))$ along $A\mapsto dc$, which is a nonzero multiple of
\int\mathrm{dvol}\,\big(\lambda,\rho([dc,\lambda])\big).

With the pairing of Definition [1.5](#b-00091) these two contributions cancel, because $\{S,S\}=0$; reversing the sign of the $(\lambda^*,\lambda)$ pair relative to the $(A,A^*)$ pair therefore turns this part of $\{S,S\}$ into twice the $(A,A^*)$ contribution. This functional is nonzero when $[\mathfrak g,\mathfrak g]
eq0$: choose $X,Y,Z\in\mathfrak g$ with $(X,[Z,Y])
eq0$, compactly supported $\Sigma$-valued functions $s_1,s_2$ and a compactly supported function $f$ with $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(df,\Gamma(s_1,s_2))
eq0$, and put $\lambda=r_1s_1X+r_2s_2Y$, $c=r_3fZ$ with $r_1,r_2,r_3$ odd as in Definition [1.13](#b-00162). Using $r_2r_3r_1=-r_1r_3r_2$, $(Y,[Z,X])=-(X,[Z,Y])$ and the symmetry of $\Gamma$,
\int\mathrm{dvol}\,\big(\lambda,\rho([dc,\lambda])\big)=2\,r_1r_3r_2\,(X,[Z,Y])\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(df,\Gamma(s_1,s_2))\neq0 .

This proves the first of the last two items when the $(\lambda^*,\lambda)$ sign is reversed, alone or together with the $(c^*,c)$ sign. Next consider the part with field content $(c,c,A^*)$ and no $A$. The $(\lambda^*,\lambda)$ pair contributes nothing to it. The $(A,A^*)$ pair contributes the variation of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,([A,c],A^*)$ along $A\mapsto dc$, which is $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,([dc,c],A^*)$ up to the sign of the pair, and the $(c^*,c)$ pair contributes the variation of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dc,A^*)$ along $c\mapsto\tfrac12[c,c]$, which is $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,([dc,c],A^*)$ up to the product of the sign of the pair and the sign of the term $\tfrac12([c,c],c^*)$. They cancel with the data of Definitions [1.5](#b-00091) and [1.8](#b-00106), so reversing the $(c^*,c)$ sign alone, or the sign of $\tfrac12([c,c],c^*)$ alone, turns this part into twice $\pm\int\mathrm{dvol}\,([dc,c],A^*)$. On $c=r_1f_1X+r_2f_2Y$ with $[X,Y]\neq0$,
\int\mathrm{dvol}\,([dc,c],A^*)=r_1r_2\int\mathrm{dvol}\,\big([X,Y],\,(d(f_1f_2),A^*|_V)\big),
which is nonzero for a suitable compactly supported $A^*|_V$. ∎
Remark 1.15 (Exact verification of identities of local functionals).

Propositions [1.9](#b-00118) and [1.14](#b-00173) use the following exact computation. For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ and $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(3)$ fix bases of $\mathfrak g$, of $V_{10}$ and of $\Sigma\oplus\Sigma^*$ in which the bracket, the pairings, $\rho$ and $\Gamma$ have Gaussian-rational entries. The density of each local functional of this chapter, and of each bracket of two of them, is then a polynomial in the jets of the components of the six fields with Gaussian-rational coefficients, computed in exact arithmetic. A local functional $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,D$ without constant term vanishes on $\mathscr E_c$ when all Euler–Lagrange derivatives of $D$ vanish identically: for $e\in\mathscr E_c$, after integration by parts with compact support, $\frac{d}{ds}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,D(se)$ is the integral of the Euler–Lagrange derivatives of $D$ at $se$ paired with $e$ (odd components multiplied by odd elements of an auxiliary nilpotent ring, as in Definition [1.13](#b-00162)), so $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,D(se)$ is independent of $s$ and equals its value $0$ at $s=0$. Conversely, a nonzero Euler–Lagrange derivative shows that the functional is nonzero. Statements that a bracket vanishes for every element of $\Sigma$ are established on every element of a basis of $\Sigma$; this suffices, because the bracket is linear in that element.
2. Superconformal symmetry as an equivariant action

The dilatation of a composite operator, and every other superconformal transformation, acts on the fields of $\mathcal N=4$ super Yang–Mills theory [ESW, Def 2.4, §10.3] up to gauge transformations and equations of motion. In the BV formalism this structure is a Maurer–Cartan element of a Chevalley–Eilenberg complex, an $L_\infty$ action in the sense of [ESW, Def 1.26–1.27], and it is the classical input of the equivariant observables used later. [ESW, (32)–(34), Thm 3.3] construct it for the Poincaré supersymmetry algebra; the special conformal transformations and the special supercharges require Weyl weights, a compensating term with the six scalars, and an R-symmetry rotation in the odd bracket. This chapter realises $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$, the complexification of $\mathfrak{psu}(2,2|4)$ [SW, (7)], on Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$, fixes the sign conventions of the complex, writes the action $S+S^{(1)}+S^{(2)}$, and proves its master equation for every gauge algebra.
2.1 The algebra $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ in complexified Euclidean form

Throughout, $x\in V$ denotes the position on $\mathbb R^4$ and $E$ the Euler vector field $E(x)=x$ of [SW, (3)]; in this chapter $E$ always means this vector field. For a vector field $v$ on $V_{10}$, $(v,-)$ is its metric dual one-form, $L_v$ the Lie derivative [ESW, (32)], $v(-)$ the derivative along $v$, and $\operatorname{div}v$ the divergence, $L_v\,\mathrm{dvol}=(\operatorname{div}v)\,\mathrm{dvol}$.
Definition 2.1 (Even part).
The even part of $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ is the Lie algebra of vector fields on $V_{10}=V\oplus W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ spanned by
• translations $x\mapsto v_1$, $v_1\in V$;
• rotations, the linear vector fields given by elements of $\mathfrak{so}(V)$;
• the dilatation $\Delta=2E$, the generator $\Delta=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1\,|\,0)$ of [SW, (17)], with $\mathrm{ad}_\Delta=-2$ on translations (Remark [2.6](#b-00254));
• special conformal fields $x\mapsto(x,x)v_1-2(v_1,x)x$, $v_1\in V$, the special conformal field of [SW, (3)] along $v_1$;
• linear vector fields on $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ given by elements of $\mathfrak{so}(W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)$,
with the bracket $[v,v']=v(v')-v'(v)$. The first four kinds are the conformal Killing vector fields of $V$; together with $\mathfrak{so}(W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)$ the even part has dimension $15+15=30$.
Definition 2.2 (Odd part).

The odd part of $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ is $\Pi(\Sigma\oplus\Sigma^*)$. An element $Q_1\in\Sigma$ is realised by the constant spinor $Q_1$, and an element $Q_2\in\Sigma^*$ by the $\Sigma$-valued function $x\mapsto\rho(x)Q_2$. Together these span the conformal Killing spinors
x\mapsto Q_1+\rho(x)Q_2,\qquad Q_1\in\Sigma,\ Q_2\in\Sigma^* .
Supercharge spinors always carry a subscript, $Q_1,Q_2,\dots$, and each formula states whether they lie in $\Sigma$ or in $\Sigma^*$; the unsubscripted $Q$ is the differential of Chapter 1.
Definition 2.3 (Bracket).
On two even elements the bracket of $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ is the bracket of vector fields, $[v,v']=v(v')-v'(v)$. For an even element $v$ and an odd element,
[v,\,Q_1+\rho(x)Q_2]=v(Q_1+\rho(x)Q_2)+\tfrac14\rho(d(v,-))(Q_1+\rho(x)Q_2)-\tfrac18(\operatorname{div}v)(Q_1+\rho(x)Q_2), \tag{2.1}
where $\rho$ of the two-form $d(v,-)$ means $\rho\circ q$ [ESW, (29)]; the right-hand side is again a conformal Killing spinor. For two odd elements, with $Q_1,Q_3\in\Sigma$ and $Q_2,Q_4\in\Sigma^*$,
[Q_1+\rho(x)Q_2,\ Q_3+\rho(x)Q_4]=\Big(x\mapsto\Gamma\big(Q_1+\rho(x)Q_2,\,Q_3+\rho(x)Q_4\big)\big|_V\Big)+\big(\text{rotation of }W_{\mathbb R}^\perp\big), \tag{2.2}
where $|_V$ is the orthogonal projection $V_{10}\to V$ and the rotation of $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ is the element of $\mathfrak{so}(W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)$ with matrix elements
\big(w,(\text{rotation of }W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)\,w'\big)=(\rho(q(w\wedge w'))Q_1,Q_4)+(\rho(q(w\wedge w'))Q_3,Q_2),\qquad w,w'\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp .

The $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$-components of $\Gamma$ drop out of the bracket, as in the dimensional reduction of the supertranslation algebra [ESW, §2.6, Prop 2.20]; they reappear in $S^{(2)}$ (Definition [2.15](#b-00332)). The coefficient $1$ in front of the rotation of $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ is fixed by the super-Jacobi identity on triples in $\Sigma\times\Sigma\times\Sigma^*$: each term of the Jacobi sum of three odd elements contains exactly one odd–odd bracket, so the sum is affine in this coefficient; it vanishes at $1$ and is nonzero at $0$ (Remark [2.18](#b-00352)), so $1$ is its unique zero.
Proposition 2.4 (Brackets of the named generators).
• For $Q_1,Q_2\in\Sigma$: $[Q_1,Q_2]=\Gamma(Q_1,Q_2)|_V$, a translation; this is [ESW, Def 2.5] after reduction.
• For $Q_1,Q_2\in\Sigma^*$: $[Q_1,Q_2]=-\big(x\mapsto(x,x)v_1-2(v_1,x)x\big)$ with $v_1=\Gamma(Q_1,Q_2)|_V$, a special conformal field.

• For $Q_1\in\Sigma$, $Q_2\in\Sigma^*$: $[Q_1,Q_2]=\big(x\mapsto\Gamma(Q_1,\rho(x)Q_2)|_V\big)+(\text{rotation of }W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)$ as in Definition [2.3](#b-00215); the dilatation part of the first summand is $\tfrac12(Q_1,Q_2)\,\Delta$, and the rest is a rotation of $V$.
• For a translation $x\mapsto v_1$: $[v_1,Q_1]=0$ for $Q_1\in\Sigma$ and $[v_1,Q_2]=\rho(v_1)Q_2\in\Sigma$ for $Q_2\in\Sigma^*$.
• For a special conformal field $x\mapsto(x,x)v_1-2(v_1,x)x$: its bracket with $Q_1\in\Sigma$ is $\rho(v_1)Q_1\in\Sigma^*$, and with $Q_2\in\Sigma^*$ it is $0$.
• $[\Delta,Q_1]=-Q_1$ for $Q_1\in\Sigma$ and $[\Delta,Q_2]=+Q_2$ for $Q_2\in\Sigma^*$.
Proof.
The first two items follow from [(2.2)](#b-00219): for $Q_2=Q_4=0$ the rotation of $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ vanishes; for $Q_1=Q_3=0$ it vanishes as well, and for $v\in V$
(v,\Gamma(\rho(x)Q_1,\rho(x)Q_2))=(\rho(x)\rho(v)\rho(x)Q_1,Q_2)=2(v,x)(x,\Gamma(Q_1,Q_2))-(x,x)(v,\Gamma(Q_1,Q_2)),
using $\rho(x)\rho(v)\rho(x)=2(v,x)\rho(x)-(x,x)\rho(v)$ from the Clifford relation and $(\rho(x)Q_1,Q_2)=(Q_1,\rho(x)Q_2)$. Projecting to $V$ gives $-\big((x,x)v_1-2(v_1,x)x\big)$.

For $Q_1\in\Sigma$, $Q_2\in\Sigma^*$ and $v\in V$, $(v,\Gamma(Q_1,\rho(x)Q_2))=(\rho(x)\rho(v)Q_1,Q_2)$; the part symmetric under $x\leftrightarrow v$ is $\tfrac12(\rho(x)\rho(v)+\rho(v)\rho(x))=(x,v)$, so the linear vector field $x\mapsto\Gamma(Q_1,\rho(x)Q_2)|_V$ equals $(Q_1,Q_2)\,E=\tfrac12(Q_1,Q_2)\,\Delta$ plus an antisymmetric linear field, i.e. a rotation.

For the even–odd brackets use [(2.1)](#b-00217). Proposition 2.5 (Identification with $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$).
The bracket of Definition [2.3](#b-00215) has the following properties.
• The dimension is $30|32$, and the bracket of two elements of the ten named subspaces lies in their span.
• The bracket is graded antisymmetric and satisfies the super-Jacobi identity.

• The $V$-part of every odd–odd bracket is a conformal Killing vector field of $V$; the rotation of $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ is nonzero for $\Sigma\times\Sigma^*$ and vanishes for $\Sigma\times\Sigma$ and $\Sigma^*\times\Sigma^*$.

• The block rule of the supermatrix presentation [SW, (17), (19)] holds for every pair of the ten named subspaces: their bracket lies in the block with the row of the first subspace and the column of the second when the column of the first equals the row of the second, plus the block with the row of the second and the column of the first when the column of the second equals the row of the first, and vanishes otherwise.
• $\mathrm{ad}_\Delta$ is diagonal on the named subspaces with the eigenvalues of the table above, which are those of $\Delta=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1\,|\,0)$ in [SW, (17)].
• The Killing form $\mathrm{str}(\mathrm{ad}_{x_1}\mathrm{ad}_{x_2})$ for $x_1,x_2\in\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$, with $\mathrm{str}$ the supertrace [SW, after (17)], vanishes identically.

• The algebra equals its derived algebra and has trivial centre; its even part is the sum of the two commuting ideals formed by the conformal Killing vector fields of $V$ and by $\mathfrak{so}(W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)$, each of dimension $15$ with nondegenerate Killing form.
These are the properties by which the algebra is identified with the complexification $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ of $\mathfrak{psu}(2,2|4)$ [SW, (7), (17)].
Proof.

The dimension count is $4+6+1+4+15=30$ and $16+16=32$. Every other item is a bilinear or trilinear identity in the arguments, or a statement about the structure constants; each is established on all ordered pairs and all ordered triples of elements of a basis adapted to the ten named subspaces (Remark [2.18](#b-00352)), hence for all arguments. ∎

2.5 The master equation
External input 2.17 (Poincaré supersymmetry, ten dimensions).

[ESW, Thm 3.3, Lemmas 3.4–3.7, (32)–(34)] and [ESW, Prop 2.20]: for every $\mathfrak g$, the functionals [(2.5)](#b-00309) on $\mathfrak{iso}(V)\oplus\mathfrak{so}(W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)$, [(2.6)](#b-00312) and [(2.8)](#b-00334) on $\Sigma\times\Sigma$ satisfy every component of [(2.4)](#b-00285) with arguments in the subalgebra generated by translations, $\mathfrak{so}(V)$, $\mathfrak{so}(W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)$ and $\Sigma$, with $d_{CE}$ the differential [(2.3)](#b-00269) used in the proof of [ESW, Lemma 3.6].
Remark 2.18 (Exact verification on a basis).

The computer-assisted statements of this chapter are exact identities established on a basis. Fix a basis of $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ adapted to the ten named subspaces, with $4+3+3+1+4+15$ even and $8+8+8+8$ odd elements, in which $\rho$, $\Gamma$ and the pairing $\Sigma\otimes\Sigma^*\to\mathbb C$ have Gaussian-rational entries. The bracket of Definition [2.3](#b-00215) is computed in exact arithmetic on every ordered pair of basis elements; its values are expanded in the basis, and graded antisymmetry, the super-Jacobi identity on every ordered triple, the Killing form and the block rule on every ordered pair, the eigenvalues of $\mathrm{ad}_\Delta$, the derived algebra, the centre and the Killing forms of the two even ideals are computed from these structure constants. With the coefficient $0$ in place of $1$ in front of the rotation of $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ in [(2.2)](#b-00219), the super-Jacobi identity fails. For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ and $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(3)$, with the data of Remark [1.15](#b-00197), every component of [(2.4)](#b-00285) of arity $1$, $2$ and $3$ is evaluated on every unordered tuple of basis elements, repetitions allowed, with at least two odd elements in arity $3$; each is a local functional whose density is a polynomial in the jets of the fields with Gaussian-rational coefficients, and it vanishes when all its Euler–Lagrange derivatives vanish identically (Remark [1.15](#b-00197)). All these identities are multilinear in their arguments, and the components of [(2.4)](#b-00285) are graded antisymmetric under exchange of arguments (Definition [2.7](#b-00259)); the identities on basis tuples therefore hold for all arguments.
Lemma 2.19 (Colour reduction).

Consider local functionals that are finite sums of terms, each the product of a polynomial in the jets of the $V_{10}$-, spinor- and form-components of the fields, independent of $\mathfrak g$, and a tree tensor in the $\mathfrak g$-components of at most five fields: a multilinear form on $\mathfrak g^k$, $k\le5$, obtained from copies of $([-,-],-)$ by contraction with the inverse pairing $(-,-)^{-1}$ along a tree, or the pairing $(-,-)$ itself for $k=2$. If the Euler–Lagrange derivatives of the density of such a functional vanish identically for $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(2)$, they vanish identically for every Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ with a nondegenerate invariant symmetric pairing.
Proof.

By invariance of the pairing, every tree tensor with $k$ legs is a sign times $(b(X_1,\dots,X_{k-1}),X_k)$ for a bracket monomial $b$ of $X_1,\dots,X_{k-1}\in\mathfrak g$, each used once. Hence the tree tensors with $k$ legs are the values of a linear map, natural in $\mathfrak g$ and equivariant under permutations of the legs, from the space of formal trees modulo antisymmetry and the Jacobi identity, which is the multilinear part of the free Lie algebra on $k-1$ letters, of dimension $(k-2)!$. For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ this map has rank $1$, $1$, $2$, $6$ for $k=2,3,4,5$, computed exactly, so it is injective for $k\le5$, and averaging a left inverse over the permutations of the legs gives an equivariant left inverse. A functional of the stated form is therefore the evaluation in $\mathfrak g$ of a formal expression, a sum of jet polynomials times formal trees. Its Euler–Lagrange derivative along a field, paired with a fixed element of $\mathfrak g$ treated as one more leg, is again of this form, because differentiation acts on the jet polynomials and leaves the tree. The equivariant left inverse acts on the trees alone; applied to the vanishing $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ evaluation it shows that the formal Euler–Lagrange derivatives vanish, hence their evaluations vanish for every $\mathfrak g$. ∎
Theorem 2.20 (Master equation of the equivariant action).

For every Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ with a nondegenerate invariant symmetric pairing, $S_{\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)}=S+S^{(1)}+S^{(2)}$, with $S^{(1)}$, $S^{(2)}$ of Definitions [2.12](#b-00307)–[2.15](#b-00332) and $S^{(k\ge3)}=0$, is an action of $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ on $(\mathscr E,\langle\,,\rangle,S)$: it satisfies [(2.4)](#b-00285), and $I_{\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)}=I+S^{(1)}+S^{(2)}$ satisfies $(d_{CE}+Q)I_{\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)}+\tfrac12\{I_{\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)},I_{\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)}\}=0$.
Proof.

By Lemma [2.11](#b-00289) it suffices to prove the components. Arity $0$ is Proposition [1.14](#b-00173). The components of arity $\ge4$, and of arity $3$ with at most one or with three odd arguments, hold for every $\mathfrak g$ by Proposition [2.16](#b-00341). The remaining components, of arities $1$ and $2$ and of arity $3$ with exactly two odd arguments, vanish for $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ and $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(3)$ for all arguments (Remark [2.18](#b-00352)). Each of them is of the form of Lemma [2.19](#b-00354): every term of $S$, $S^{(1)}$, $S^{(2)}$ is a tree tensor in at most four, three and two $\mathfrak g$-components respectively, built from $(-,-)$ and $[-,-]$; the bracket of Definition [1.6](#b-00095) contracts one leg of each factor with the inverse pairing and joins two trees into a tree; so every term has at most $4+3-2=5$ legs. 3. Costello's data with a UV boundary

Costello's renormalisation needs a gauge-fixing operator $Q^{GF}$, the heat kernel of $H=[Q,Q^{GF}]$ and the propagator $P(\varepsilon,\infty)=\int_\varepsilon^\infty(Q^{GF}\otimes1)K_t\,dt$ [C07, §6.5], and its axioms [C07, Def 4.3.3] are formulated on a compact manifold; [C07, §5.2] records that Yang–Mills theory in second-order form lies outside them. On Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$ we keep a single regulator, the lower Schwinger limit $\varepsilon$, and set the upper limit to $\infty$, so that $\varepsilon$ is the single scale of the construction. This chapter constructs a Feynman-gauge operator $Q^{GF}$ that satisfies three of the five axioms, identifies the two that fail, and proves the identities that hold with these data: $QP(\varepsilon,\infty)=K_\varepsilon$, the UV-boundary identity, the acyclicity of $Q$ at scale $\infty$ on sections with vanishing moments together with the zero-mode classes that $Q$ has on compactly supported sections, and the one-loop formula for the graph expansion.

Remark 3.4 (Names of the adjointness relations in the sources).

[C07, §4.3] calls $Q$ “self adjoint” and [C07, Def 4.3.3(1)] calls $Q^{GF}$ “skew self adjoint”; [C07, §1, §1.1, §2.1] and [CG2, §7.2.1] use the opposite names, $Q$ skew self adjoint and $Q^{GF}$ self adjoint. The printed adjointness relation of [ESW, Def 1.16] is discussed in Remark [1.12](#b-00153).
Proposition 3.5 (Axioms of a gauge-fixing operator).
Of the conditions of [C07, Def 4.3.3], three hold:
• (1), read as in Remark [3.4](#b-00395): Proposition [3.3](#b-00383);
• (2): every component of $Q^{GF}$ has order $0$ or $1$;
• (4): $H=d^*d+dd^*$, the componentwise Laplacian, is a generalised Laplacian (Proposition [3.2](#b-00375)).
Condition (3) fails: $(Q^{GF})^2$ vanishes on the slots of $c$, $A$, $\lambda$, $\lambda^*$, and
(Q^{GF})^2A^*=2\,d^*(A^*|_V)\ \ (\text{in the slot of }c),\qquad (Q^{GF})^2c^*=-2\,dc^*\ \ (\text{in the slot of }A|_V).
Condition (5) fails: $\operatorname{Im}Q\cap\operatorname{Im}Q^{GF}\neq0$, since for every nonzero $c\in\mathscr E_c$ in the ghost slot
Qc=-dc=Q^{GF}\big(\tfrac12dc\ \text{in the slot of }A^*|_V\big).
Moreover $\operatorname{Im}Q^{GF}$ pairs nontrivially with itself: for $e_0$ in the $A^*$ slot and $e_1$ in the $c^*$ slot,
\langle Q^{GF}e_0,Q^{GF}e_1\rangle=-2\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(e_0,de_1).
Proof.

$(Q^{GF})^2A^*=Q^{GF}(-2A^*)=-2\big(-d^*(A^*|_V)\big)$ and $(Q^{GF})^2c^*=Q^{GF}(dc^*)=-2\,dc^*$; on the other slots the image of $Q^{GF}$ lies in the slots of $c$ and $\lambda$, where $Q^{GF}$ vanishes. For (5), $Q^{GF}(\tfrac12dc)=-2\cdot\tfrac12dc$. The last formula is $\langle-2e_0,de_1\rangle$ with $-2e_0$ in the $A$ slot. ∎
Remark 3.6 (Consequences of the two failures).

Three statements of [C07] use (3) or (5): [C07, Lemma 6.5.1] ($P(0,\infty)$ inverts $Q\colon\operatorname{Im}Q^{GF}\to\operatorname{Im}Q$; its proof uses $(Q^{GF})^2=0$), the real-slice Gaussian over $(\operatorname{Im}Q^{GF})_{\mathbb R}$ of [C07, §6.6], and [C07, Lemma 6.6.2]. Indeed $\operatorname{Im}Q^{GF}$ contains the whole $A$ slot, on which $\langle e,Qe\rangle$ has the longitudinal zero eigenvector (Remark [1.10](#b-00130)). The arguments below use $Q^2=0$, $H=[Q,Q^{GF}]$, $[Q,H]=0$ and the adjointness relations; Theorem [3.19](#b-00485) takes the place of [C07, Lemma 6.5.1].
Remark 3.7 (Feynman gauge).

In momentum space the $A\otimes A$ component of the propagator $P(0,\infty)$ (Proposition [3.11](#b-00430) at $\varepsilon=0$) is $2(-,-)^{-1}\otimes(\text{inverse metric of }V_{10})\,|p|^{-2}$. It is the inverse of the second variation of $-\big(\tfrac12\langle A,QA\rangle-\tfrac14\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V)\big)=\tfrac14\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(A,HA)$, i.e. the covariance of the weight $e^{+S/\hbar}$ for the Yang–Mills kinetic term completed by the Feynman-gauge term $-\tfrac14(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V)$; it has the eigenvalue $2(-,-)^{-1}|p|^{-2}$, positive, in all ten directions of $V_{10}$. Restricted to $\lambda$, the propagator $P(0,\infty)$ is minus the inverse of the second variation of $\tfrac12\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(\lambda,{\not d}\lambda)$.
3.2 Heat kernel and propagator
Definition 3.8 (Heat kernel).

For $t>0$, $K_t\in\mathscr E\otimes\mathscr E$ is the kernel with the components of $K_0$ (Definition [1.6](#b-00095)) with $\delta(x-y)$ replaced by $(4\pi t)^{-2}e^{-|x-y|^2/4t}$; in momentum space this factor is $e^{-t|p|^2}$. Then $K_t\star e=e^{-tH}e$ [C07, §6.5; C07, §15.2]. The kernel
L_t=(Q^{GF}\otimes1)K_t
represents $Q^{GF}e^{-tH}$ [C07, §6.5]. On $\mathbb R^4$,
K_\infty:=\lim_{t\to\infty}K_t=0,
pointwise in $x-y$, and in momentum space for every $p\neq0$.
Proposition 3.9 (Heat-kernel identities).
(Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q)K_t=0,\qquad \frac{d}{dt}K_t+(Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q)L_t=0\qquad[\text{C07, §6.5}].
Proof.

$K_t=(e^{-tH}\otimes1)K_0$, $[Q,H]=0$ and $(Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q)K_0=0$ give the first identity. For the second, odd operators on different tensor factors anticommute, $(1\otimes Q)(Q^{GF}\otimes1)=-(Q^{GF}\otimes1)(1\otimes Q)$, and $(1\otimes Q)K_t=-(Q\otimes1)K_t$, so
(Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q)L_t=(QQ^{GF}\otimes1)K_t+(Q^{GF}Q\otimes1)K_t=(H\otimes1)K_t=-\frac{d}{dt}K_t .
Definition 3.10 (Propagator).
P(\varepsilon,\infty)=\int_\varepsilon^\infty L_t\,dt=\int_\varepsilon^\infty(Q^{GF}\otimes1)K_t\,dt\qquad[\text{C07, §6.5}],\qquad \varepsilon>0 .

The component in a row labelled by two slots in the table below is the value of $\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}$ [C07, §6.4] on the product of a coordinate functional of the first slot at $x$ and one of the second slot at $y$, in this order.

Proposition 3.12 (The two UV-boundary kernels).
(Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q)P(\varepsilon,\infty)=K_\varepsilon, \tag{3.1}
\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}P(\varepsilon,\infty)=-\varepsilon L_\varepsilon . \tag{3.2}
Proof.
By Proposition [3.9](#b-00421),
(Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q)P(\varepsilon,\infty)=\int_\varepsilon^\infty(Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q)L_t\,dt=-\int_\varepsilon^\infty\frac{d}{dt}K_t\,dt=K_\varepsilon-K_\infty=K_\varepsilon .

This is [C07, Lemma 10.2.1] with the upper scale at $\infty$ and $K_\infty=0$. In position space the scalar core of [(3.1)](#b-00446) is $d^*d\,\frac{1-e^{-|x-y|^2/4\varepsilon}}{4\pi^2|x-y|^2}=(4\pi\varepsilon)^{-2}e^{-|x-y|^2/4\varepsilon}$. The second identity is the fundamental theorem of calculus applied to $\int_\varepsilon^\infty L_t\,dt$. ∎
Remark 3.13 (Two objects at $t=\varepsilon$).

The lower end of the Schwinger integral carries two different kernels. By [(3.2)](#b-00447), $L_\varepsilon=(Q^{GF}\otimes1)K_\varepsilon$ governs the $\varepsilon$-dependence of every graph: for a graph $\gamma$ whose value is the integral of $f_\gamma$ over the Schwinger times $t_e\in[\varepsilon,\infty)$ of its edge set $E(\gamma)$ [C07, §15.5], $\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}$ of the value is minus the sum over $e\in E(\gamma)$ of $\varepsilon f_\gamma$ with $t_e=\varepsilon$, that is, with the edge $e$ carrying $L_\varepsilon$. The singular coefficients ($\varepsilon^{-1}$, $\log\varepsilon$) and the scaling behaviour therefore sit on $L_\varepsilon$ edges. By [(3.1)](#b-00446), $K_\varepsilon$ governs the action of $Q$ (Theorem [3.17](#b-00464)): the obstruction to the quantum master equation and the $Q$-variation of observables sit on edges carrying $K_\varepsilon$, or $K_\varepsilon-K_0$, and on the counterterm vertices $-QI^{CT}[\varepsilon]-\{I,I^{CT}[\varepsilon]\}_\varepsilon$ (Definition [3.15](#b-00457); the counterterm $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ is constructed in Chapter 4), together with their $\delta$-derivatives for observables (Chapter 5).
3.3 The UV-boundary identity
Remark 3.14 (Functionals on $\mathbb R^4$).

On $\mathbb R^4$ the operators $\partial_{K_t}$ and $\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}$ [C07, §6.4] and the brackets below act on functionals of compactly supported sections, $\mathscr O(\mathscr E_c)\supset\mathscr O_l(\mathscr E)$ [C07, Def 4.2.2]. The interaction, its counterterms and their flows are taken modulo constants [CG2, §7.2.6]; the observables of Chapter 5 keep their constant terms, which depend on the four-form $\omega$ and carry the subtraction of the expectation value. A local functional $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(\text{density})$, such as $S$, $I$ or a counterterm, is a density modulo total derivatives, and on it these operators are evaluated graph by graph (Proposition [3.22](#b-00513)), with compactly supported legs. For the interaction and its counterterms constants are discarded because a contraction that uses every field of a translation-invariant functional is proportional to the volume of $\mathbb R^4$. If the Taylor component of a functional, evaluated on compactly supported sections in its remaining arguments, is an integrable kernel in the two contracted positions, its contraction with $K_t$ is bounded by $(4\pi t)^{-2}$ times the integral of the absolute value of that kernel and tends to $0$ as $t\to\infty$. This applies to every local functional $\int\omega\,(\text{density})$ with $\omega$ a compactly supported four-form [CG2, Lemma 10.1.1.3], to every local functional $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(\text{density})$ at least quadratic in the fields, and to the bracket of two such functionals: a contraction of two legs at one point is a density times $(4\pi t)^{-2}$, and a contraction between two such functionals pairs two compactly supported densities through $K_t$. For a linear functional $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(c^*,X)$, $X\in\mathfrak g$, the contraction integrates $K_t$ over one position, and the integral of the scalar factor $(4\pi t)^{-2}e^{-|x-y|^2/4t}$ over $x$ equals $1$ for every $t$; these linear functionals are the zero-mode classes of Theorem [3.19](#b-00485).
Definition 3.15 (Scale-$\varepsilon$ Laplacian and bracket).

\Delta_\varepsilon=-\partial_{K_\varepsilon}\quad[\text{C07, §10.1}],\qquad \{f,g\}_\varepsilon=\Delta_\varepsilon(fg)-\Delta_\varepsilon(f)g-(-1)^{|f|}f\Delta_\varepsilon(g)\quad[\text{CG2, §7.2.8}],

the second with the Laplacian $\Delta_\varepsilon$ of [C07] in the product rule of [CG2]. At scale $\infty$ the kernel is $K_\infty:=0$ (Definition [3.8](#b-00415)); accordingly $\Delta_\infty:=-\partial_{K_\infty}=0$ and $\{-,-\}_\infty=0$ identically, on every functional, and this is the scale-$\infty$ structure used throughout. On functionals whose contracted Taylor components are integrable kernels (Remark [3.14](#b-00455)), in particular on local functionals with a compactly supported four-form, on local functionals $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(\text{density})$ at least quadratic in the fields, and on brackets of two such, it is also the limit $t\to\infty$ of $\Delta_t$ and $\{-,-\}_t$.
Definition 3.16 (Renormalisation group flow).
For an even $\phi\in\mathrm{Sym}^2\mathscr E$ and an even functional $J$, at least cubic modulo $\hbar$,
W(\phi,J)=\hbar\log\big(e^{\hbar\partial_\phi}e^{J/\hbar}\big)\qquad[\text{CG2, §7.2.7}],

which is $\Gamma(\phi,J)$ of [C07, Def 6.6.1]. The letter $W$ with two arguments always denotes this flow; $W$ alone is the multiplicity space of [ESW, §10], and $\Gamma$ is reserved for the $\Gamma$-pairing of [ESW, (28)].
Theorem 3.17 (UV-boundary identity).
On functionals with values in $C^\bullet(\mathfrak{psl}(4|4))$ (Chapter 2), as formal power series in $\hbar$,
(d_{CE}+Q)\,e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}=e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}\,(d_{CE}+Q+\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon). \tag{3.3}
Here $Q^{GF}$ is the operator of Definition [3.1](#b-00371).
Proof.
By [C07, §6.4], $[\partial_\phi,Q]=\partial_{Q\phi}$ for $\phi\in\mathrm{Sym}^2\mathscr E$, with $Q$ acting on $\mathscr E\otimes\mathscr E$ as $Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q$. With [(3.1)](#b-00446),

\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}Q-Q\,\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}=\partial_{K_\varepsilon}=-\Delta_\varepsilon ,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad Q\,\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}=\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}Q+\Delta_\varepsilon .
The operators $\partial_\phi$ mutually commute [C07, §6.4], so $\Delta_\varepsilon$ commutes with $\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}$, and by induction on $n$
Q\,\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}^n=\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}^nQ+n\,\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}^{n-1}\Delta_\varepsilon .
Multiplying by $\hbar^n/n!$ and summing over $n$,
Q\,e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}=e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}Q+\hbar\,e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}\Delta_\varepsilon .

Finally $d_{CE}$ acts on the arguments in $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ and $\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}$ on the fields; $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ is a kernel on the fields, independent of the arguments of the cochains, so $[\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)},d_{CE}]=0$. Each step uses $Q^2=0$, [(3.1)](#b-00446) and the algebra of the operators $\partial_\phi$. ∎
Corollary 3.18 (Master equations at the two ends).

Let $J$ be an even functional with values in $C^\bullet(\mathfrak{psl}(4|4))[[\hbar]]$, at least cubic modulo $\hbar$ when the arguments of the cochains are counted as fields, as in [CG2, §13.2.2], and let $W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J)=\hbar\log\big(e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}e^{J/\hbar}\big)$ be its flow (Definition [3.16](#b-00460)). Then
(d_{CE}+Q+\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon)e^{J/\hbar}=0\iff(d_{CE}+Q)\,e^{W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J)/\hbar}=0,
and the two sides are equivalent to
(d_{CE}+Q)J+\tfrac12\{J,J\}_\varepsilon+\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon J=0,\qquad (d_{CE}+Q)\,W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J)=0 .
Proof.

Apply [(3.3)](#b-00466) to $e^{J/\hbar}$; the operator $e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}$ is invertible. This is [C07, Lemma 10.2.2] with the second scale at $\infty$, where $\Delta_\infty=0$. For an even $J$, the product rule of Definition [3.15](#b-00457), applied to the powers $J^n$, gives $\Delta_\varepsilon e^{J/\hbar}=e^{J/\hbar}\big(\hbar^{-1}\Delta_\varepsilon J+\tfrac12\hbar^{-2}\{J,J\}_\varepsilon\big)$, while $d_{CE}+Q$ is a derivation, $(d_{CE}+Q)e^{J/\hbar}=\hbar^{-1}e^{J/\hbar}(d_{CE}+Q)J$; this is the equivalence of [C07, §10.1] with $\Delta_\varepsilon$ in place of $\Delta_0$. ∎
3.4 Acyclicity at scale infinity

For a kernel $\phi\in\mathscr E\otimes\mathscr E$ write $\phi\star$ for the operator it represents [C07, §6.3]. Thus $K_t\star=e^{-tH}$, and $P(\varepsilon,\infty)\star=\int_\varepsilon^\infty Q^{GF}e^{-tH}dt$; $P(0,\infty)\star$ is the limit $\varepsilon\to0$. A Schwartz section of the BV bundle is a section whose components are Schwartz functions on $\mathbb R^4$; its moments are the integrals $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,f\,e$ with $f$ a polynomial function on $\mathbb R^4$. A Schwartz section is moment-free when all its moments vanish, equivalently when its Fourier transform (Chapter 1) vanishes to infinite order at $p=0$. The moment-free Schwartz sections form a closed subspace of the Schwartz sections, with the induced topology.
Theorem 3.19 (Acyclicity at scale $\infty$).

For every $\alpha\in\mathscr E_c$ the integral $P(0,\infty)\star\alpha=\int_0^\infty Q^{GF}e^{-tH}\alpha\,dt$ converges to a smooth section, bounded together with its first derivatives by a multiple of $(1+|x|)^{-2}$, and
Q\big(P(0,\infty)\star\alpha\big)+P(0,\infty)\star(Q\alpha)=\alpha ; \tag{3.4}
in kernel form, $(Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q)P(0,\infty)=K_0$. Moreover:

• The moment-free Schwartz sections form a space stable under $Q$, $Q^{GF}$, $e^{-tH}$ and $P(0,\infty)\star$, on which $P(0,\infty)\star$ acts continuously and [(3.4)](#b-00487) holds. Thus $P(0,\infty)\star$ is a contracting homotopy for $Q$ there: every moment-free Schwartz section $e$ with $Qe=0$ equals $Q\big(P(0,\infty)\star e\big)$, with $P(0,\infty)\star e$ moment-free.

• Zero-mode classes. Let $e_0$ be a section in the slot of $c$, of $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ or of $\lambda$ whose components are polynomial functions on $\mathbb R^4$, with $Qe_0=0$: a constant ghost $e_0=X\in\mathfrak g$, a section of $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ with harmonic polynomial components, or a polynomial solution of ${\not d}e_0=0$. The linear functional $e\mapsto\langle e_0,e\rangle$ on $\mathscr E_c$ is $Q$-closed and is $Q$-exact for no $e_0\neq0$, and it vanishes on moment-free Schwartz sections. For a constant ghost $X$ it is $-\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(c^*,X)$. For each bound on the polynomial degree of $e_0$ these functionals span a finite-dimensional space.
Proof.

Compactly supported sections. Each component of $e^{-tH}\alpha$ is the convolution of a component of $\alpha$ with $(4\pi t)^{-2}e^{-|x|^2/4t}$, so $e^{-tH}\alpha$ and its first derivatives are bounded by $(4\pi t)^{-2}$ times $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,|\alpha|$ and $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,|d\alpha|$, and by the suprema of $|\alpha|$ and $|d\alpha|$ for $t\le1$. Since $Q^{GF}$ has constant coefficients and order at most $1$, $\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^4}|Q^{GF}e^{-tH}\alpha|$ is integrable on $(0,\infty)$; the same bounds for the derivatives allow $Q$ to pass under the integral. At a point $x$ with $\operatorname{dist}(x,\operatorname{supp}\alpha)\ge1$, $|e^{-tH}\alpha(x)|\le(4\pi t)^{-2}e^{-\operatorname{dist}(x,\operatorname{supp}\alpha)^2/4t}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,|\alpha|$, and
\int_0^\infty(4\pi t)^{-2}e^{-\operatorname{dist}(x,\operatorname{supp}\alpha)^2/4t}\,dt=\frac{1}{4\pi^2\operatorname{dist}(x,\operatorname{supp}\alpha)^2},
which gives the bound by a multiple of $(1+|x|)^{-2}$; the first derivatives obey the same bound. Since $[Q,H]=0$, $Q^{GF}e^{-tH}Q\alpha=Q^{GF}Qe^{-tH}\alpha$, and
The limit vanishes because $|e^{-tH}\alpha|\le(4\pi t)^{-2}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,|\alpha|$; this is $K_\infty=0$. The kernel form is [(3.1)](#b-00446) at $\varepsilon\to0$ with $K_\varepsilon\to K_0$.

Moment-free sections. In momentum space $Q$ and $Q^{GF}$ act by multiplication with the matrices of polynomials in $p$ of Proposition [1.11](#b-00135) and Definition [3.1](#b-00371), $e^{-tH}$ by $e^{-t|p|^2}$, and $P(0,\infty)\star$ by the matrix of $Q^{GF}$ times $\int_0^\infty e^{-t|p|^2}dt=|p|^{-2}$. The first three preserve Schwartz functions of $p$ that vanish to infinite order at $p=0$. For such a function $h$ and every $n$, Taylor's formula at $p=0$ bounds every derivative $\partial^\beta h$ on $|p|\le1$ by $|p|^n$ times a multiple of the supremum of the derivatives of $h$ of order $n+|\beta|$ on the unit ball, while every derivative of order $k$ of $|p|^{-2}$ is bounded by a multiple of $|p|^{-2-k}$; by the Leibniz rule every derivative of order $k$ of $|p|^{-2}h$ is bounded on $0<|p|\le1$ by $|p|^{n-2-k}$ times continuous seminorms of $h$. Hence $|p|^{-2}h$ extends smoothly by $0$ at $p=0$ and vanishes there to infinite order; on $|p|\ge1$ the derivatives of $|p|^{-2}$ are bounded, so rapid decay and the seminorm bounds persist. This proves stability and continuity. For $p\neq0$ the matrices satisfy
