The derivation $Q$ of [C07, §6.2] acts on an $n$-linear graded-symmetric functional $F$ of parity $|F|$ by
QF=(-1)^{|F|}\,F\circ\Big(\sum_{j=1}^n1^{\otimes(j-1)}\otimes Q\otimes1^{\otimes(n-j)}\Big),

the operator in brackets being the tensor-product differential of [C07, §6.2], with the Koszul rule for odd operators on tensor factors: in $F(e+rQe,\dots)$ with $e$ even and $r$ an odd element of an auxiliary nilpotent ring [C07, Lemma 6.4.1, proof], the element $r$ passes through $F$.
Corollary 3.20 (Functionals at scale $\infty$).

Let $n\ge1$ and let $F$ be a continuous graded-symmetric $n$-linear functional on moment-free Schwartz sections with $F\circ\big(\sum_{j=1}^n1^{\otimes(j-1)}\otimes Q\otimes1^{\otimes(n-j)}\big)=0$. Then
F=\Big(F\circ\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n1^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes P(0,\infty)\star\otimes1^{\otimes(n-i)}\Big)\circ\Big(\sum_{j=1}^n1^{\otimes(j-1)}\otimes Q\otimes1^{\otimes(n-j)}\Big),

and the functional $F\circ\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n1^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes P(0,\infty)\star\otimes1^{\otimes(n-i)}$ is continuous, graded symmetric and of parity $|F|+1$; $F$ equals $(-1)^{|F|+1}$ times $Q$ of it. Hence the complex of continuous polynomial functionals on moment-free Schwartz sections, without constant term, is acyclic for $Q$: every $Q$-closed functional without constant term is $Q$-exact.
Proof.

By Theorem [3.19](#b-00485), $P(0,\infty)\star$ acts continuously on moment-free Schwartz sections, so the composite functional is continuous; averaging over the $n$ factors keeps it graded symmetric, and $P(0,\infty)\star$ is odd, which gives the parity. Odd operators acting on different tensor factors anticommute, so the graded commutator of $Q$ on the $j$-th factor with $P(0,\infty)\star$ on the $i$-th factor vanishes for $i\neq j$, and for $i=j$ it is the identity of the $i$-th factor by [(3.4)](#b-00487). Summing over $i,j$ and dividing by $n$, the graded commutator of the tensor-product differential with the averaged operator $\frac1n\sum_i1^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes P(0,\infty)\star\otimes1^{\otimes(n-i)}$ is $\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathrm{id}=\mathrm{id}$. Composing with $F$ and using $F\circ\big(\sum_j1^{\otimes(j-1)}\otimes Q\otimes1^{\otimes(n-j)}\big)=0$ gives the displayed identity, and the action of $Q$ on functionals of parity $|F|+1$ gives the last statement. ∎
Remark 3.21 (Where the content of an operator lies).

At scale $\infty$ the differential on functionals is $d_{CE}+Q$ ($\Delta_\infty=0$, $\{-,-\}_\infty=0$, Definition [3.15](#b-00457)). On moment-free Schwartz sections the cohomology of $Q$ on functionals without constant term is zero (Corollary [3.20](#b-00504)): every $Q$-closed functional is $Q$ of a nonlocal functional built with $P(0,\infty)\star$. On compactly supported sections $Q$ has nonzero classes, among them the zero-mode classes of Theorem [3.19](#b-00485), the pairings with polynomial zero modes of $Q$, such as $-\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(c^*,X)$ for a constant ghost $X$. The list of Theorem [3.19](#b-00485) is a list of examples: the slot of $A|_V$ contributes further classes. For $a,b\in V$ with $(a,b)=0$ and $a,b$ linearly independent, the one-form $e_0=(a,x)\,(b,-)$ satisfies $d^*e_0=-(a,b)=0$ and $d^*de_0=0$, hence $Qe_0=-\tfrac12d^*de_0=0$, while $de_0=(a,-)\wedge(b,-)\neq0$. The functional $e\mapsto\langle e_0,e\rangle$ is $Q$-closed; a $Q$-exact linear functional depends on the component of $e$ in the slot of $A^*|_V$ through its image under $d^*$ alone, which vanishes on $d^*\beta$ for every compactly supported two-form $\beta$, while $\langle e_0,d^*\beta\rangle$ is $\pm\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(de_0,\beta)$, nonzero for suitable $\beta$; so this class is nonzero. The zero-mode classes vanish on moment-free sections, sit at $p=0$, are independent of $\varepsilon$, and are finitely many in each polynomial degree and infinitely many in all; products of them give nonlinear classes. On moment-free Schwartz sections every $Q$-closed functional without constant term therefore defines the zero class, whatever functional $O(\varepsilon)$ it is obtained from. The content of an operator is the local functional $O(\varepsilon)$ at the UV end whose flow $O[\infty]$ to scale $\infty$ [CG2, Def 8.3.1.3] has an $\varepsilon\to0$ limit; both are defined in Chapter 5. This requirement fixes the singular part of $O(\varepsilon)$ uniquely; the finite part is the scheme freedom. Correspondingly, an equation expressing $Q\,O[\infty]$ as the scale-$\infty$ observable of a second local functional has content because that functional is local, and for an operator whose observable is a cocycle, $Q\,O[\infty]=0$ (Remark [5.6](#b-00927)), the anomalous dimension is read off in the cohomology of local functionals.
3.5 The graph expansion and the one-loop formula
Proposition 3.22 (Graph expansion).
For $J=\sum_{i\ge0}\hbar^iJ_i$ as in Definition [3.16](#b-00460),
W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J)=\sum_\gamma\hbar^{\,b_1(\gamma)+\sum_v\deg v}\,\frac{1}{|\operatorname{Aut}\gamma|}\,w_\gamma\qquad[\text{C07, §15.4}],

the sum over connected graphs $\gamma$ with legs, with vertex set $V(\gamma)$ and edge set $E(\gamma)$ [C07, §15.5] (these always carry the argument $\gamma$) and first Betti number $b_1(\gamma)=|E(\gamma)|-|V(\gamma)|+1$, each vertex $v$ labelled by a Taylor component of $J_{\deg v}$ (vertices of degree $0$ at least trivalent), each edge by $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$, each leg by an argument; $|\operatorname{Aut}\gamma|$ counts the automorphisms fixing the legs, and $w_\gamma$ is obtained from the full multilinear vertex functions, contracted along the edges and summed over all component labels. Edge rule: two contracted coordinate functionals, brought adjacent by Koszul reordering, are replaced by the component of $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ in the same order (Definition [3.10](#b-00427)). At order $\hbar^1$ either $b_1(\gamma)=1$ and all vertices have degree $0$, or $b_1(\gamma)=0$ and exactly one vertex has degree $1$, for instance a counterterm vertex.
Proof.

Write $\phi=P(\varepsilon,\infty)=\sum\phi^{\prime}\otimes\phi^{\prime\prime}$. Expanding the exponentials, a term of $e^{\hbar\partial_\phi}e^{J/\hbar}$ is a set of vertices, each a factor $\hbar^{\deg v-1}J_{\deg v}$, with $|E(\gamma)|$ pairs of half-edges contracted by $\hbar\partial_\phi$; the factor $\frac12$ in $\partial_\phi=\frac12\sum\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}}\partial_{\phi^{\prime}}$ [C07, §6.4] and the factorials of the exponentials combine to $1/|\operatorname{Aut}\gamma|$, and on two coordinate functionals $\partial_\phi$ returns the component of $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ in their order. The logarithm keeps the connected graphs, and the overall factor $\hbar$ gives the power
\hbar^{1+|E(\gamma)|-|V(\gamma)|+\sum_v\deg v}=\hbar^{b_1(\gamma)+\sum_v\deg v}.
The last statement is $b_1(\gamma)+\sum_v\deg v=1$. ∎

For the one-loop formula let $\mathscr E$ be a finite-dimensional super vector space, as when the manifold of [C07, §6.6, §10.1] is a point, and let $\phi=\sum\phi^{\prime}\otimes\phi^{\prime\prime}\in\mathrm{Sym}^2\mathscr E$ be even with complex coefficients [C07, §6.4]. Let $J$ be a quadratic functional on $\mathscr E$, even as a whole, whose coefficients lie in a supercommutative algebra: the complex numbers, or an auxiliary nilpotent ring with odd elements as in [C07, Lemma 6.4.1, proof]. The one-loop operator of $(\phi,J)$ is the linear map
e\mapsto\sum\phi^{\prime}\,(-1)^{|\phi^{\prime\prime}|}\,\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}}\partial_eJ ,

i.e. $\phi$ composed with the parity operator $(-1)^{|\cdot|}$ composed with the second derivative of $J$, the right-hand slot differentiated first, with the coefficients written to the right and extended linearly over them. $\mathrm{STr}$ is the supertrace on such linear maps [CG2, §13.7.2]: on the map $e\mapsto e_0\,\ell(e)$, with $e_0\in\mathscr E$ homogeneous and $\ell$ a linear functional with values in the coefficients, it is $(-1)^{|e_0|}\ell(e_0)$.
Proposition 3.23 (One-loop formula).
As formal power series in $J$,

\hbar\log\big(e^{\hbar\partial_\phi}e^{J/\hbar}\big)\Big|_{e=0}=\hbar\sum_{n\ge1}\frac1{2n}\,\mathrm{STr}\big((\text{one-loop operator})^n\big)=-\frac\hbar2\,\mathrm{STr}\log\big(1-\text{one-loop operator}\big). \tag{3.5}
The term $n=1$ is $\hbar\,\partial_\phi J$, and the term of order $n$ is the sum of the cycles with $n$ vertices, whose automorphism group has order $2n$.
Proof.

Two identities for an even quadratic functional $F$ with coefficients as above. The second derivative $\partial_e\partial_{e'}F$ is a coefficient of parity $|e|+|e'|$ with $\partial_e\partial_{e'}F=(-1)^{|e||e'|}\partial_{e'}\partial_eF$; since $\phi$ is even, $|\phi^{\prime}|=|\phi^{\prime\prime}|$ in every term.
First, $\tfrac12\mathrm{STr}$ of the one-loop operator of $F$ is $\partial_\phi F$: by the rank-one formula,

\tfrac12\mathrm{STr}=\tfrac12\sum(-1)^{|\phi^{\prime}|+|\phi^{\prime\prime}|}\,\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}}\partial_{\phi^{\prime}}F=\tfrac12\sum\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}}\partial_{\phi^{\prime}}F=\partial_\phi F .

Second, since $\partial_\phi$ is of order two, $\partial_\phi(F_1F_2)-(\partial_\phi F_1)F_2-F_1(\partial_\phi F_2)$ is the sum of the two terms with one derivative on each factor; for $F_1$ even, the graded symmetry $\sum\phi^{\prime}\otimes\phi^{\prime\prime}=\sum(-1)^{|\phi^{\prime}||\phi^{\prime\prime}|}\phi^{\prime\prime}\otimes\phi^{\prime}$ makes the two terms equal, so this sum is $\sum(\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}}F_1)(\partial_{\phi^{\prime}}F_2)$. It is a derivation in each argument; hence, by induction on $m$,
\partial_\phi(F^m)=m\,(\partial_\phi F)\,F^{m-1}+\tfrac12m(m-1)\,F^{m-2}\sum(\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}}F)(\partial_{\phi^{\prime}}F),
\partial_\phi e^{F/\hbar}=e^{F/\hbar}\Big(\hbar^{-1}\partial_\phi F+\tfrac12\hbar^{-2}\sum(\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}}F)(\partial_{\phi^{\prime}}F)\Big).

The one-loop operator of the quadratic functional $\tfrac12\sum(\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}}F)(\partial_{\phi^{\prime}}F)$ is the square of the one-loop operator of $F$. Indeed, the Leibniz rule for the linear functionals $\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}}F$ and $\partial_{\phi^{\prime}}F$ gives two terms for the second derivative, which coincide after the graded symmetry of $\phi$ and the exchange of the two coefficients, so that

\partial_e\partial_{e'}\Big(\tfrac12\sum(\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}}F)(\partial_{\phi^{\prime}}F)\Big)=\sum(-1)^{|e'||\phi^{\prime\prime}|}\,(\partial_e\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}}F)\,(\partial_{e'}\partial_{\phi^{\prime}}F).

Writing $\phi=\sum_k\phi^{\prime}_k\otimes\phi^{\prime\prime}_k=\sum_l\phi^{\prime}_l\otimes\phi^{\prime\prime}_l$ for two copies of the same sum, the one-loop operator of this functional sends $e$ to

\sum_{l,k}\phi^{\prime}_l(-1)^{|\phi^{\prime\prime}_l|}(-1)^{|e||\phi^{\prime\prime}_k|}(\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}_l}\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}_k}F)(\partial_e\partial_{\phi^{\prime}_k}F)=\sum_{l,k}\phi^{\prime}_l(-1)^{|\phi^{\prime\prime}_l|}(\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}_l}\partial_{\phi^{\prime}_k}F)(-1)^{|\phi^{\prime\prime}_k|}(\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}_k}\partial_eF),

where the graded symmetry of $\phi$ in the index $k$ contributes $(-1)^{|\phi^{\prime\prime}_k|}$ and $\partial_e\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}_k}F=(-1)^{|e||\phi^{\prime\prime}_k|}\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}_k}\partial_eF$; the right side is the one-loop operator of $F$ applied twice to $e$.
The flow in an auxiliary formal parameter $s$. Let $J_s$ be the quadratic functional determined, as a formal power series in $s$ and in $J$, by
\frac{d}{ds}J_s=\tfrac12\sum(\partial_{\phi^{\prime\prime}}J_s)(\partial_{\phi^{\prime}}J_s),\qquad J_0=J .

By the formula for $\partial_\phi e^{F/\hbar}$ with $F=J_s$, the functional $\exp\big(\int_0^s\partial_\phi J_{s^{\prime}}\,ds^{\prime}\big)e^{J_s/\hbar}$ satisfies $\frac{d}{ds}(\cdots)=\hbar\partial_\phi(\cdots)$, as does $e^{s\hbar\partial_\phi}e^{J/\hbar}$; both equal $e^{J/\hbar}$ at $s=0$, and this equation determines the coefficient of each power of $s$ from the previous one, so they coincide. At order $m$ in $J$ the powers $s^k$ that occur have $k\le m$, because $\partial_\phi$ lowers the polynomial degree by two and $J^m$ has degree $2m$; so $s=1$ may be substituted. At the origin $e^{J_1/\hbar}$ equals $1$, hence
\hbar\log\big(e^{\hbar\partial_\phi}e^{J/\hbar}\big)\Big|_{e=0}=\hbar\int_0^1\partial_\phi J_s\,ds .

The one-loop operator of $J_s$ depends linearly on $J_s$, so by the second identity its derivative in $s$ is its square; its value at $s=0$ is the one-loop operator of $J$, and the unique formal solution is $\sum_{n\ge1}s^{n-1}(\text{one-loop operator of }J)^n$. By the first identity,

which is [(3.5)](#b-00526), with $\mathrm{STr}\log(1-\text{one-loop operator})=-\sum_{n\ge1}\frac1n\mathrm{STr}\big((\text{one-loop operator})^n\big)$. The term $n=1$ is $\hbar\,\partial_\phi J$ by the first identity. In the graph expansion with vertices $J$ the graphs without legs and with bivalent vertices are the cycles, and a cycle with $n$ vertices has $2n$ automorphisms. ∎
Remark 3.24 (Use in the field theory).

For the one-loop part of $W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I)$ at a background field configuration, $J$ is the part of $I(\text{background}+\text{fluctuation})$ quadratic in the fluctuation, $\phi=P(\varepsilon,\infty)$, $\mathrm{STr}$ includes the trace over $\mathfrak g$ and the integration over positions, and expanding in the background produces the one-loop one-particle-irreducible graphs with their external legs; the parity operator and the supertrace produce the signs of fermion and ghost loops. When the background contains odd fields, multiplied by odd elements of an auxiliary nilpotent ring as in Definition [1.13](#b-00162), the coefficients of $J$ contain odd elements, and Proposition [3.23](#b-00524) applies with these coefficients.
4. Counterterms at one loop and the quantum master equation at the UV boundary

The one-loop counterterm, the analogue on $\mathbb R^4$ at order $\hbar$ of the counterterm of [C07, Thm B] (Remark [4.9](#b-00635)), is fixed by the requirement that the order-$\hbar$ part of the flow $W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon])$ have a limit as $\varepsilon\to0$ at generic leg momenta, and it is unique among the translation-invariant and $\mathfrak g$-invariant local functionals with coefficients in the span of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $\log\varepsilon$ (Propositions [4.8](#b-00628) and [4.10](#b-00637)). The regulator, however, cuts every edge at the Schwinger time $\varepsilon$ and breaks the gauge symmetry, so the one-loop counterterm contains the mass terms $\varepsilon^{-1}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(A,A)$, whose $Q$-variation is nonzero. Transported to the UV boundary by Theorem [3.17](#b-00464), the quantum master equation then fails by a finite local functional, and a finite local counterterm has to be chosen to remove it: this is the first renormalisation condition of the theory. This chapter computes $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ in every one-loop sector of superficial degree $\ge0$, identifies its $\log\varepsilon$ part as a rescaling of the fields with vanishing component along the coupling, and evaluates the master equation at the UV boundary in the sector with legs $(c,A|_V)$, where the first finite counterterm appears.
4.1 The one-loop counterterm and its boundary form

Throughout this chapter $\mathfrak g$ is simple. Then the Killing form $\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)$ is a multiple of the invariant pairing, and the ratio $\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)/(X,Y)$, for $X,Y\in\mathfrak g$ with $(X,Y)\neq0$, is a number independent of $X$ and $Y$. Every one-loop coefficient of this chapter is a rational multiple of
\frac{\hbar\,\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2\,(X,Y)},
except the coefficients of the fourth-order adjoint traces of the quartic graphs, which are rational multiples of $\hbar/16\pi^2$. The upper Schwinger limit is $\infty$ (Chapter 3).

The value of a translation-invariant functional with $k$ legs on plane waves $e^{i(p_j,x)}$, $j=1,\dots,k$, with fibre elements as in Definition [1.13](#b-00162), is $(2\pi)^4\delta(p_1+\dots+p_k)$ times a function of $(p_1,\dots,p_k)$ on the subspace where $p_1+\dots+p_k=0$; this function is its plane-wave value. Leg momenta are generic when every leg momentum is nonzero and no sum of the momenta of a nonempty proper subset of the legs vanishes. For $k=1$ the set of generic configurations is empty; for $k\ge2$ it is the complement of finitely many proper linear subspaces of the subspace $p_1+\dots+p_k=0$, an open dense subset. A functional depending on $\varepsilon$ has a limit as $\varepsilon\to0$ at generic leg momenta when the plane-wave values of its Taylor components converge as $\varepsilon\to0$ at every generic configuration of the leg momenta. Every limit of a flow in this chapter is a limit in this sense.
Definition 4.1 (One-loop counterterm).

For a connected one-particle-irreducible graph $\gamma$ with legs, $b_1(\gamma)=1$ and all vertices labelled by $I$ (Proposition [3.22](#b-00513)), let $w_\gamma(\varepsilon)$ be its value with every edge labelled by $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ [C07, §15.4]. Every vertex of $\gamma$ lies on its cycle and carries a leg, so at generic leg momenta the momenta of distinct edges of $\gamma$ differ, and by Lemma [4.6](#b-00594), as $\varepsilon\to0$, the plane-wave value of $w_\gamma(\varepsilon)$ is the sum of multiples of negative integer powers of $\varepsilon$, a multiple of $\log\varepsilon$, and a function of $\varepsilon$ with a limit; the first two are polynomials in the leg momenta, and $\mathrm{Sing}_\varepsilon w_\gamma(\varepsilon)$ denotes the local functional whose plane-wave value is their sum [CG2, §13.7.2]. The one-loop counterterm is
I^{CT}[\varepsilon]=\hbar\sum_\gamma\frac{1}{|\operatorname{Aut}\gamma|}\,\mathrm{Sing}_\varepsilon\,w_\gamma(\varepsilon), \tag{4.1}

the sum over the connected one-particle-irreducible graphs $\gamma$ with $b_1(\gamma)=1$ and at least two legs, modulo constants. Its coefficients lie in the span of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $\log\varepsilon$ (Proposition [4.20](#b-00732)), the one-loop part of the renormalisation scheme $\mathscr A_{<0}$ [C07, Def 1.4.1; CG2, §13.7.2].

The $\varepsilon$-dependence of a graph is carried by the lower ends of its Schwinger integrals. By [(3.2)](#b-00447), $\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}P(\varepsilon,\infty)=-L_\varepsilon$ with $L_\varepsilon=(Q^{GF}\otimes1)K_\varepsilon$.
Proposition 4.2 (Boundary form of the scale derivative).
Let $\gamma$ be a graph with edge set $E(\gamma)$ [C07, §15.5], and let $w_\gamma(\varepsilon)$ be its value with every edge labelled by $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$. Then

\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}w_\gamma(\varepsilon)=\sum_{e\in E(\gamma)}w_\gamma\big(\text{edge }e\text{ labelled by }-\varepsilon L_\varepsilon,\ \text{the other edges by }P(\varepsilon,\infty)\big). \tag{4.2}

In the Schwinger form $w_\gamma(\varepsilon)=\int_{[\varepsilon,\infty)^{E(\gamma)}}f_\gamma\prod_{e}dt_e$ of [C07, §15.5], with the edge $e$ carrying $L_{t_e}$, the $e$-th term of [(4.2)](#b-00563) is
-\varepsilon\int_{[\varepsilon,\infty)^{E(\gamma)\setminus\{e\}}}f_\gamma\big|_{t_e=\varepsilon}\prod_{e'\neq e}dt_{e'} .
Proof.
The value $w_\gamma$ is multilinear in the kernels labelling the edges, so the Leibniz rule gives
\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}w_\gamma=\sum_e w_\gamma\Big(\text{edge }e\text{ labelled by }\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}P(\varepsilon,\infty)\Big),

and $\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}P(\varepsilon,\infty)=-L_\varepsilon$ by [(3.2)](#b-00447). In the Schwinger form, $\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\int_\varepsilon^\infty(\cdots)\,dt_e=-(\cdots)|_{t_e=\varepsilon}$ for each edge. ∎
Corollary 4.3 (Singular part from the boundary).
At fixed leg momenta, if the right-hand side of [(4.2)](#b-00563) equals $-a\,\varepsilon^{-1}+b$ plus a term bounded by a multiple of $\varepsilon$, with $a$, $b$ independent of $\varepsilon$, then

w_\gamma(\varepsilon)=a\,\varepsilon^{-1}+b\log\varepsilon+(\text{a function of }\varepsilon\text{ with a limit}),\qquad \mathrm{Sing}_\varepsilon w_\gamma(\varepsilon)=a\,\varepsilon^{-1}+b\log\varepsilon .
Proof.

$\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\big(w_\gamma-a\varepsilon^{-1}-b\log\varepsilon\big)=\varepsilon^{-1}\big(\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}w_\gamma+a\varepsilon^{-1}-b\big)$ is $\varepsilon^{-1}$ times a term bounded by a multiple of $\varepsilon$, hence bounded near $\varepsilon=0$, so $w_\gamma-a\varepsilon^{-1}-b\log\varepsilon$ has a limit and differs from it by a term bounded by a multiple of $\varepsilon$. ∎

blocks.source: The singular coefficients of every graph are therefore computed from graphs with one edge pinned at $t=\varepsilon$. For one-loop graphs with at most two edges, the Schwinger integrals reduce to four elementary ones after a Gaussian integral over the loop momentum.
Lemma 4.4 (Gaussian integral over the loop momentum).
Let $t_1,t_2>0$, $p\in V$, and let the numerator be a polynomial function of $p_1\in V$ of degree at most two. Then

the positive Laplacian, minus the sum of the second derivatives along an orthonormal basis, being taken in the variable $p_1$. For one edge, $\int\frac{d^4p_1}{(2\pi)^4}e^{-t|p_1|^2}=(16\pi^2t^2)^{-1}$.
Proof.
Completing the square and integrating the Gaussian,

The normalised Gaussian average in the shifted variable has vanishing odd moments, and its second moment sends $(v,p_1)(v',p_1)$ to $(v,v')/(2(t_1+t_2))$ for $v,v'\in V$. A polynomial of degree at most two is its value at the centre plus a linear term plus its quadratic part; the average of the quadratic part is $\frac{1}{4(t_1+t_2)}$ times the sum of the second derivatives along an orthonormal basis, i.e. $-\frac{1}{4(t_1+t_2)}$ times the positive Laplacian of the numerator in $p_1$. ∎
Lemma 4.5 (Elementary Schwinger integrals).
For $p\neq0$, modulo functions of $\varepsilon$ with a limit as $\varepsilon\to0$ ($\mathscr A_{\ge0}$ of [C07, Def 1.4.1]),
Proof.

The integrands are symmetric in $t_1,t_2$, so by Proposition [4.2](#b-00561) each $\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}$ equals $-2\varepsilon$ times the integral over $t\in[\varepsilon,\infty)$ of the integrand at $t_1=\varepsilon$, $t_2=t$. On the pinned edge the exponent satisfies $0\le\frac{\varepsilon t|p|^2}{\varepsilon+t}\le\varepsilon|p|^2$, so $e^{-\varepsilon t|p|^2/(\varepsilon+t)}$ equals $1-\frac{\varepsilon t|p|^2}{\varepsilon+t}$ plus a remainder between $0$ and $\tfrac12\varepsilon^2|p|^4$, uniformly in $t$. Corollary [4.3](#b-00570) with $(a,b)$ equal to $(\tfrac14,\tfrac16|p|^2)$, $(0,-1)$, $(0,-\tfrac16)$ gives the three expansions. The one-edge integral is exact. ∎
Lemma 4.6 (Singular part of a one-loop graph).

Let $\gamma$ be a connected one-particle-irreducible graph with $b_1(\gamma)=1$, so that every vertex lies on the cycle and $|E(\gamma)|=|V(\gamma)|$. Let its vertex functions be polynomials in the momenta, up to a factor depending on the leg momenta alone (such as the Fourier transform of a four-form at minus the total leg momentum, Chapter 5), and let its numerator, the product of the vertex functions and of the polynomial factors of the edge components of $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ (Proposition [3.11](#b-00430)), be homogeneous in the loop momentum and the leg momenta; for vertices labelled by $I$ and legs in fixed slots this holds by Lemma [4.18](#b-00722). Its superficial degree is the degree of the numerator plus $4-2|E(\gamma)|$. Let the leg momenta be such that the momenta of any two distinct edges differ by a nonzero vector. Then, at these leg momenta and as $\varepsilon\to0$,
w_\gamma(\varepsilon)=\sum_{1\le k\le\frac12(\text{superficial degree})}\varepsilon^{-k}\,a_k+b\,\log\varepsilon+(\text{a function of }\varepsilon\text{ with a limit}),

where $a_k$ and $b$ are polynomials in the leg momenta, $a_k$ homogeneous of degree (superficial degree)$-2k$ and $b$ homogeneous of degree equal to the superficial degree, and $\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}$ of the function with a limit tends to $0$. In particular the sum of the terms with $\varepsilon^{-k}$ and $\log\varepsilon$ is the plane-wave value of a local functional, $\mathrm{Sing}_\varepsilon w_\gamma(\varepsilon)$, and it vanishes when the superficial degree is negative.
Proof.

Let the edge $e\in E(\gamma)$ carry the momentum $p_1-q_e$, with $p_1$ the loop momentum and $q_e$ a sum of leg momenta, so that $q_e\neq q_f$ for $e\neq f$. By Proposition [3.11](#b-00430), $w_\gamma(\varepsilon)$ is the integral over $p_1$, with the measure $d^4p_1/(2\pi)^4$, of the numerator times $\prod_ee^{-\varepsilon|p_1-q_e|^2}/|p_1-q_e|^2$, and $e^{-\varepsilon|k|^2}/|k|^2=\int_\varepsilon^\infty e^{-t|k|^2}dt$ introduces a Schwinger time $t_e$ for each edge. By Tonelli's theorem,

\int\frac{d^4p_1}{(2\pi)^4}\int_{[\varepsilon,\infty)^{E(\gamma)}}\big|\text{numerator}\big|\,e^{-\sum_et_e|p_1-q_e|^2}\prod_edt_e=\int\frac{d^4p_1}{(2\pi)^4}\,\big|\text{numerator}\big|\prod_e\frac{e^{-\varepsilon|p_1-q_e|^2}}{|p_1-q_e|^2},

and the right side is finite: the points $p_1=q_e$ are distinct, near each of them exactly one factor is singular, $|p_1-q_e|^{-2}$ being integrable near $p_1=q_e$ in four dimensions, and the Gaussian factors bound the polynomial numerator at large $|p_1|$. By Fubini's theorem, $w_\gamma(\varepsilon)$ is the integral over $t\in[\varepsilon,\infty)^{E(\gamma)}$ of the integral over $p_1$, with the measure $\prod_edt_e\,d^4p_1/(2\pi)^4$, of $\exp\big(-\sum_et_e|p_1-q_e|^2\big)$ times the numerator. Write $\tau=\sum_et_e$. Completing the square,
\sum_et_e|p_1-q_e|^2=\tau\Big|p_1-\sum_e\frac{t_e}{\tau}\,q_e\Big|^2+\tau\cdot\frac12\sum_{e,f}\frac{t_e}{\tau}\frac{t_f}{\tau}|q_e-q_f|^2 ,
and the Gaussian integral over $p_1$, with the moments of Lemma [4.4](#b-00577) (each contracted pair of loop momenta gives $(2\tau)^{-1}$ times the metric), gives

w_\gamma(\varepsilon)=\sum_{j\ge0}\int_{[\varepsilon,\infty)^{E(\gamma)}}\frac{(\text{numerator})_j}{16\pi^2\,\tau^{2+j}}\,\exp\Big(-\tau\cdot\frac12\sum_{e,f}\frac{t_e}{\tau}\frac{t_f}{\tau}|q_e-q_f|^2\Big)\prod_edt_e ,

where $(	ext{numerator})_j$, the part with $j$ contracted pairs, is a polynomial in the ratios $t_e/	au$ and the leg momenta, homogeneous of degree (degree of the numerator)$-2j$, and zero when $2j$ exceeds the degree of the numerator. Put $m_j=j+2-|E(\gamma)|$; then $(	ext{numerator})_j
eq0$ implies $2m_j\le$ (superficial degree). The ratios $t_e/	au$ range over the simplex $\sum_et_e/	au=1$, and $\prod_edt_e$ is $	au^{|E(\gamma)|-1}d	au$ times the Lebesgue measure of the simplex. Since $\sum_{e
eq f}t_et_f/	au^2=1-\sum_et_e^2/	au^2\ge1-\max_et_e/	au$, the factor multiplying $	au$ in the exponent is at least one half of the smallest of the numbers $|q_e-q_f|^2$, $e
eq f$, times $1-\max_et_e/	au$, and $	au(1-\max_et_e/	au)$ is the sum of the Schwinger times other than the largest.

The region $\tau\ge1$. The integrand of the $j$-th term is bounded by a multiple of $\tau^{-2-j}$ times the exponential of minus a positive multiple of the sum of the Schwinger times other than the largest. Integrating these times against the exponential, and the largest time, which is at least $\tau/|E(\gamma)|\ge1/|E(\gamma)|$, against $\tau^{-2-j}$, gives a bound independent of $\varepsilon$; by dominated convergence this part has a limit as $\varepsilon\to0$.

The region $\tau\le1$. If $m_j<0$, the integrand times $\tau^{|E(\gamma)|-1}$ is bounded by a multiple of $\tau^{-1-m_j}$, which is integrable, and the part has a limit. If $m_j\ge0$, expand the exponential to order $m_j$. The remainder is bounded by $1/(m_j+1)!$ times the $(m_j+1)$-th power of the exponent, so its contribution is bounded by a multiple of $\tau^{-2-j+m_j+1}\tau^{|E(\gamma)|-1}=\tau^0$ and has a limit. The term of order $i\le m_j$ is the integral, over the part of the simplex where $\min_et_e/\tau\ge\varepsilon$, of $(16\pi^2\,i!)^{-1}(\text{numerator})_j$ times the $i$-th power of minus the factor multiplying $\tau$ in the exponent, times

\int_{\varepsilon/\min_e(t_e/\tau)}^{1}\tau^{-1-(m_j-i)}\,d\tau=\begin{cases}\dfrac{\varepsilon^{-(m_j-i)}\big(\min_et_e/\tau\big)^{m_j-i}-1}{m_j-i}, & i<m_j,\\[2mm] \log\big(\min_et_e/\tau\big)-\log\varepsilon, & i=m_j.\end{cases}

The part of the simplex where $\min_et_e/\tau<\varepsilon$ has measure at most a multiple of $\varepsilon$, the function $(\min_et_e/\tau)^{m_j-i}$ is at most $\varepsilon^{m_j-i}$ there, and $\log(\min_et_e/\tau)$ is integrable on the simplex. Hence the term of order $i<m_j$ is $\varepsilon^{-(m_j-i)}$ times an integral over the whole simplex plus a function with a limit, and the term of order $m_j$ is $-\log\varepsilon$ times an integral over the whole simplex plus a function with a limit. These integrals over the simplex, of polynomials in the ratios and the leg momenta times $(\min_et_e/\tau)^{m_j-i}$, are polynomials in the leg momenta, homogeneous of degree (degree of the numerator)$-2j+2i$, which equals (superficial degree)$-2(m_j-i)$. Collecting the powers $k=m_j-i$ gives the expansion, with $1\le k\le m_j\le\frac12$(superficial degree); for negative superficial degree every $m_j$ with $(\text{numerator})_j\neq0$ is negative, and the singular part vanishes.

Finally, $\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}$ of the function with a limit tends to $0$. That function is the sum, over $j$ and $i$, of the following pieces; in the second and third item the simplex integrand of the term of order $i$ is $(16\pi^2\,i!)^{-1}(\text{numerator})_j$ times the $i$-th power of minus the factor multiplying $\tau$ in the exponent, a polynomial in the ratios and the leg momenta.

• The integrals over $t\in[\varepsilon,\infty)^{E(\gamma)}$ restricted to $\tau\ge1$, those restricted to $\tau\le1$ with $m_j<0$, and the remainders of the expansion of the exponential on $\tau\le1$. By Proposition [4.2](#b-00561), $\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}$ of each is minus $\varepsilon$ times its integrals over the faces $t_e=\varepsilon$; by the bounds above these face integrals are bounded on $\tau\ge1$ and bounded by a multiple of $1+|\log\varepsilon|$ on $\tau\le1$, the integrand being at most a multiple of $\tau^{1-|E(\gamma)|}$ there.

• For the term of order $i<m_j$, with $k=m_j-i$: $-k^{-1}\varepsilon^{-k}h(\varepsilon)$, where $h(\varepsilon)$ is the integral of the simplex integrand times $(\min_et_e/\tau)^k$ over the part of the simplex where $\min_et_e/\tau<\varepsilon$; and $-k^{-1}$ times the integral of the simplex integrand over the part where $\min_et_e/\tau\ge\varepsilon$, which comes from the $-1$ in the integral over $\tau$.

• For the term of order $m_j$: $h(\varepsilon)\log\varepsilon$, where $h(\varepsilon)$ is the integral of the simplex integrand over the part where $\min_et_e/\tau<\varepsilon$; and the integral of the simplex integrand times $\log(\min_et_e/\tau)$ over the part where $\min_et_e/\tau\ge\varepsilon$.

The part of the simplex where $\min_et_e/\tau<s$ is the union over $e$ of the parts where $t_e/\tau<s$. For a function continuous on the part where $\min_et_e/\tau\ge s_0$, its integral over the part where $\min_et_e/\tau\ge s$, $s\ge s_0$, is therefore differentiable in $s$, with derivative minus a sum of integrals of the function over the faces where $\min_et_e/\tau=s$, each face having $(|E(\gamma)|-2)$-dimensional measure at most that of a face of the simplex; the same holds, with the opposite sign and $s_0=0$, for the integral of a function continuous on the simplex over the part where $\min_et_e/\tau<s$, and that integral is at most the maximum of the absolute value of the function there times a multiple of $s$. In the second item the integrand of $h$ is at most a multiple of $\varepsilon^k$ where $\min_et_e/\tau<\varepsilon$, so $h(\varepsilon)$ and $\varepsilon\frac{dh}{d\varepsilon}$ are bounded by multiples of $\varepsilon^{k+1}$, and $\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\big(\varepsilon^{-k}h(\varepsilon)\big)=-k\varepsilon^{-k}h(\varepsilon)+\varepsilon^{1-k}\frac{dh}{d\varepsilon}$ is bounded by a multiple of $\varepsilon$; $\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}$ of the integral over the part where $\min_et_e/\tau\ge\varepsilon$ is bounded by a multiple of $\varepsilon$. In the third item $h(\varepsilon)$ and $\varepsilon\frac{dh}{d\varepsilon}$ are bounded by multiples of $\varepsilon$, so $\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\big(h(\varepsilon)\log\varepsilon\big)=h(\varepsilon)+\varepsilon\frac{dh}{d\varepsilon}\log\varepsilon$ is bounded by a multiple of $\varepsilon(1+|\log\varepsilon|)$; and $\log(\min_et_e/\tau)=\log\varepsilon$ on the faces where $\min_et_e/\tau=\varepsilon$, so $\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}$ of the integral over the part where $\min_et_e/\tau\ge\varepsilon$ is bounded by a multiple of $\varepsilon|\log\varepsilon|$. Every piece has $\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}$ tending to $0$. ∎
Lemma 4.7 (One-loop graphs as trees with a one-loop vertex).

Consider the graphs of Proposition [3.22](#b-00513), with labelled legs, whose vertices are labelled by Taylor components of $I$, except at most one vertex of valence at least $1$, the marked vertex, labelled by a Taylor component of a further functional (in Chapter 5, the operator $O$). For a connected graph $\Gamma$ with $b_1(\Gamma)=1$, let $\gamma$ be its cycle together with the vertices on the cycle, the remaining half-edges at these vertices being the legs of $\gamma$, and let $T$ be the tree obtained from $\Gamma$ by contracting $\gamma$ to one vertex $s$, whose half-edges are the legs of $\gamma$.

• $\gamma$ is connected and one-particle-irreducible with $b_1(\gamma)=1$. The automorphisms of $T$ fixing the legs are the identity, and so are those of every tree with the given legs whose vertices are labelled as above except one distinguished vertex $s$. Restriction to $\gamma$ is a bijection from the automorphisms of $\Gamma$ fixing the legs to the automorphisms of $\gamma$ fixing the legs of $\gamma$. The value $w_\Gamma$ is $w_T$ with $s$ labelled by the multilinear form $w_\gamma$ in the half-edges of $s$.

• The sum of $w_\Gamma/|\operatorname{Aut}\Gamma|$ over the connected graphs $\Gamma$ with $b_1(\Gamma)=1$ and the given legs equals the sum of $w_T/|\operatorname{Aut}T|=w_T$ over the trees $T$ with the given legs and one vertex $s$, labelled by the Taylor component, with legs the half-edges of $s$, of the sum of $w_\gamma/|\operatorname{Aut}\gamma|$ over the connected one-particle-irreducible graphs $\gamma$ with $b_1(\gamma)=1$.

• A connected one-particle-irreducible graph with $b_1=1$, one leg and all vertices labelled by $I$ is a cubic vertex of $I$ with one edge from the vertex to itself, and its value is $0$ before any integration over positions or momenta.
Proof.

First item. A connected graph with $b_1=1$ contains exactly one cycle. Every vertex of $\gamma$ lies on it, so removing an edge of $\gamma$ leaves $\gamma$ connected, and $b_1(\gamma)=|E(\gamma)|-|V(\gamma)|+1=1$. Contracting the cycle lowers $b_1$ by one, so $T$ is a tree.

Let $T$ be such a tree, with distinguished vertex $s$. An automorphism $\alpha$ of $T$ fixing the legs preserves the labels of the vertices, so it fixes $s$ and the marked vertex. For a vertex $v\neq s$, the vertices beyond $v$ are $v$ and the vertices separated from $s$ by $v$. A vertex beyond $v$ at maximal distance from $s$ has one half-edge towards $s$ and its other half-edges are legs; if it is labelled by $I$ it has at least two legs. Hence the vertices beyond $v$ carry a leg or include the marked vertex. Let $v^{\prime}\neq v$ be a second vertex different from $s$, the two being exchanged if $v$ lies beyond $v^{\prime}$. If $v^{\prime}$ lies beyond $v$ and $v$ is labelled by $I$, then $v$ has, besides its half-edges towards $s$ and towards $v^{\prime}$, a further half-edge, which is a leg or leads to vertices beyond $v$ and not beyond $v^{\prime}$ that carry a leg or include the marked vertex; if $v^{\prime}$ lies beyond $v$ and $v$ is the marked vertex, the vertices beyond $v$ include the marked vertex and those beyond $v^{\prime}$ exclude it; if neither lies beyond the other, the two sets of vertices beyond them are disjoint, and each carries a leg or includes the marked vertex. In every case $v$ and $v^{\prime}$ differ in the set of legs carried by the vertices beyond them or in whether these include the marked vertex. Both data are preserved by $\alpha$, so $\alpha$ fixes every vertex. A tree has no two edges with the same ends and no edge from a vertex to itself, so $\alpha$ fixes every edge, and, with the legs, every half-edge.

An automorphism of $\Gamma$ fixing the legs maps the cycle to itself and therefore induces an automorphism of $T$ fixing the legs, which is the identity. It fixes every vertex outside the cycle and every half-edge outside the edges of the cycle, the legs of $\gamma$ included, so it restricts to an automorphism of $\gamma$ fixing the legs of $\gamma$, and this restriction determines it. Conversely, an automorphism of $\gamma$ fixing its legs extends by the identity to an automorphism of $\Gamma$ fixing the legs.

The value $w_\Gamma$ is the contraction of the tensor product of the vertex functions along the edges of $\Gamma$, with the edge rule of Proposition [3.22](#b-00513). The contractions along different edges commute [C07, §6.4], so contracting the edges of the cycle first gives $w_\gamma$, a multilinear form in the half-edges of $s$, and the remaining contractions give $w_T$ with $s$ labelled by $w_\gamma$.

Second item. By the first item the half-edges of $s$ are determined by $T$ and its legs, and $\Gamma\mapsto(T,\gamma)$, with the legs of $\gamma$ identified with the half-edges of $s$, is a bijection from the isomorphism classes of connected graphs with $b_1=1$ and the given legs to the pairs consisting of an isomorphism class of trees $T$ with the given legs and a vertex $s$, and an isomorphism class of connected one-particle-irreducible graphs $\gamma$ with $b_1(\gamma)=1$ whose legs are the half-edges of $s$; the inverse glues $\gamma$ into $T$ in place of $s$. With $|\operatorname{Aut}\Gamma|=|\operatorname{Aut}\gamma|$, $|\operatorname{Aut}T|=1$ and the linearity of $w_T$ in the label of $s$,

\sum_\Gamma\frac{w_\Gamma}{|\operatorname{Aut}\Gamma|}=\sum_T\sum_\gamma\frac{1}{|\operatorname{Aut}\gamma|}\,w_T\big(s\text{ labelled by }w_\gamma\big)=\sum_T\frac{1}{|\operatorname{Aut}T|}\,w_T\Big(s\text{ labelled by }\sum_\gamma\frac{w_\gamma}{|\operatorname{Aut}\gamma|}\Big).

Third item. A cycle with $n$ vertices of valence at least three has at least $n$ legs, so one leg forces $n=1$ and a cubic vertex, two of whose slots are joined by the edge. By Definition [1.13](#b-00162), every cubic vertex function of $I$, namely $A\,A\,A$ (which contains $(A|_V)^3$ and $A|_V(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})^2$), $\lambda\,\lambda\,A$, $A\,c\,A^*$, $c\,\lambda\,\lambda^*$ and $c\,c\,c^*$, is the form $(X_1,[X_2,X_3])$ in the $\mathfrak g$-factors $X_1,X_2,X_3$ of its three legs, up to sign, times a factor independent of them; by the invariance of $(-,-)$ and the antisymmetry of the bracket, $(X_1,[X_2,X_3])$ is totally antisymmetric. The $\mathfrak g$-factor of every component of $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ is a multiple of $(-,-)^{-1}$ (Proposition [3.11](#b-00430)), which is symmetric. The contraction of two arguments of a totally antisymmetric form with a symmetric tensor is $0$, so the vertex with two of its slots joined is the zero functional, before any integration. ∎
Proposition 4.8 (Existence of the limit).
The order-$\hbar$ part of $W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon])$ has a limit as $\varepsilon\to0$ at generic leg momenta.
Proof.

By Proposition [3.22](#b-00513) with $J=I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$, the order-$\hbar$ part is $\hbar$ times the sum of $w_\Gamma/|\operatorname{Aut}\Gamma|$ over the connected graphs $\Gamma$ with $b_1(\Gamma)=1$ and vertices labelled by $I$, plus $\hbar$ times the sum of $w_T/|\operatorname{Aut}T|$ over the trees $T$ with one vertex $s$ labelled by a Taylor component of $-\hbar^{-1}I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ and the other vertices labelled by $I$. By Lemma [4.7](#b-00615) (without marked vertex), $|\operatorname{Aut}T|=1$ for these trees, and the first sum is the sum over the same trees of $w_T$ with $s$ labelled by the sum of $w_\gamma/|\operatorname{Aut}\gamma|$ over the connected one-particle-irreducible graphs $\gamma$ with $b_1(\gamma)=1$. A cycle of vertices of valence at least three carries legs, so every such $\gamma$ has legs; those with one leg have value $0$ (Lemma [4.7](#b-00615)), and $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ has no Taylor component with one leg (Definition [4.1](#b-00556)). By [(4.1)](#b-00558), the order-$\hbar$ part is therefore $\hbar$ times the sum over the trees $T$ whose vertex $s$ has at least two half-edges of $w_T$ with $s$ labelled by
\sum_\gamma\frac{1}{|\operatorname{Aut}\gamma|}\Big(w_\gamma(\varepsilon)-\mathrm{Sing}_\varepsilon w_\gamma(\varepsilon)\Big),

the sum over the $\gamma$ whose legs are the half-edges of $s$. For a fixed number of legs this sum is finite: a tree with $r$ vertices labelled by $I$ and a vertex $s$ with $m$ half-edges has $r$ edges and at least $3r+m-2r=r+m$ legs, and a cycle with $m$ legs has at most $m$ vertices.

Fix generic leg momenta. Each edge of $T$ separates $T$ into two parts, and each part carries a leg: in the part without $s$, a vertex at maximal distance from $s$ carries at least two legs; in the part with $s$, the vertex $s$ has, besides the half-edge on the path from $s$ to the edge, a further half-edge, which is a leg or leads to vertices separated from $s$ and from the edge, among which a vertex at maximal distance from $s$ carries at least two legs. Hence the edge carries the sum of the momenta of a nonempty proper subset of the legs, a nonzero momentum $k$, and its edge factor, a polynomial times $e^{-\varepsilon|k|^2}/|k|^2$ (Proposition [3.11](#b-00430)), converges to the polynomial times $|k|^{-2}$. The half-edges of $s$ carry the sums of the momenta of disjoint nonempty sets of legs, one set for each half-edge. Two distinct edges of the cycle of $\gamma$ cut it into two arcs, each containing a vertex, and every vertex of $\gamma$ carries a leg of $\gamma$; the momenta of the two edges differ by the sum of the momenta entering $\gamma$ along one arc, the sum of the momenta of a nonempty proper subset of the legs of $T$, which is nonzero. By Lemma [4.6](#b-00594), with the homogeneity of Lemma [4.18](#b-00722), the plane-wave value of $w_\gamma(\varepsilon)-\mathrm{Sing}_\varepsilon w_\gamma(\varepsilon)$ at these momenta has a limit as $\varepsilon\to0$. The plane-wave value of $w_T$ is the sum, over the components of the internal slots, of the products of the vertex functions of $T$, of its edge factors and of this value, a finite sum of products of functions of $\varepsilon$ with limits. ∎
Remark 4.9 (Relation with Theorem B).

[C07, Thm B] constructs, on a compact manifold with a finite upper scale, a counterterm at all orders in $\hbar$, unique among the local functionals with coefficients in $\mathscr A_{<0}$, for which the flow of the interaction minus the counterterm has a limit as $\varepsilon\to0$ as a functional; at one loop, its part with $k$ legs is the singular part of the order-$\hbar$, $k$-leg part of the flow of the interaction minus the counterterms with fewer legs, and it is independent of the upper scale [C07, §1.5]. Definition [4.1](#b-00556) and Propositions [4.8](#b-00628) and [4.10](#b-00637) give its analogue on $\mathbb R^4$ with upper scale $\infty$, for the even, local, at least cubic interaction $I$ of [(1.3)](#b-00159), in the following scope: the order is $\hbar$; the singular parts are computed graph by graph on the one-particle-irreducible graphs, and the one-particle-reducible graphs carry them through their cycles (Lemma [4.7](#b-00615)); the limit is the limit of plane-wave values at generic leg momenta; and uniqueness holds among the translation-invariant and $\mathfrak g$-invariant local functionals whose coefficients lie in a space of functions of $\varepsilon$ containing $\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $\log\varepsilon$ in which every function with a limit as $\varepsilon\to0$ is zero.
Proposition 4.10 (Uniqueness of the one-loop counterterm).

Let $I^{\prime}$ be a local functional of order $\hbar$, without constant term, invariant under translations and under the adjoint action of $\mathfrak g$, whose coefficients lie in a space of functions of $\varepsilon$ containing $\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $\log\varepsilon$ in which every function with a limit as $\varepsilon\to0$ is zero, for instance the span of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $\log\varepsilon$, or a complement $\mathscr A_{<0}$ of $\mathscr A_{\ge0}$ containing them [C07, Def 1.4.1]. If the order-$\hbar$ part of $W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I-I^{\prime})$ has a limit as $\varepsilon\to0$ at generic leg momenta, then $I^{\prime}=I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$.
Proof.

The vertex functions of $I$ and the components of $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ are translation invariant, and their $\mathfrak g$-factors are built from the bracket, $(-,-)$ and $(-,-)^{-1}$; so $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$, and with it the difference $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]-I^{\prime}$, is invariant under translations and under the adjoint action of $\mathfrak g$, with coefficients in the given space of functions. A translation-invariant local functional with one leg is, modulo total derivatives, the integral of a constant linear form on the fibre of the bundle of fields. The fibre is $\mathfrak g$ tensored with a representation of $\mathrm{Spin}(4,\mathbb C)\times\mathrm{Spin}(6,\mathbb C)$ (Chapter 1), so a $\mathfrak g$-invariant linear form on it lies in the tensor product of the invariant linear forms on $\mathfrak g$ with the dual of that representation; the invariant linear forms on $\mathfrak g$ are, through $(-,-)$, the centre of $\mathfrak g$, which is $0$ for $\mathfrak g$ simple. Hence the difference has no Taylor component with one leg, and by hypothesis none without legs.

The order-$\hbar$ parts of $W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I-I^{\prime})$ and $W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon])$ differ by $\hbar$ times the sum of the trees with one vertex labelled by a Taylor component of $\hbar^{-1}(I^{CT}[\varepsilon]-I^{\prime})$ and all other vertices labelled by $I$ (Proposition [3.22](#b-00513)). That vertex has at least two half-edges, so, as in the proof of Proposition [4.8](#b-00628), every edge of such a tree carries a nonzero momentum at generic leg momenta. By the hypothesis and Proposition [4.8](#b-00628), the sum of the trees has a limit at generic leg momenta. Suppose the difference is nonzero, and let $k\ge2$ be the smallest number of legs of its nonzero Taylor components. A tree with $r\ge1$ vertices labelled by $I$, each with at least three half-edges, has $r$ edges, and its vertex labelled by the difference has at least $k$ half-edges, so it has at least $k+3r-2r=k+r$ legs; the $k$-leg part of the sum of the trees is therefore the $k$-leg Taylor component of $\hbar^{-1}(I^{CT}[\varepsilon]-I^{\prime})$ itself, which then has a limit at generic leg momenta. Its plane-wave value is a finite sum of products of linearly independent coefficient functions of $\varepsilon$ with polynomials in $(p_1,\dots,p_k)$ on the subspace where $p_1+\dots+p_k=0$. At a generic configuration this sum is a function of $\varepsilon$ in the given space with a limit, hence zero, and by linear independence every polynomial vanishes there. The generic configurations are dense in the subspace, so the polynomials vanish on it. A polynomial vanishing on that subspace is a combination of the components of $p_1+\dots+p_k$ with polynomial coefficients, the plane-wave value of a total derivative; so the $k$-leg component is zero, a contradiction. ∎

4.3 Cubic and quartic graphs

The cubic and quartic parts of $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ are organised by the Weyl weights of Example [2.13](#b-00317): $A$ has weight $1$, $\lambda$ weight $\tfrac32$, $c$ weight $0$, and the antifields $A^*,\lambda^*,c^*$ the complementary weights $3,\tfrac52,4$, so that each pairing of a field with its antifield has weight $4$. The weight of a local functional $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(\cdots)$ is the sum of the weights of its fields plus the number of its derivatives, and every term of $S$ has weight $4$. The superficial degree of a graph is $4$ minus the sum of the weights of its legs: $2$ for $(A,A)$, $1$ for $(\lambda,\lambda)$, $(c,A^*)$, $(A|_V,A|_V,A|_V)$, $(A|_V,A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp},A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$, and $0$ for the other cubic and the quartic leg sets below.
Lemma 4.18 (Weights of the singular coefficients).

Let $\gamma$ be a one-loop one-particle-irreducible graph with vertices labelled by $I$. Its superficial degree in the sense of Lemma [4.6](#b-00594) is $4$ minus the sum of the weights of its legs. The coefficient of $\varepsilon^{-k}$ in its singular part is a local functional of weight $4-2k$, and the coefficient of $\log\varepsilon$ a local functional of weight $4$; in particular the coefficient of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ has weight $2$.
Proof.

In momentum space, a vertex with fields of total weight $4-k$ is a polynomial of degree $k$ in the momenta, since every term of $S$ has weight $4$; an edge component of $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ between slots of total weight $2+k$ is a polynomial of degree $k$ times $\int_\varepsilon^\infty e^{-t_e|\text{momentum}|^2}dt_e$ (Proposition [3.11](#b-00430): degree $0$ for $A\otimes A$, $1$ for $c\otimes A^*$ and $\lambda\otimes\lambda$). Each internal half-edge contributes its weight once to a vertex and once to an edge, so, for legs in fixed slots and every assignment of slots to the internal half-edges, the numerator of $\gamma$ is homogeneous of degree $4|V(\gamma)|-2|E(\gamma)|$ minus the sum of the weights of the legs, in the loop momentum $p_1$ and the leg momenta, which is the homogeneity required in Lemma [4.6](#b-00594); with $|E(\gamma)|=|V(\gamma)|$ at one loop, its degree plus $4-2|E(\gamma)|$ is $4$ minus the sum of the weights of the legs. By Lemma [4.6](#b-00594) the coefficient of $\varepsilon^{-k}$ is a polynomial in the leg momenta, homogeneous of degree (superficial degree)$-2k$, and that of $\log\varepsilon$ is homogeneous of degree equal to the superficial degree. The weight of such a local coefficient is the sum of the leg weights, $4-$(superficial degree), plus its degree in the momenta, which gives $4-2k$ and $4$. ∎
Lemma 4.19 (Local functionals of weight at most four).

Let a local functional of degree $0$, without constant term, have weight at most $4$ and be invariant under $\mathrm{Spin}(4,\mathbb C)\times\mathrm{Spin}(6,\mathbb C)$ and the adjoint action of $\mathfrak g$. If it is even, it is a linear combination of: in weight $2$, $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(A|_V,A|_V)$ and $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp},A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$; in weight $4$, functionals whose monomials have one of the field contents
In weights $1$ and $3$ there are none.
Proof.

As functionals, $c$ has degree $+1$, $A^*$ and $\lambda^*$ degree $-1$, $c^*$ degree $-2$, and $A,\lambda$ degree $0$ (Chapter 1). Degree $0$ requires the number of $c$ to equal the number of $A^*$ and $\lambda^*$ plus twice the number of $c^*$, and weight at most $4$ allows at most one antifield. With $c^*$ (weight $4$): $c\,c\,c^*$. With $A^*$ (weight $3$): one $c$ and weight at most $1$ more, i.e. $c\,A^*$ with one derivative or $c\,A\,A^*$; invariance pairs $A^*|_V$ with the derivative or with $A|_V$, and $A^*|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ with $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$. With $\lambda^*$ (weight $\tfrac52$): one $c$ and, by $\mathrm{Spin}(4,\mathbb C)$, one spinor $\lambda$. Without antifields there is no $c$; the monomials are built from $A$, $\lambda$ and derivatives, with an even number of spinors. $\mathrm{Spin}(6,\mathbb C)$ admits invariants of an even number of vectors of $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ (the invariant volume form of $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ needs six) and $\mathrm{Spin}(4,\mathbb C)$ of an even number of vector indices from $A|_V$ and the derivatives. In weight $2$ this leaves $(A|_V)^2$, $(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})^2$; in weight $4$ the listed contents, a single $A$ with three derivatives being a total derivative; in weight $1$ the single $A$, without invariant; in weight $3$ the contents $A^3$, $A\,A$ with one derivative, $c\,A^*$, each with an odd number of vector indices of $V$ or of $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$, and $\lambda\lambda$, whose components lie in $S_+\otimes S_-$ (a vector of $V$) or in $W\otimes W$, $W^*\otimes W^*$ (without $SL(4,\mathbb C)$-invariant); all of these have vanishing invariants. ∎
Proposition 4.20 (Structure of the one-loop counterterm).

$I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ is the sum of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ times the mass term of Theorem [4.16](#b-00707) and $\log\varepsilon$ times a local functional of weight $4$ with the field contents of Lemma [4.19](#b-00726). Its $\log\varepsilon$ part is therefore determined by the one-particle-irreducible one-loop graphs with the leg sets $(A|_V,A|_V)$, $(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp},A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$, $(\lambda,\lambda)$, $(c,A^*|_V)$, the eight cubic sets $(A|_V,A|_V,A|_V)$, $(A|_V,A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp},A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$, $(\lambda,\lambda,A|_V)$, $(\lambda,\lambda,A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$, $(c,A|_V,A^*|_V)$, $(c,A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp},A^*|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$, $(c,\lambda,\lambda^*)$, $(c,c,c^*)$, and the three quartic sets $(A|_V)^4$, $(A|_V)^2(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})^2$, $(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})^4$.
Proof.

By Lemmas [4.6](#b-00594) and [4.18](#b-00722), the singular part of a one-particle-irreducible one-loop graph with vertices labelled by $I$ consists of $\varepsilon^{-k}$ times a local functional of weight $4-2k$, $1\le k\le\frac12(\text{superficial degree})$, and $\log\varepsilon$ times a local functional of weight $4$, and it vanishes when the superficial degree is negative. The slots of every vertex of $I$ have degrees adding to $0$, and so have the two slots joined by every nonzero component of $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ (Proposition [3.11](#b-00430): $A\otimes A$, $c\otimes A^*|_V$, $A^*|_V\otimes c$, $\lambda\otimes\lambda$); hence the legs of every graph have degrees adding to $0$. With the degrees of the proof of Lemma [4.19](#b-00726), a set of $n$ legs with degrees adding to $0$ has weight at least $n$: every leg other than $c$ has weight at least $1$, every $c$ has weight $0$ and degree $+1$, and the antifields exceed weight $1$ by $\tfrac32$ per unit of negative degree or more ($A^*$: $3=1+2$, $\lambda^*$: $\tfrac52=1+\tfrac32$, $c^*$: $4=1+\tfrac32\cdot2$), so the weight is at least $n-(\text{number of }c)+\tfrac32(\text{number of }c)\ge n$. The graphs with one leg have value $0$ (Lemma [4.7](#b-00615)). Hence the superficial degree, $4$ minus the weight of the legs, is at most $2$, and negative for five or more legs; by Lemma [4.6](#b-00594) no power $\varepsilon^{-k}$ with $k\ge2$ occurs, and the coefficient of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ has weight $2$. $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ is invariant under $\mathrm{Spin}(4,\mathbb C)\times\mathrm{Spin}(6,\mathbb C)$ and the adjoint action of $\mathfrak g$ (proof of Theorem [4.16](#b-00707)), so by Lemma [4.19](#b-00726) the coefficient of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ is a combination of the two mass terms, computed in Theorem [4.16](#b-00707), and the coefficient of $\log\varepsilon$ has the listed contents. ∎
4.3.1 Cubic graphs

Every cubic graph below has vanishing coefficient of $\varepsilon^{-1}$, in accordance with Lemma [4.18](#b-00722). Its $\log\varepsilon$ coefficient, as a multilinear form in the three legs, is a rational multiple of the tree vertex function of Definition [1.13](#b-00162) with the same legs; the tables give these multiples, in units of $\hbar\,\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)/(16\pi^2(X,Y))$. The tree vertices are: the $(A|_V)^3$ and $A|_V(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})^2$ parts of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,\big(-\tfrac12(dA,\tfrac12[A\wedge A])\big)$; the $A|_V$ and $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ parts of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,\tfrac12(\lambda,({\not d}_A-{\not d})\lambda)$; the $A|_V$ and $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ parts of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,([A,c],A^*)$; $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,([c,\lambda],\lambda^*)$; $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,\tfrac12([c,c],c^*)$.

4.3.2 Quartic graphs

For the quartic sets leg $j\in\{1,2,3,4\}$ carries a decomposable fibre element $(v_j,-)\otimes X_j$ with $X_j\in\mathfrak g$, $v_j\in V$ for a leg $A|_V$ and $v_j\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ for a leg $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$; in the set $(A|_V)^2(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})^2$ legs $1,2$ are $A|_V$ and legs $3,4$ are $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$. A multilinear form is determined by its values on such legs, and by Lemma [4.18](#b-00722) the $\log\varepsilon$ coefficients are independent of the momenta. They are written in the basis of products of a colour factor and a Lorentz factor:

• colour factors: the pairing $([X_1,X_2],[X_3,X_4])$ of the bracket of the colour elements of legs $1,2$ with the bracket of those of legs $3,4$; the pairing $([X_1,X_4],[X_2,X_3])$; and the averaged trace $\tfrac1{24}\sum_{\text{orderings}}\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_{X_1}\mathrm{ad}_{X_2}\mathrm{ad}_{X_3}\mathrm{ad}_{X_4})$, the fourth-order adjoint trace averaged over the $24$ orderings of $X_1,\dots,X_4$. The third pairing $([X_1,X_3],[X_2,X_4])$ is the sum of the first two, by the Jacobi identity and the invariance of $(-,-)$.
• Lorentz factors: $(v_1,v_2)(v_3,v_4)$, $(v_1,v_3)(v_2,v_4)$, $(v_1,v_4)(v_2,v_3)$, products of metric pairings.

The two bracket pairings carry the unit $\hbar\,\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)/(16\pi^2(X,Y))$, the averaged trace the unit $\hbar/16\pi^2$. On such legs, by the Hodge normalisation of Definition [1.8](#b-00106),

4.3.3 The logarithmic part as a rescaling of the fields

Write $\int(A,A^*)$, $\int(\lambda^*,\lambda)$, $\int(c^*,c)$ for the local functionals $e\mapsto\langle e_A,e_{A^*}\rangle$, $\langle e_{\lambda^*},e_\lambda\rangle$, $\langle e_{c^*},e_c\rangle$, the pairing of Definition [1.5](#b-00091) applied to the components of the field $e$ in the two slots of a pair, the even member first; the first uses all ten components of $A$. For a monomial in the fields, let $n_A,n_{A^*},n_\lambda,n_{\lambda^*},n_c,n_{c^*}$ denote the numbers of its factors of each kind.
Lemma 4.21 (The bracket as a field count).
For every monomial $F$ in the fields,
\Big\{\int(A,A^*),F\Big\}=(n_A-n_{A^*})F,\qquad \Big\{\int(\lambda^*,\lambda),F\Big\}=(n_{\lambda^*}-n_\lambda)F,\qquad \Big\{\int(c^*,c),F\Big\}=(n_{c^*}-n_c)F .
Hence, on every monomial of $S$,
\Big\{2\int(A,A^*)-4\int(\lambda^*,\lambda)-\int(c^*,c),\,F\Big\}=\big(2(n_A-n_{A^*})+4(n_\lambda-n_{\lambda^*})+(n_c-n_{c^*})\big)F .
Proof.

By Definition [1.6](#b-00095), the kernel $K_0$ pairs each even member $A,\lambda^*,c^*$ with its odd partner $A^*,\lambda,c$ with the coefficient $-\delta(x-y)$ times the inverse fibre pairing, which is the structure $K_0=-\sum(x_i\otimes\xi_i+\xi_i\otimes x_i)$, $\Delta_0=\sum\partial_{x_i}\partial_{\xi_i}$ of [C07, §10.1] for the manifold a point, in the notation of loc. cit.: $x_i$ an even coordinate and $\xi_i$ its odd partner, applied pointwise at each position. For one pair, $x_i\xi_i$ is odd, and

The bracket with a fixed functional is a derivation, because $\Delta_0$ is a second-order operator, so $\{x_i\xi_i,-\}=x_i\partial_{x_i}-\xi_i\partial_{\xi_i}$ counts $x_i$ minus $\xi_i$. The three functionals of the lemma are the sums of $x_i\xi_i$ over the components, with $x_i$ the even member, which gives the three identities; the combination follows by linearity. ∎
Theorem 4.22 (The logarithmic part of the one-loop counterterm).
The $\log\varepsilon$ part of $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ is
\frac{\hbar\,\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\,\log\varepsilon\,\big(Q+\{I,-\}\big)\Big(2\int(A,A^*)-4\int(\lambda^*,\lambda)-\int(c^*,c)\Big). \tag{4.6}

Equivalently, it multiplies each monomial of $S$ by $2(n_A-n_{A^*})+4(n_\lambda-n_{\lambda^*})+(n_c-n_{c^*})$: the bracket acts as a weighted field count with weights $2$ for $A$, $4$ for $\lambda$, $1$ for $c$, and the opposite weights for the antifields.
Proof.
The functional $2\int(A,A^*)-4\int(\lambda^*,\lambda)-\int(c^*,c)$ is odd. By Proposition [1.11](#b-00135), $Q$ applied to it equals its bracket with $\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle$, so
by the graded symmetry of Definition [1.6](#b-00095), $S$ being even. By Lemma [4.21](#b-00796), this bracket multiplies the terms of $S$ by

These are the computed multiples: the quadratic ones by Theorem [4.16](#b-00707) and Remark [4.17](#b-00716) (with the coefficient $0$ of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V)$, absent from $S$), the cubic ones $6,6,10,10,1,1,1,1$ by the totals of the eight cubic tables, and the quartic ones $8,8,8$ by the totals of the three quartic tables. In the cubic and quartic sets the computed coefficient equals the multiple of the tree vertex as a multilinear form, including the two chirality structures of $(\lambda,\lambda,A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$ and of $(c,\lambda,\lambda^*)$. By Proposition [4.20](#b-00732) these leg sets carry the whole $\log\varepsilon$ part of $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$, so the two local functionals coincide. ∎
Corollary 4.23 (The coupling counterterm vanishes at one loop).

Suppose the $\log\varepsilon$ part of $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ is written as $\frac{\hbar\,\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\log\varepsilon$ times the sum of $\{S,-\}$ of an element of the span of $\int(A|_V,A^*|_V)$, $\int(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp},A^*|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$, $\int(c^*,c)$ and the two chiral parts of $\int(\lambda^*,\lambda)$, and a multiple of $S$. Then the multiple of $S$ is $0$ and the element is $2\int(A,A^*)-4\int(\lambda^*,\lambda)-\int(c^*,c)$. The same holds with $S$ replaced by its classical part, the terms of $S$ without antifields. Since the coupling constant sits in $(-,-)$ and enters $S$ as an overall factor, the one-loop $\log\varepsilon$ counterterm is a rescaling of the fields with vanishing component along the coupling.
Proof.

By Lemma [4.21](#b-00796), $\{S,-\}$ of an element of the span multiplies each monomial of $S$ by a sum of field counts weighted by the coefficients of the element, additive over the factors of the monomial, and a multiple of $S$ adds the same number to every monomial. The terms of $S$ built from $A|_V$ alone contain $2$, $3$, $4$ factors $A|_V$, with computed multiples $4$, $6$, $8$: an additive weight times $2,3,4$ plus a common constant fits $4,6,8$ with weight $2$ and constant $3\cdot4-2\cdot6=0$. With the constant $0$: the kinetic terms of $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ and $\lambda$ give the weight $2$ of $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ and the sum $8$ of the two chiral weights of $\lambda$; the vertex $\lambda\lambda A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$, whose two structures have both $\lambda$ of the same chirality, gives each chiral weight $(10-2)/2=4$; the ghost kinetic term $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dc,A^*)$ gives the weight $-1+2=1$ of $c$; the remaining eight multiples are then reproduced. For the classical part: by Lemma [4.21](#b-00796) every term of $S$ containing an antifield has $n_c-n_{c^*}=1$ and every classical term has $n_c=n_{c^*}=0$, so $S$ minus its classical part equals $\{S,-\int(c^*,c)\}$, an element of the span; replacing $S$ by its classical part shifts the element by a multiple of $\int(c^*,c)$ and leaves the multiple unchanged. ∎
Remark 4.24 (The mass term has nonzero BV variation).

The $\varepsilon^{-1}$ part of $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$, the mass term $\frac{\hbar\,\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\tfrac94\varepsilon^{-1}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(A,A)$, has nonzero variation under $Q+\{I,-\}$. Indeed $\{I,\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(A,A)\}$ pairs the $A^*$ of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,([A,c],A^*)$ with $A$ and is a multiple of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,([A,c],A)=-\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(c,[A,A])=0$, the bracket $[A,A]$ contracting the symmetric metric with the antisymmetric bracket of $\mathfrak g$. By Proposition [1.11](#b-00135), $Q$ inserts $Qc=-dc$ into the slot of $A|_V$, so

\big(Q+\{I,-\}\big)\Big(\frac{\hbar\,\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\tfrac94\varepsilon^{-1}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(A,A)\Big)=-\frac{\hbar\,\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\tfrac92\varepsilon^{-1}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dc,A|_V).
This is the breaking of the gauge symmetry by the regulator. The next section shows how the master equation at the UV boundary absorbs it and what it leaves behind.
4.4 The quantum master equation at the UV boundary
Definition 4.25 (Defect vertex).
For an even functional $J$ with values in $\mathbb C[[\hbar]]$, at least cubic modulo $\hbar$, the defect vertex at scale $\varepsilon$ is the odd functional
QJ+\tfrac12\{J,J\}_\varepsilon+\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon J,
with $\Delta_\varepsilon$ and $\{-,-\}_\varepsilon$ of Definition [3.15](#b-00457). By Corollary [3.18](#b-00476), its vanishing is the quantum master equation at scale $\varepsilon$.
Proposition 4.26 (The $Q$-variation at scale $\infty$ is the flow of the defect).
On functionals without superconformal ghosts,

Q\,W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J)=e^{-W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J)/\hbar}\,e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}\Big(\big(QJ+\tfrac12\{J,J\}_\varepsilon+\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon J\big)\,e^{J/\hbar}\Big). \tag{4.7}

Thus $Q\,W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J)$ is the sum of the connected graphs with exactly one vertex labelled by the defect vertex, all other vertices by $J$, and all edges by $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$, with the weights of Proposition [3.22](#b-00513) [C07, §15.4].
Proof.

For an even $J$, the product rule of Definition [3.15](#b-00457) gives $(Q+\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon)e^{J/\hbar}=\hbar^{-1}\big(QJ+\tfrac12\{J,J\}_\varepsilon+\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon J\big)e^{J/\hbar}$, as in the proof of Corollary [3.18](#b-00476). Theorem [3.17](#b-00464) without superconformal ghosts gives

Q\,e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}e^{J/\hbar}=e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}\big(Q+\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon\big)e^{J/\hbar}=\hbar^{-1}e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}\Big(\big(QJ+\tfrac12\{J,J\}_\varepsilon+\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon J\big)\,e^{J/\hbar}\Big).

The left side is $Q\,e^{W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J)/\hbar}=\hbar^{-1}\big(Q\,W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J)\big)e^{W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J)/\hbar}$, $Q$ being a derivation; multiplying by $\hbar\,e^{-W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J)/\hbar}$ gives [(4.7)](#b-00830). Expanding $e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}$ into graphs as in Proposition [3.22](#b-00513), the right side of [(4.7)](#b-00830) is the sum of the graphs with exactly one vertex labelled by the defect vertex; the factor $e^{-W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J)/\hbar}$, the exponential of the connected graphs of $J$, removes the components without that vertex, which leaves the connected graphs. ∎

With $\Delta_\infty=0$ and $\{-,-\}_\infty=0$, the quantum master equation at scale $\infty$ for the renormalised flow is $Q\lim_{\varepsilon\to0}W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J)=0$ (Corollary [3.18](#b-00476)). Its failure at order $\hbar$ is the order-$\hbar$ part of $\lim_{\varepsilon\to0}Q\,W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon])$. By [(4.7)](#b-00830) it is a sum of graphs with one defect vertex, among them trees of $I$ attached to that vertex; it is the flow to scale $\infty$ of an effective defect vertex, the one-loop obstruction. On a compact manifold with a finite upper scale the obstruction is the local functional of [C07, Prop 12.0.3], closed and independent of $\varepsilon$ by [C07, Lemma 12.0.4]; on $\mathbb R^4$ with upper scale $\infty$ these properties are part of Step 2. In the sector with legs $(c,A|_V)$ no tree of $I$ contributes at order $\hbar$, and the limit computed below is itself local.
Proposition 4.27 (The defect vertex at one loop).
For $J=I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$, with $I$ the classical interaction [(1.3)](#b-00159),

QJ+\tfrac12\{J,J\}_\varepsilon+\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon J=\tfrac12\big(\{I,I\}_\varepsilon-\{I,I\}\big)+\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon I-Q\,I^{CT}[\varepsilon]-\{I,I^{CT}[\varepsilon]\}_\varepsilon+(\text{terms of order }\hbar^2). \tag{4.8}
The first term is the bracket built from $\Delta_\varepsilon-\Delta_0=-\partial_{K_\varepsilon-K_0}$, i.e. two vertices of $I$ joined by one special edge carrying
K_\varepsilon-K_0=-\int_0^\varepsilon(H\otimes1)K_t\,dt,
which in momentum space is $e^{-\varepsilon|p|^2}-1$ times the components of $K_0$; its Schwinger time lies in $[0,\varepsilon]$.
Proof.

Expanding $QJ+\tfrac12\{J,J\}_\varepsilon+\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon J$ with $J=I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ and $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ of order $\hbar$: at order $\hbar^0$, $QI+\tfrac12\{I,I\}_\varepsilon$; at order $\hbar$, $-QI^{CT}[\varepsilon]-\tfrac12\big(\{I,I^{CT}[\varepsilon]\}_\varepsilon+\{I^{CT}[\varepsilon],I\}_\varepsilon\big)+\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon I$, where the two brackets of even functionals coincide; the rest is $\tfrac12\{I^{CT}[\varepsilon],I^{CT}[\varepsilon]\}_\varepsilon-\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$, of order $\hbar^2$. The classical master equation (Proposition [1.14](#b-00173)) gives $QI=-\tfrac12\{I,I\}$, with $\{-,-\}$ built from $\Delta_0$ (Definition [1.6](#b-00095)). From $K_t=(e^{-tH}\otimes1)K_0$, $\frac{d}{dt}K_t=-(H\otimes1)K_t$, and integration from $0$ to $\varepsilon$ gives the special edge; in momentum space $e^{-tH}$ is $e^{-t|p|^2}$. ∎

At order $\hbar$, the graphs of [(4.7)](#b-00830) with two legs are: the term $-QI^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ as a vertex; the bubbles formed by the two vertices of $\tfrac12(\{I,I\}_\varepsilon-\{I,I\})$, joined by the special edge and one edge $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$; and one-particle-reducible graphs in which a loop closes at a single cubic vertex. The term $\{I,I^{CT}[\varepsilon]\}_\varepsilon$ has at least three legs.
Lemma 4.28 (Two-leg sectors of degree one).

An invariant local functional of degree $1$ with two legs and weight at most $4$ is a combination of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dc,A|_V)$ (weight $2$) and $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*dc,d^*A|_V)$ (weight $4$). In particular the sectors with legs $(c,A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$ and $(c,\lambda)$ vanish.
Proof.

Degree $1$ with two legs requires one $c$ and one leg of degree $0$, $A$ or $\lambda$. The invariant pairings of a scalar with a spinor and with a vector of $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ vanish. With $A|_V$: one derivative in weight $2$, $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dc,A|_V)$; three derivatives in weight $4$, where $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dc,d^*dA|_V)=\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d\,dc,dA|_V)=0$ and $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dc,dd^*A|_V)=\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*dc,d^*A|_V)$. ∎

blocks.source: Lemma 4.29 (Graphs with one special edge).

The plane-wave value of each bubble of the first figure is $\varepsilon^{-1}$ times a multiple of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dc,A|_V)$ plus a multiple of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*dc,d^*A|_V)$ plus a term bounded by a multiple of $\varepsilon$, with vanishing coefficient of $\log\varepsilon$.
Proof.

The special edge carries $-\int_0^\varepsilon(\cdots)e^{-t_1|p_1|^2}dt_1$ and the other edge $\int_\varepsilon^\infty(\cdots)e^{-t_2|p_1-p|^2}dt_2$. After the Gaussian integral over $p_1$ (Lemma [4.4](#b-00577), extended to the polynomial numerators of degree three of these graphs by the same moments), the integrand is $(t_1+t_2)^{-2}e^{-t_1t_2|p|^2/(t_1+t_2)}$ times a sum of terms $(t_1+t_2)^{-m}$, $m\ge0$, with polynomial coefficients in $\frac{t_1}{t_1+t_2}$ and $p$. On $[0,\varepsilon]\times[\varepsilon,\infty)$ the exponent satisfies $0\le\frac{t_1t_2|p|^2}{t_1+t_2}\le t_1|p|^2\le\varepsilon|p|^2$, so its exponential is a power series in $\varepsilon|p|^2$ with uniform remainders. Substituting $\varepsilon t_1$, $\varepsilon t_2$ for $t_1$, $t_2$ maps the region to $[0,1]\times[1,\infty)$, on which $(t_1+t_2)^{-2-m}$ is integrable, and each term becomes an integer power of $\varepsilon$ times a convergent integral. Hence the value is a series in integer powers of $\varepsilon$; by Lemma [4.28](#b-00846) the coefficients of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $\varepsilon^0$ are the two listed functionals. ∎
