Table 4.17. The one-loop part of $Q\,W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon])$ with legs $(c,A|_V)$, graph by graph, in units of $\hbar\,\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)/(16\pi^2(X,Y))$. Each bubble has weight $1$: the $\tfrac12$ of $\tfrac12\{I,I\}$ cancels against the two assignments of the two vertices. Every entry has vanishing $\log\varepsilon$ coefficient.
Theorem 4.30 (The one-loop obstruction in the sector $(c,A|_V)$).

The part of $Q\,W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon])$ of order $\hbar$ with legs $(c,A|_V)$ has the following $\varepsilon$-expansion: the special-edge bubbles contribute $-\tfrac92\,\varepsilon^{-1}$ times $\frac{\hbar\,\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dc,A|_V)$, the vertex $-QI^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ contributes $+\tfrac92\,\varepsilon^{-1}$ times the same functional, the coefficient of $\log\varepsilon$ is $0$, and the limit is

-\frac{27}{8}\,\frac{\hbar\,\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*dc,d^*A|_V)=\frac{27}{16}\,\frac{\hbar\,\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\;Q\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V). \tag{4.9}
The sectors $(c,A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$ and $(c,\lambda)$ of the one-loop obstruction vanish.
Proof.

By Proposition [4.26](#b-00828) and [(4.8)](#b-00839), the order-$\hbar$ part with two legs is the sum of the graphs listed before Lemma [4.28](#b-00846). The one-particle-reducible graphs vanish: a loop closing at one cubic vertex contracts two legs of a vertex of the form $([X,Y],Z)$ with $(-,-)^{-1}$ and gives $\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X)=0$ or the contraction of the antisymmetric bracket with the symmetric $(-,-)^{-1}$, both zero. The same argument gives $\Delta_\varepsilon I=0$: $K_\varepsilon$ pairs a field with its antifield, the vertices of $I$ containing an antifield are $([A,c],A^*)$, $([c,\lambda],\lambda^*)$, $\tfrac12([c,c],c^*)$, and each self-contraction is a trace of $\mathrm{ad}$. The five bubbles are given in the table; their $\varepsilon^{-1}$ coefficients sum to $-\tfrac94+\tfrac18-\tfrac92+2+\tfrac18=-\tfrac92$, and by Lemma [4.29](#b-00852) they have vanishing $\log\varepsilon$ coefficient. By Theorem [4.16](#b-00707) and Remark [4.24](#b-00819), $-QI^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ restricted to $(c,A|_V)$ is $-\tfrac94\cdot(-2)=\tfrac92$ times $\varepsilon^{-1}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dc,A|_V)$ in the unit; its $\log\varepsilon$ part restricted to $(c,A|_V)$ vanishes, because $Q\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dA,dA)$ contains $d\,dc=0$, $Q\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dc,A^*)$ restricted to $(c,A|_V)$ is $-\tfrac12\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dc,d^*dA|_V)=-\tfrac12\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d\,dc,dA|_V)=0$, and the coefficient of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V)$ is $0$. The finite parts sum to $-\tfrac58-\tfrac1{12}-\tfrac54-\tfrac43-\tfrac1{12}=-\tfrac{81}{24}=-\tfrac{27}8$. Finally $Q\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V)=2\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*(-dc))=-2\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*dc,d^*A|_V)$, so $-\tfrac{27}8=\tfrac{27}{16}\cdot(-2)$. The last statement is Lemma [4.28](#b-00846). ∎
Remark 4.31 (The obstruction as the longitudinal part of the two-point function).

$Q$ preserves the polynomial degree of functionals, so the part of $Q\,W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon])$ with legs $(c,A|_V)$ at order $\hbar$ is $Q$ applied to the order-$\hbar$ quadratic part of $W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon])$: the renormalised two-point function, whose limit as $\varepsilon\to0$ at nonzero momentum exists by Theorem [4.16](#b-00707) and Proposition [4.8](#b-00628). $Q$ annihilates its $(c,A^*)$ part on $(c,A|_V)$, since $\iota_p$ of $|p|^2A|_V-p\,\iota_pA|_V$ is $0$, and its transverse $A|_V$ part, which depends on $A|_V$ through $dA|_V$. Hence the cancellation of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ and the vanishing of $\log\varepsilon$ in Theorem [4.30](#b-00858) follow from Theorem [4.16](#b-00707), and the obstruction is $Q$ of the longitudinal part of the renormalised $A|_V$ two-point function at scale $\infty$. A longitudinal quadratic functional of $A|_V$ is $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,G\,d^*A|_V)$ for a translation-invariant operator $G$ on functions, and $Q$ sends it to $-2\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*dc,G\,d^*A|_V)$; comparing with [(4.9)](#b-00860) shows that $G$ is the constant $\tfrac{27}{16}$ in the unit, so the longitudinal part is the local functional
\frac{27}{16}\,\frac{\hbar\,\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V).

Equivalently, $Q$ applied to the longitudinal parts of the graphs of the $A|_V$ two-point function, with every edge cut off at $\varepsilon$, sums to $-\tfrac92\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $-\tfrac{27}8$ times the functionals of [(4.9)](#b-00860); there the gauge bubble and the ghost loop carry separate $\log(\varepsilon|p|^2)$ and $\log2$ terms in their longitudinal parts, which cancel in their sum. Theorem [4.30](#b-00858) is the evaluation of the same quantity through the UV-boundary identity, on graphs with one special edge confined to $[0,\varepsilon]$.
Theorem 4.32 (The finite counterterm in the sector $(c,A|_V)$).
Replace the renormalised interaction $I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ by
I-\frac{27}{16}\,\frac{\hbar\,\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V)-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]. \tag{4.10}

Then $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ at one loop is unchanged, the order-$\hbar$ part of the flow has a limit at generic leg momenta, and the part with legs $(c,A|_V)$ of the one-loop obstruction vanishes. The added term is local, even, of degree $0$ and weight $4$, independent of $\varepsilon$, and invariant under translations, $\mathrm{Spin}(4,\mathbb C)\times\mathrm{Spin}(6,\mathbb C)$, the adjoint action of $\mathfrak g$ and the dilatation. Among the quadratic functionals of $A|_V$ of weight $4$ and degree $0$, it is unique up to adding multiples of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dA|_V,dA|_V)$, which is $Q$-closed.
Proof.

The added term is of order $\hbar$, so at order $\hbar$ it enters the flow as a tree vertex, with a limit as $\varepsilon\to0$, and leaves the one-loop singular parts unchanged. In [(4.8)](#b-00839) it adds $-Q$ of itself at order $\hbar$, and $-\{I,\cdot\}_\varepsilon$ of itself, which has at least three legs. By Theorem [4.30](#b-00858) and $Q\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V)=-2\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*dc,d^*A|_V)$, the $(c,A|_V)$ part becomes $-\tfrac{27}{8}+\tfrac{27}{16}\cdot2=0$ in the unit. Invariance under the dilatation holds because the weight is $4$. For uniqueness: by Lemma [4.19](#b-00726), the quadratic functionals of $A|_V$ of weight $4$ are spanned by $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dA|_V,dA|_V)$ and $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V)$; the first is $Q$-closed, since $d\,dc=0$, and the second has $Q$-variation $-2\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*dc,d^*A|_V)\neq0$, so the coefficient $\tfrac{27}{16}$ of the second is forced. ∎
Remark 4.33 (Renormalisation conditions belong to the definition of the theory).

$I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ is purely singular, and unique among the translation-invariant and $\mathfrak g$-invariant local functionals of Proposition [4.10](#b-00637) (the one-loop analogue of [C07, Thm B], in the scope of Remark [4.9](#b-00635)); the finite term of [(4.10)](#b-00870) is a finite change of the interaction, $I\mapsto I-\tfrac{27}{16}\frac{\hbar\,\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V)$, of the kind that lifts a theory across a $Q$-exact obstruction in [C07, Lemma 12.0.4]. The order-$\hbar$ part of the regulated flow with $I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ has a finite limit at generic leg momenta (Proposition [4.8](#b-00628)) and fails the master equation at scale $\infty$ by a finite local amount; the master equation forces the coefficient $\tfrac{27}{16}$ and leaves the $Q$-closed finite counterterms, such as multiples of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dA,dA)$, free. This choice is a renormalisation condition, and it is part of the definition of the quantum theory: every observable $O[\infty]$ is built from the flow of the interaction, and changes with it. In this program it is the first instance of that statement; the same mechanism recurs for the equivariant counterterms of the superconformal ghosts.
Remark 4.34 (The cubic sector of the obstruction).

The one-loop obstruction also has components with three legs: $(c,A|_V,A|_V)$, $(c,A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp},A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$, $(c,\lambda,\lambda)$ and $(c,c,A^*|_V)$. They are sums of triangles and quartic-vertex bubbles with one special edge, of the vertex $-\{I,I^{CT}[\varepsilon]\}_\varepsilon$, and of one-particle-reducible graphs in which $-QI^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ is joined to $I$ by an edge $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$. The finite term of [(4.10)](#b-00870) changes them by $-\{I,\cdot\}$ of itself, a nonzero functional built from $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,([A,c],A^*)$. The full one-loop master equation, i.e. the vanishing of the obstruction in all sectors after a finite counterterm, is the subject of Step 2.
Proposition 4.35 (The finite counterterm under special conformal transformations).

Let $v$ be the special conformal field $x\mapsto(x,x)v_1-2(v_1,x)x$, $v_1\in V$ (Definition [2.1](#b-00203)), acting on $A|_V$ by the Lie derivative $L_v$ (Definition [2.12](#b-00307)). The derivative of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V)$ along $A|_V\mapsto L_vA|_V$ is
2\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*L_vA|_V)=-8\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,\iota_{v_1}A|_V)\neq0,
while for translations, rotations and the dilatation $2E$ the derivative vanishes.
Proof.

For a conformal Killing field $v$ of $V$, the symmetric part of the derivative of $(v,-)$ is $\tfrac14\operatorname{div}v$ times the metric; taking one more divergence, $d^*d$ applied to the components of $v$ is $\tfrac12\operatorname{grad}(\operatorname{div}v)$. The Lie derivative of the one-form $A|_V$ is $v(A|_V)+A|_V\circ(\text{derivative of }v)$, and the divergence of this expression, with the two identities above, is
d^*(L_vA|_V)=v(d^*A|_V)+\tfrac12(\operatorname{div}v)\,d^*A|_V+\tfrac12\,\iota_{\operatorname{grad}(\operatorname{div}v)}A|_V .
Hence

and integration by parts cancels the first two terms, since $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,v(\cdot)=-\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(\operatorname{div}v)(\cdot)$. For the special conformal field, $\operatorname{div}v=-8(v_1,x)$ (Chapter 2) and $\operatorname{grad}(\operatorname{div}v)=-8v_1$, which gives the stated value. For translations and rotations $\operatorname{div}v=0$, and for $2E$, $\operatorname{div}v=8$ is constant. ∎

The finite counterterm of Theorem [4.32](#b-00868) is the Feynman-gauge longitudinal term, and Proposition [4.35](#b-00878) shows that it breaks the special conformal symmetry. In Step 2 the components of the equivariant counterterms along the special conformal generators have to absorb this variation, or exhibit it as part of an obstruction.
Remark 4.36 (Method of computation).

Each per-graph coefficient of this chapter is an exact rational number. It is obtained in an explicit realisation of $V_{10}$, $\Sigma$ and $\mathfrak g$ over $\mathbb Q(i)$, with the loop momentum integrated as a Gaussian (Lemma [4.4](#b-00577)) and the $\varepsilon$-expansion taken on the graphs with one pinned edge (Proposition [4.2](#b-00561)), in exact rational arithmetic; for the two-point graphs the polarisations and momenta are symbolic. For the cubic and quartic sets each multilinear form is determined by exact linear algebra on a basis of the $\mathrm{Spin}(4,\mathbb C)\times\mathrm{Spin}(6,\mathbb C)$-invariant multilinear forms of the given legs, including the parity-odd ones, from evaluations at integer polarisations and momenta drawn uniformly from a finite set of integers. A nonzero polynomial vanishes at such a point with probability at most its total degree divided by the size of the set (Schwartz–Zippel), so the sampled system has full rank with high probability; full rank is then established exactly, and the solution is exact. The colour factors are reduced exactly for a general simple $\mathfrak g$, and the resulting rational multiples of $\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)/(X,Y)$ are the same in the explicit realisations $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ and $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(3)$. The sector $(c,A|_V)$ of the obstruction is also given by $Q$ of the renormalised two-point function (Remark [4.31](#b-00864)).
5. Local operators: from functionals to local $O(\varepsilon)$

The insertion of a composite operator into a one-loop graph diverges as $\varepsilon\to0$, and Costello's construction asks for a family $O(\varepsilon)$ whose flow to scale $\infty$ has a limit. At scale $\infty$, however, $K_\infty=0$ and $P(0,\infty)$ is a contracting homotopy for $Q$ on moment-free Schwartz sections (Chapter 3), so a general functional family $O(\varepsilon)$ produces the zero class on moment-free Schwartz sections. The content of an operator is therefore the requirement that $O(\varepsilon)$ be local, $O(\varepsilon)=O-\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ with coefficients in $\mathrm{span}\{\varepsilon^{-1},\log\varepsilon\}$: locality and the existence of the limit fix the singular part, and the finite part is the scheme. This chapter sets up $O(\varepsilon)$ and $O[\infty]$, proves $O(\varepsilon)=O$ for single letters at one loop, and computes $O(\varepsilon)$ for the scalar bilinears graph by graph.
5.1 Observables as first-order deformations
Definition 5.1 (Background field and the family $I+\delta O$).
A background field is a compactly supported four-form $\omega\in\Omega^4_c(\mathbb R^4)$ [CG2, Lemma 10.1.1.3]. A local operator is a local functional
O=\int\omega\,(\text{density}),

linear in $\omega$, whose density is a polynomial in the fields and their derivatives at a point; the Weyl weight $w_O$ of $O$ is the sum of the Weyl weights of the fields in the density ($c$: $0$, $A$: $1$, $\lambda$: $\tfrac32$, $A^*$: $3$, $\lambda^*$: $\tfrac52$, $c^*$: $4$) plus the number of derivatives. For $O$ of cohomological degree $i$, $\delta$ is a square-zero parameter of degree $-i$ [CG2, Def 8.3.1.1], and $I+\delta O$ is a family of interactions over $\mathbb C[\delta]/\delta^2$; by [CG2, after Def 8.3.1.3] it satisfies the axioms of a family of theories over $\mathbb C[\delta]/\delta^2$ except locality of the flowed functionals. The scalar bilinears and the letters $\int\omega\,(X,\iota_wA)$, $\int\omega\,(X,\iota_v(A|_V))$, $\int\omega\,(\zeta,\lambda)$ have $i=0$; the ghost letter $\int\omega\,(X,c)$ has $i=1$, and then $\delta$ has degree $-1$.
The square-zero parameter $\delta$ is written without argument; the delta distribution is always written with its argument, as in $\delta(x-y)$.
Definition 5.2 (The local family and the observable at scale $\infty$).

Let $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ be the one-loop counterterm of $I$ (Definition [4.1](#b-00556); the analogue of [C07, Thm B], Remark [4.9](#b-00635)), and write the counterterm of the family $I+\delta O$ as $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]+\delta\,\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$. Put

O(\varepsilon):=O-\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon],\qquad O[\infty]:=\lim_{\varepsilon\to0}\partial_\delta W\big(P(\varepsilon,\infty),\,I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]+\delta\,O(\varepsilon)\big), \tag{5.1}

with $W$ the flow of Definition [3.16](#b-00460) [CG2, §7.2.7]. With the global ghosts of $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$, $I$ is replaced by the equivariant interaction $I_{\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)}=I+S^{(1)}+S^{(2)}$ [ESW, Rem 1.29] (Definition [2.10](#b-00281)) and $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ by the counterterm of the family $I_{\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)}+\delta O$ over $C^\bullet(\mathfrak{psl}(4|4))$:

O(\varepsilon):=O-\partial_\delta I^{CT}_{\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)}[\varepsilon],\qquad O[\infty]:=\lim_{\varepsilon\to0}\partial_\delta W\big(P(\varepsilon,\infty),\,I_{\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)}-I^{CT}_{\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)}[\varepsilon]+\delta\,O(\varepsilon)\big).

Both are cochains on $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$; their components of arity $0$ are the functionals [(5.1)](#b-00901). This chapter computes the components of arity $0$; the components with arguments in $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ involve the counterterms of $I_{\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)}$ along the ghosts; Chapter 6 treats the dilatation through the scaling covariance, and the ghost components are part of Step 2 (Chapter 7).

At scale $\infty$ the differential on observables is $(d_{CE}+Q)O[\infty]$, since the scale-$\infty$ structure is defined by the kernel $K_\infty:=0$, so that $\Delta_\infty=0$ and $\{-,-\}_\infty=0$ (Definition [3.15](#b-00457)) [CG2, Def 8.3.1.3, Prop 13.4.0.1].
[C07, Thm B] is stated for interactions that are at least cubic modulo $\hbar$, and $\delta O$ is quadratic for the operators below. The construction of [C07, Thm B] is applied graph by graph:
Proposition 5.3 (Counterterms of the family).

Let $O$ be a homogeneous local operator. At order $\hbar$ there is a unique local functional $\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ with coefficients in the span of the negative integer powers of $\varepsilon$ and of $\log\varepsilon$, a subspace of $\mathscr A_{<0}$ [C07, Def 1.4.1; CG2, §13.7.2], such that the limit [(5.1)](#b-00901) exists at generic leg momenta. It is the singular part of the sum of the one-loop graphs in which the vertex $O$ lies on the cycle, each evaluated with $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$; for $w_O\le3$ its coefficients lie in $\mathrm{span}\{\varepsilon^{-1},\log\varepsilon\}$.
Proof.

By Proposition [3.22](#b-00513), the order-$\hbar$ part of $\partial_\delta W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]+\delta O)$ is a sum over connected graphs with exactly one vertex $O$ (since $\delta^2=0$) and either one cycle and vertices $I$, or no cycle and one vertex $-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$. Every vertex of $I$ is at least trivalent and $O$ occurs once, so for a fixed number of legs the sum is finite. Three classes occur.

• $O$ lies off the cycle. Removing the edges that join $O$ to the rest leaves a one-loop graph without $O$; the corresponding tree graph with the vertex $-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ in its place cancels its singular part by Lemma [4.7](#b-00615), with $O$ as the marked vertex, and Definition [4.1](#b-00556), and the trees joining $O$ converge to trees with $P(0,\infty)$, because $P(\varepsilon,\infty)-P(0,\infty)=-\int_0^\varepsilon L_t\,dt$ is bounded by a multiple of $\varepsilon$ at fixed nonzero momentum.

• $O$ lies on the cycle. The vertex function of $O$ is a polynomial in the momenta times the Fourier transform of $\omega$ at minus the total momentum of its legs (Lemma [5.8](#b-00946)), and the numerator is homogeneous, $O$ being homogeneous, so by Lemma [4.6](#b-00594) the singular part of such a graph is a local functional with coefficients in the span of the negative powers of $\varepsilon$ and of $\log\varepsilon$, and the tree with the vertex $-\delta\,\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ in place of the cycle removes it (Lemma [4.7](#b-00615), with $O$ as the marked vertex). Its superficial degree is $w_O$ minus the sum of the Weyl weights of the legs (proof of Proposition [5.13](#b-01000)), at most $w_O$, so for $w_O\le3$ the powers $\varepsilon^{-k}$, $k\ge2$, are absent.
• Trees with the vertex $-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ and with $O$: already paired in the first class.

Uniqueness: two such counterterms differ by a local functional with coefficients in $\mathscr A_{<0}$ whose tree-level flow has a limit. The part of that flow with as many legs as the component of the difference with the fewest legs is that component itself, which therefore has a limit and vanishes; by induction on the number of legs, as in Proposition [4.10](#b-00637), the difference vanishes. ∎
Proposition 5.4 (Local representatives).
Let $O$ be a homogeneous local operator.
• Two local families $O(\varepsilon)$, $O^{\prime}(\varepsilon)$ for which the limit [(5.1)](#b-00901) exists have the same singular part.

• Adding to $O(\varepsilon)$ an $\varepsilon$-independent local functional of order $\hbar$ adds to $O[\infty]$, at order $\hbar$, the flow of that functional to scale $\infty$ through trees with vertices $I$.

• Let $F$ be a continuous polynomial functional of moment-free Schwartz sections, without constant term, with $QF=0$. Then $F$ is $Q$-exact (Corollary [3.20](#b-00504)). On compactly supported sections the $Q$-closed functionals carry in addition nonzero classes, among them the zero-mode classes of Theorem [3.19](#b-00485) and Remark [3.21](#b-00510), finitely many in each polynomial degree and infinitely many in all.
Consequently a statement about $O[\infty]$ has content when it is written in the form
(d_{CE}+Q)\,O[\infty]=(\text{a local functional})[\infty],
and, for an operator whose observable is a cocycle (Remark [5.6](#b-00927)), an anomalous dimension is read off in the cohomology of local functionals.
Proof.

The first item is the uniqueness part of Proposition [5.3](#b-00907). The second follows from linearity of [(5.1)](#b-00901) in the $\delta$-component: at order $\hbar$ the added functional enters through its tree-level flow. The third item is Corollary [3.20](#b-00504), which rests on the homotopy identity $Q\,P(0,\infty)\star+P(0,\infty)\star\,Q=\mathrm{id}$ of Theorem [3.19](#b-00485) on moment-free Schwartz sections; the classes on compactly supported sections are those described in Theorem [3.19](#b-00485) and Remark [3.21](#b-00510). Every observable $O[\infty]$ that extends to a continuous functional on moment-free Schwartz sections, with $(d_{CE}+Q)O[\infty]=0$ there, therefore lies in the image of $Q$ on such functionals; what it records about $O$ is the local functional $O(\varepsilon)$, through the first two items. ∎
Remark 5.5 (Where the content of an operator lies).

By Proposition [5.4](#b-00915), the singular part of $O(\varepsilon)$ is uniquely fixed and the finite part is the scheme freedom; this is the statement of Remark [3.21](#b-00510) for operators. In the rest of this chapter $\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ is computed; its $\log\varepsilon$ part is the input of the anomalous dimensions in Chapter 6.
Remark 5.6 (The cocycle condition).
Reading the dilatation component of Chapter 6 as the anomalous dimension of a cohomology class requires $O[\infty]$ to be a cocycle at arity zero,
Q\,O[\infty]=0\qquad\text{at order }\hbar,

the part linear in $\delta$ of the quantum master equation of the family $I+\delta O$ at scale $\infty$. For $O$ with $(Q+\{I,-\})O=0$, Proposition [4.26](#b-00828) applied to $J=I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]+\delta O(\varepsilon)$ expresses $Q\,O[\infty]$ at order $\hbar$ as the limit of the graphs with one vertex labelled by the part of the defect vertex linear in $\delta$: the special edge $K_\varepsilon-K_0$ between $I$ and $O$, from $\{I,O\}_\varepsilon-\{I,O\}$; the vertices $-Q\,\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]-\{I,\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]\}_\varepsilon$ and $-\{I^{CT}[\varepsilon],O\}_\varepsilon$; the self-contraction $\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon O$, zero for operators without antifields; and the trees joining $O$ to the action defect of Proposition [4.27](#b-00837), whose cubic sector is open (Remark [4.34](#b-00876)). For the scalar bilinears the local output of Weyl weight $2$, ghost degree $1$ and colour singlet includes functionals of the type $\int\omega\,(dc,A|_V)$. A nonzero result of this kind is removed by a finite local counterterm of Weyl weight $w_O$ added to $O(\varepsilon)$, for instance a multiple of $\int\omega\,(A|_V,A|_V)$, since
Q\int\omega\,(A|_V,A|_V)=-2\int\omega\,(dc,A|_V).

Such a counterterm is independent of $\varepsilon$ and of order $\hbar$; by Proposition [5.4](#b-00915) it adds to $O[\infty]$ the flow of a local functional of the same Weyl weight, and it leaves the $\log\varepsilon$ coefficients of this chapter and the dilatation coefficients of Chapter 6 unchanged. The evaluation of these graphs is part of Step 2 (Chapter 7).
5.2 Tools for one-loop insertions
The gauge algebra $\mathfrak g$ is simple. The inverse pairing $(-,-)^{-1}\in\mathfrak g\otimes\mathfrak g$ is symmetric, and a bilinear form on $\mathfrak g$ can be evaluated on it.
Lemma 5.7 (Colour contractions).
For $X_1,X_2\in\mathfrak g$:
• the bracket $[-,-]$ evaluated on $(-,-)^{-1}$ is $0$;

• for every linear map of $\mathfrak g$, the bilinear form $(Z,Z^{\prime})\mapsto(Z,\text{the map applied to }Z^{\prime})$ evaluated on $(-,-)^{-1}$ is the trace $\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}$ of the map; in particular $(-,-)$ evaluated on $(-,-)^{-1}$ is $\dim\mathfrak g$, and $(X_1,[-,-])$ and $(-,[X_1,-])$ evaluated on $(-,-)^{-1}$ are $0$;
• the bilinear form $([X_1,-],[X_2,-])$ evaluated on $(-,-)^{-1}$ is $-\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_{X_1}\mathrm{ad}_{X_2})$;

• for all $X,Y\in\mathfrak g$ with $(X,Y)\neq0$, the ratio $\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)/(X,Y)$ is the same number, and $\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_{X_1}\mathrm{ad}_{X_2})=\frac{\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{(X,Y)}\,(X_1,X_2)$.
Proof.

The bracket is antisymmetric and $(-,-)^{-1}$ is symmetric. The inverse pairing is characterised by the property that contracting its second factor with $(Z,-)$ returns $Z$; hence the bilinear form of a linear map, evaluated on $(-,-)^{-1}$, is the trace of the map. By invariance, $(X_1,[Z,Z^{\prime}])=([X_1,Z],Z^{\prime})=-(Z,[X_1,Z^{\prime}])$, which is the case of the map $-\mathrm{ad}_{X_1}$, of trace $0$ because $\mathrm{ad}_{X_1}$ is antisymmetric for $(-,-)$, and $(-,[X_1,-])$ is the case of $\mathrm{ad}_{X_1}$; and $([X_1,Z],[X_2,Z^{\prime}])=-(Z,[X_1,[X_2,Z^{\prime}]])$ is the case of $-\mathrm{ad}_{X_1}\mathrm{ad}_{X_2}$. For simple $\mathfrak g$ every invariant symmetric bilinear form is a multiple of $(-,-)$, which gives the last item. ∎
In the following, the number
\frac{\hbar\,\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2\,(X,Y)}
is the unit of every one-loop coefficient; it is negative when $(-,-)$ is positive definite on the compact real form.
Lemma 5.8 (Vertex functions on decomposable legs).

Give each leg of a vertex a fibre element $(v,-)\otimes Z$ with $v\in V_{10}$ and $Z\in\mathfrak g$; by linearity this determines every vertex function. The quartic vertex function [(1.5)](#b-00167) with legs $(v_j,-)\otimes Z_j$, $j=1,\dots,4$, equals

the three terms belonging to the pairings $(12|34)$, $(13|24)$, $(14|23)$ of the legs. The cubic vertex function [(1.4)](#b-00166) with two legs $(w,-)\otimes Z$, $(w^{\prime},-)\otimes Z^{\prime}$, $w,w^{\prime}\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$, of incoming momenta $p$, $p^{\prime}$, and one leg $(v,-)\otimes Z^{\prime\prime}$, $v\in V$, equals
-\frac i2\,(v,p^{\prime}-p)\,(w,w^{\prime})\,\big(Z^{\prime\prime},[Z,Z^{\prime}]\big); \tag{5.3}
The vertex function of $\int\omega\,(\iota_{w_1}A,\iota_{w_2}A)$ on legs $(v,-)\otimes Z$, $(v^{\prime},-)\otimes Z^{\prime}$ is
\big[(w_1,v)(w_2,v^{\prime})+(w_1,v^{\prime})(w_2,v)\big](Z,Z^{\prime}),
times the Fourier transform of $\omega$ at minus the total momentum of the legs.
Proof.

With $A_j=(v_j,-)\otimes Z_j$, the two-form $[A_1\wedge A_2]$ of Chapter 1 is $(v_1,-)\wedge(v_2,-)\otimes[Z_1,Z_2]$, because $[A_1\wedge A_2](e,e^{\prime})=(v_1,e)(v_2,e^{\prime})[Z_1,Z_2]-(v_1,e^{\prime})(v_2,e)[Z_1,Z_2]$, and likewise for every pair of legs. Polarising the normalisation of the Hodge pairing in Definition [1.8](#b-00106) gives

and likewise for the other two pairings, which gives [(5.2)](#b-00948). In [(1.4)](#b-00166), $\iota_pA(p_j)=(v_j,p)Z_j$ and $[A(p_i),A(p_j)]=(v_i,v_j)[Z_i,Z_j]$. With legs $1,2$ along $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ and leg $3$ along $V$, the momenta lie in $V\perp W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$, so $(v_1,p)=(v_2,p)=0$ and $(v_2,v_3)=(v_3,v_1)=0$; the second and third terms of [(1.4)](#b-00166) vanish and the first is $-\tfrac i2(v_3,p_2-p_1)(v_1,v_2)(Z_3,[Z_1,Z_2])$, which is [(5.3)](#b-00950). The last item is the multilinear part of $(\iota_{w_1}A,\iota_{w_2}A)$ on two plane waves (Definition [1.13](#b-00162)). ∎
Lemma 5.9 (Insertion on a cycle).

Expand around a background consisting of two plane waves with fibre elements $A(p_1)$, $A(p_2)$, as in Remark [3.24](#b-00547). The part of the order-$\hbar$ term of $\partial_\delta W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I+\delta O)$ that is bilinear in $A(p_1)$, $A(p_2)$ and comes from cycles through the vertex $O$ whose edges all lie in the $A$ slot is $\hbar$ times the sum of
• $\tfrac12$ times each bubble: the cycle through $O$ and one quartic vertex carrying both external legs;
• $1$ times each triangle: the cycle through $O$, a cubic vertex carrying $A(p_1)$ and a cubic vertex carrying $A(p_2)$, traversed in one orientation.

In each cycle the internal legs are contracted along the edges with the $A\otimes A$ component of $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ (Proposition [3.11](#b-00430)): an edge of momentum $p$ replaces the fibre elements $(v,-)\otimes Z$, $(v^{\prime},-)\otimes Z^{\prime}$ at its two ends by $2$ times the inverse metric in $v\otimes v^{\prime}$ and $(-,-)^{-1}$ in $Z\otimes Z^{\prime}$, times $\int_\varepsilon^\infty e^{-t|p|^2}dt=e^{-\varepsilon|p|^2}|p|^{-2}$, and the loop momentum $p$ is integrated with $\int d^4p/(2\pi)^4$.
Proof.

On the $A$ slots the parity operator and the supertrace of Proposition [3.23](#b-00524) are trivial, and the one-loop operator is $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ composed with the second derivative of $I+\delta O$ in the fluctuation. The $\delta$-derivative of $\frac1{2n}\mathrm{STr}$ of its $n$-th power is $\frac12\mathrm{STr}$ of the product of $n-1$ factors built from $I$ and one factor built from $O$. The second derivative of $O$ is its vertex function with both legs internal, since $O$ is quadratic. For $n=2$ the factor built from $I$ is bilinear in the two external legs through the quartic vertex: by Definition [1.13](#b-00162) the part of the quartic term of $I$ quadratic in the fluctuation and bilinear in $A(p_1)$, $A(p_2)$ is one half of [(1.5)](#b-00167) with two internal legs, whose second derivative is [(1.5)](#b-00167) with two legs open; this gives the weight $\tfrac12$. For $n=3$ the two factors built from $I$ each carry one external leg through a cubic vertex; the two orders of these factors give equal traces, since all second derivatives and $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ are symmetric and the trace is invariant under transposition and cyclic permutation, so $\tfrac12$ times their sum is one triangle with weight $1$. ∎
The singular parts are read off from the following lemma, which also locates them on the lower end $t=\varepsilon$ of the Schwinger integrals (Remark [3.13](#b-00452)).
Lemma 5.10 (Logarithmic coefficient from the UV boundary).
Let $\gamma$ be a one-loop graph with edge set $E(\gamma)$ [C07, §15.5], $|E(\gamma)|\ge2$, whose value is

F_\gamma(\varepsilon)=\int_{[\varepsilon,\infty)^{E(\gamma)}}\prod_{e\in E(\gamma)}dt_e\int\frac{d^4p}{(2\pi)^4}\,\big(\text{numerator of }\gamma\big)(p)\,\exp\Big(-\sum_{e\in E(\gamma)}t_e|p+p_e|^2\Big)\qquad[\text{C07, §15.4}],

with generic $p_e\in V$ and a numerator that is a polynomial in $p$ and the $p_e$, homogeneous of degree $2|E(\gamma)|-4$; let $\big(\text{numerator of }\gamma\big)_{\rm top}$ be its part of degree $2|E(\gamma)|-4$ in $p$, and write
\text{(average)}=\frac1{2\pi^2}\int_{|p|=1}\big(\text{numerator of }\gamma\big)_{\rm top}(p)\,d\mathrm{area}(p)
for its average over the unit sphere of $V$, of area $2\pi^2$. Then

and each of the $|E(\gamma)|$ terms of the sum tends to $\frac{1}{|E(\gamma)|}\cdot\frac{\text{(average)}}{16\pi^2}$. The coefficient of $\log\varepsilon$ in $F_\gamma(\varepsilon)$ is $-\frac{\text{(average)}}{16\pi^2}$, and each edge carries the fraction $\frac1{|E(\gamma)|}$ of it.

The first identity is Proposition [4.2](#b-00561). Fix an edge $e$. As in the proof of Lemma [4.6](#b-00594), with $\tau=\varepsilon+\sum_{e^{\prime}\neq e}t_{e^{\prime}}$, the Gaussian integral over $p$ writes the value of $\gamma$ with $t_e=\varepsilon$ fixed as

\sum_{j=0}^{|E(\gamma)|-2}\int_{[\varepsilon,\infty)^{E(\gamma)\setminus e}}\frac{(\text{numerator})_j}{16\pi^2\,\tau^{2+j}}\exp\Big(-\tau\cdot\frac12\sum_{e^{\prime},e^{\prime\prime}}\frac{t_{e^{\prime}}}{\tau}\frac{t_{e^{\prime\prime}}}{\tau}|p_{e^{\prime}}-p_{e^{\prime\prime}}|^2\Big)\prod_{e^{\prime}\neq e}dt_{e^{\prime}} ,
the exponent being $\ge0$. The term $j=|E(\gamma)|-2$ contracts all loop momenta of the top-degree part, so in polar coordinates

The terms $j\le|E(\gamma)|-3$, of lower degree in $p$, are bounded separately. Their integrands are bounded by a multiple of $\tau^{-2-j}$ times the exponential; on $\tau\ge1$ the integral is bounded as in the proof of Lemma [4.6](#b-00594), and on $\tau\le1$ it is bounded by a multiple of $\int_0^1(\varepsilon+\rho)^{|E(\gamma)|-4-j}\,d\rho$, with $|E(\gamma)|-4-j\ge-1$, hence by a multiple of $1+|\log\varepsilon|$. Multiplied by $\varepsilon$ these terms tend to $0$. This proves the limit of each of the $|E(\gamma)|$ terms, and summing over the edges gives the limit in [(5.4)](#b-00972). in position space this is the singular part $-\frac{\log\varepsilon}{16\pi^2}\,\delta(x-y)$ of the square of $\frac{1-e^{-|x-y|^2/4\varepsilon}}{4\pi^2|x-y|^2}$.
5.3 Single letters
Proposition 5.11 (Letters).
Let $X\in\mathfrak g$, $w\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$, $v\in V$ and $\zeta\in\Sigma^*\otimes\mathfrak g$. For each of the letters
\int\omega\,(X,\iota_wA),\qquad \int\omega\,(X,\iota_v(A|_V)),\qquad \int\omega\,(\zeta,\lambda),\qquad \int\omega\,(X,c),
one has $\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]=0$ at one loop, hence
O(\varepsilon)=O . \tag{5.5}
Proof.

The vertex $O$ is univalent, and a cycle passes through every one of its vertices along two edges; hence $O$ lies off the cycle in every one-loop graph, and by Proposition [5.3](#b-00907) $\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$, the singular part of the graphs with $O$ on the cycle, is $0$. The graphs with $O$ off the cycle consist of a one-loop graph with the vertices of $I$, joined to $O$ by a tree. If the one-loop graph has one external leg, it is a cubic vertex of $I$ with two of its legs joined by an edge; every cubic vertex of $I$ has the form $(Z_1,[Z_2,Z_3])$ in its colour factors (Chapter 1), and joining two of its legs evaluates $(Z_1,[-,-])$ or $(-,[Z_2,-])$ on $(-,-)^{-1}$, which is $0$ by Lemma [5.7](#b-00935). If the one-loop graph has more external legs, its singular part is cancelled by the tree with the vertex $-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ (first class in the proof of Proposition [5.3](#b-00907)). ∎

All vertices of $I$ have Weyl weight $4$ (fields plus derivatives), so a one-loop graph with one vertex $O$ has superficial degree $w_O$ minus the sum of the Weyl weights of its external legs, i.e. $2$ minus that sum. Its external legs have total cohomological degree $0$; an external $c$ (weight $0$) needs an antifield (weight $\ge\frac52$) to compensate its degree, and two $\lambda$ have weight $3$. A single external $\lambda$, of weight $\tfrac32$, is excluded: every vertex of $I$ and of $O$ contains an even number of factors $\lambda$, $\lambda^*$, and every edge carrying the $\lambda\otimes\lambda$ component of $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ joins two of them, so the number of external legs $\lambda$, $\lambda^*$ is even; equivalently, the element $-1$ of $\mathrm{Spin}(4,\mathbb C)$, which acts by $-1$ on $S_\pm$ and trivially on $V$, preserves the action and the regulator and changes the sign of every functional with an odd number of spinor legs. The external legs of degree $\ge0$ graphs are therefore none, one $A$, or two $A$. The element $-1$ of $SO(W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)$ lies in the image of $\mathrm{Spin}(6;\mathbb C)$ and is a symmetry of the action and of the regulator ($H$ and $Q^{GF}$ commute with $\mathrm{Spin}(6;\mathbb C)$); it fixes $w_1w_2$ and changes the sign of every functional with an odd number of $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ legs, so the singular parts with one $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ leg, or with legs $A|_V$, $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$, vanish. Both edges at $O$ are $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ edges. A cycle that enters a Yukawa vertex along $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ continues along $\lambda$ and needs an external $\lambda$; a cycle that enters the vertex $([A,c],A^*)$ along $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ leaves it along $c$ or along $A^*|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$; $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ has no component in the slot of $A^*|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ (Proposition [3.11](#b-00430)), and if the cycle leaves along $c$, through the $c\otimes A^*|_V$ component, the leg $A^*|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ of that vertex is external, of weight $3$, which is excluded. Hence the cycle passes through cubic vertices of type $A|_V(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})^2$ and quartic vertices, with at most two external legs: one cubic vertex gives (b), one quartic vertex gives (c) or (e), and two cubic vertices give (d) or (f), according to whether the edge between them is $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ or $A|_V$. ∎

Remark 5.19 (Method of computation).

The entries of the table of Proposition [5.14](#b-01009) are exact rational multiples of $\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)/(X,Y)$. In explicit realisations of $V_{10}$, of the Clifford module and of $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ and $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(3)$, the Schwinger integrals of each graph are integrated in closed form in exact rational arithmetic and the singular part is read off from the exact $\varepsilon$-expansion; the multiples are the same for both gauge algebras, and the colour factors are reduced for a general simple $\mathfrak g$ by Lemma [5.7](#b-00935). 6. The dilatation component and anomalous dimensions

The dilatation is the simplest superconformal component of the BV transformation of an operator. The classical theory is invariant under the rescaling of the fields by their Weyl weights, and the regulator breaks this invariance through $\varepsilon$ alone: the rescaling maps $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ to $P(s^2\varepsilon,\infty)$. Consequently the scale dependence of $O[\infty]$ is carried by the $\log\varepsilon$ parts of $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ and of $\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$, and by Theorem [4.22](#b-00805) (the logarithmic part of the one-loop counterterm) the part coming from the action is a field redefinition. This chapter proves these statements, computes the resulting coefficients for the scalar bilinears and the single letters, shows how the boundary graphs with an $L_\varepsilon$ edge produce them, and states the identification with the equivariant dilatation cochain as the task of Step 2, together with the graphs that Step 2 must evaluate.
6.1 Scaling covariance of the regulator

Lemma 6.2 (Scaling of the data).
• $\langle\sigma_s e_0,\sigma_s e_1\rangle=\langle e_0,e_1\rangle$ and $(\sigma_s\otimes\sigma_s)K_t=K_{s^2t}$.
• $\sigma_s Q=Q\sigma_s$, $\sigma_s Q^{GF}=s^2Q^{GF}\sigma_s$ and $\sigma_s H=s^2H\sigma_s$; on functionals $\sigma_s$ commutes with $Q$ and with the bracket.

• $\sigma_s S=S$ and $\sigma_s I=I$. A local functional $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(\text{density})$ whose density has Weyl weight $k$ (fields plus derivatives) satisfies $\sigma_s\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(\text{density})=s^{k-4}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(\text{density})$; for example $\sigma_s\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(A,A)=s^{-2}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(A,A)$.
• For a local operator $O$, $\sigma_s O$ is $O$ with $\omega$ replaced by $s^{w_O}$ times the pullback of $\omega$ along $x\mapsto s^{-1}x$, and $s\frac{d}{ds}\big|_{s=1}\sigma_s O=(E+w_O)\,O$.
Proof.

For the pairing substitute $x=sy$, $\mathrm{dvol}(x)=s^4\mathrm{dvol}(y)$; the two weights add up to $4$. The scalar factor of $K_t$ (Definition [3.8](#b-00415)) becomes $s^{-4}(4\pi t)^{-2}e^{-|x-y|^2/4s^2t}=(4\pi s^2t)^{-2}e^{-|x-y|^2/4s^2t}$. An operator with $j$ derivatives from a slot of Weyl weight $k$ to a slot of Weyl weight $k^{\prime}$ is multiplied by $s^{k+j-k^{\prime}}$ under conjugation by $\sigma_s$. For the arrows of $Q$ (Proposition [1.11](#b-00135)) the exponent is $0+1-1$, $1+2-3$, $3+1-4$, $\tfrac32+1-\tfrac52$, all $0$; for the arrows of $Q^{GF}$ (Definition [3.1](#b-00371)) it is $3+0-1$, $1+1-0$, $4+1-3$, $\tfrac52+1-\tfrac32$, all $2$; hence also for $H=[Q,Q^{GF}]$. Every term of [(1.1)](#b-00108) has a density of Weyl weight $4$: for example $1+1+2$ for $(dA,dA)$, $\tfrac32+\tfrac32+1$ for $(\lambda,{\not d}\lambda)$, $0+1+3$ for $(dc,A^*)$ and $([A,c],A^*)$, $0+\tfrac32+\tfrac52$, $0+0+4$, and $4$ for the cubic and quartic gauge terms. For a density of Weyl weight $k$, $(\text{density})(\sigma_s^{-1}e)(x)=s^{k}(\text{density})(e)(sx)$, and $\int\mathrm{dvol}(x)\,s^k(\text{density})(sx)=s^{k-4}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(\text{density})$. With $\omega$ in place of $\mathrm{dvol}$ the same substitution moves the factor $s^{w_O}$ and the dilation onto $\omega$, and $s\frac{d}{ds}\big|_{s=1}s^{w_O}(\text{density})(sx)=(w_O+E)(\text{density})(x)$. ∎
Proposition 6.3 (Scaling covariance).
For every $s>0$ and $\varepsilon>0$,
(\sigma_s\otimes\sigma_s)\,P(\varepsilon,\infty)=P(s^2\varepsilon,\infty),\qquad \sigma_s\,\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}=\partial_{P(s^2\varepsilon,\infty)}\,\sigma_s , \tag{6.1}
and for every even functional $J$ as in Definition [3.16](#b-00460),
\sigma_s\,W\big(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J\big)=W\big(P(s^2\varepsilon,\infty),\sigma_s J\big). \tag{6.2}
Proof.
By Lemma [6.2](#b-01076), $(\sigma_s\otimes\sigma_s)L_t=(\sigma_s Q^{GF}\otimes\sigma_s)K_t=s^2(Q^{GF}\otimes1)K_{s^2t}=s^2L_{s^2t}$, and
(\sigma_s\otimes\sigma_s)\,P(\varepsilon,\infty)=\int_\varepsilon^\infty s^2L_{s^2t}\,dt=\int_{s^2\varepsilon}^\infty L_{t}\,dt=P(s^2\varepsilon,\infty).

For linear functionals $\ell_1,\ell_2$, the operator $\partial_\phi$ of [C07, §6.4] gives $\partial_\phi\big((\ell_1\circ\sigma_s^{-1})(\ell_2\circ\sigma_s^{-1})\big)=(\ell_1\otimes\ell_2)\big((\sigma_s^{-1}\otimes\sigma_s^{-1})\phi\big)$; since $\partial_\phi$ is determined by its values on products of two linear functionals and $\sigma_s$ is an even algebra automorphism of functionals, $\partial_\phi\,\sigma_s=\sigma_s\,\partial_{(\sigma_s^{-1}\otimes\sigma_s^{-1})\phi}$. With $\phi=P(s^2\varepsilon,\infty)$ and the first identity for $s^{-1}$ this is the second identity in [(6.1)](#b-01085). Then $\sigma_s e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}e^{J/\hbar}=e^{\hbar\partial_{P(s^2\varepsilon,\infty)}}e^{\sigma_s J/\hbar}$, and taking $\hbar\log$ gives [(6.2)](#b-01087). ∎
Lemma 6.4 (Covariance of the counterterms).

For a local family $J=I+\delta O$ with $O$ homogeneous, let $J^{CT}[\varepsilon]=I^{CT}[\varepsilon]+\delta\,\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ be its one-loop counterterm (Proposition [5.3](#b-00907)). Then the counterterm of the family $\sigma_s J=I+\delta\,\sigma_s O$ at the cutoff $s^2\varepsilon$ is
(\sigma_s J)^{CT}[s^2\varepsilon]=\sigma_s\big(J^{CT}[\varepsilon]\big)+2\log s\;\sigma_s\big(\text{coefficient of }\log\varepsilon\text{ in }J^{CT}[\varepsilon]\big). \tag{6.3}
In particular $\sigma_s$ maps the coefficient of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ in $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ to $s^{-2}$ times itself and fixes the coefficient of $\log\varepsilon$.
Proof.

At one loop $W$ is affine in the counterterm, which enters through its tree-level flow. By [(6.2)](#b-01087), $W(P(s^2\varepsilon,\infty),\sigma_s J-\sigma_s J^{CT}[\varepsilon])=\sigma_s W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J-J^{CT}[\varepsilon])$ has a limit as $\varepsilon\to0$, and so has $W(P(s^2\varepsilon,\infty),\sigma_s J-(\sigma_s J)^{CT}[s^2\varepsilon])$. The difference of the two counterterms is a local functional whose tree-level flow has a limit, and its part without $\delta$ is invariant under translations and under the adjoint action of $\mathfrak g$, which $\sigma_s$ preserves; so, as in the uniqueness parts of Propositions [4.10](#b-00637) and [5.3](#b-00907), their singular parts in $\varepsilon$ coincide. Write $(\sigma_s J)^{CT}[\varepsilon^{\prime}]$ as $\varepsilon^{\prime-1}$ times one local functional plus $\log\varepsilon^{\prime}$ times another. At $\varepsilon^{\prime}=s^2\varepsilon$, $\log\varepsilon^{\prime}=\log\varepsilon+2\log s$ and $\varepsilon^{\prime-1}=s^{-2}\varepsilon^{-1}$; matching the coefficients of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $\log\varepsilon$ with those of $\sigma_s J^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ gives [(6.3)](#b-01094), the constant $2\log s$ times the $\log\varepsilon$ coefficient being the remainder. Let $\gamma$ be a one-loop graph whose value has the expansion $(\varepsilon^{-1}\text{-coefficient})\,\varepsilon^{-1}+(\log\varepsilon\text{-coefficient})\log\varepsilon+(\text{a function with a limit})$. Then

The term $2\varepsilon^{-1}(\varepsilon^{-1}\text{-coefficient})$ is the scaling $s\frac{d}{ds}\big|_{s=1}$ of the counterterm $-(\varepsilon^{-1}\text{-coefficient})\,\varepsilon^{-1}$ under $\sigma_s$ (Lemma [6.4](#b-01092)). Proof.

By Proposition [4.2](#b-00561), $\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}(\text{value of }\gamma)=-\varepsilon\sum_e(\text{value with }t_e=\varepsilon)$, and $\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}$ of the expansion is $-(\varepsilon^{-1}\text{-coefficient})\varepsilon^{-1}+(\log\varepsilon\text{-coefficient})+(\text{a function tending to }0)$. Multiply by $2$ and add $2\varepsilon^{-1}(\varepsilon^{-1}\text{-coefficient})$. ∎
